item.title: ACC 303 Notes Module 1
item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques Module: Module 1: Probability Foundations & Sampling Theory Target Reading: Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) Ch. 1 & 8; Kothari (2e) Ch. 1 & 4; Gujarati & Porter (5e) App. A (A.1–A.6) Syllabus Focus: Population vs. sample, census vs. sample survey, qualitative vs. quantitative variables, 4 levels of measurement, probability & non-probability sampling designs (SRS, Systematic, Stratified Neyman allocation, Cluster), sampling vs. non-sampling errors, standard error of the mean, Finite Population Correction (FPC), and Central Limit Theorem (CLT). Key Definition Statistical analysis is fundamental to modern business decision-making and econometric modeling. The term statistics carries two distinct definitions based on context: Plural Sense ("statistics"): Numerical facts, figures, or data collected for analysis (e.g., inflation rate of , quarterly GDP growth of , or average hourly wage of ). Singular Sense ("statistics"): The scientific discipline and methodology concerning the collection, organization, presentation, analysis, and interpretation of data to assist in making effective decisions under conditions of uncertainty. Statistical methods are formally bifurcated into two primary branches based on research objectives and data availability: Descriptive Statistics: Statistical procedures and graphical techniques utilized to organize, summarize, and present raw numerical data in an informative, structured format. Primary Tools: Frequency tables, histograms, bar charts, pie charts, scatter plots, measures of location (mean, median, mode), and measures of dispersion (variance, standard deviation, interquartile range). Scope: Confined strictly to the observed dataset; no probabilistic conclusions are extended to unobserved entities. Inferential Statistics: The body of statistical methods used to draw inferences, conclusions, or estimates about unknown population parameters based strictly on sample statistics. Primary Tools: Probability distributions, point and interval estimation, parametric and non-parametric hypothesis testing, Analysis of Variance (ANOVA), and regression analysis. Scope: Evaluates risks and uncertainty by applying probability theory to quantify the margin of error (sampling error) inherent in generalizing from a sample to an entire population. To conduct empirical research, the domain of inquiry must be clearly conceptualized: Methodological Trade-offs: A Census eliminates sampling error because every population unit is examined. However, for large or infinite populations, a census is economically prohibitive, time-consuming, physically impossible (e.g., measuring lifespan of industrial batteries), or destructive (e.g., blood testing). Furthermore, censuses accumulate non-sampling and administrative errors as grows. A Sample Survey dramatically reduces data collection costs, accelerates research timelines, and allows deeper data probing. However, it introduces sampling error due to random variations between sample statistics and true population parameters. A variable is a quantity or characteristic that can take on different numerical values or categories across observations. Qualitative (Attribute/Categorical) Variable: A non-numeric characteristic where individual observations are classified into distinct categories (e.g., gender, PC brand preference, marital status, state of residence). Summarized using counts, frequencies, and percentages. Quantitative Variable: A variable that is expressed numerically. Discrete Quantitative Variable: A variable that can assume only distinct, clearly separated integer values with "gaps" between possible values. Discrete variables typically arise from counting operations (e.g., number of bedrooms in a house: ; number of defective components per batch). Continuous Quantitative Variable: A variable that can assume any real numerical value within a given continuous interval. Continuous variables result from measuring operations and depend on the precision of the measuring instrument (e.g., flight duration, atmospheric pressure, student GPA, body weight). The mathematical level of measurement determines the appropriate statistical tools, charts, and mathematical operations that can validly be applied to a variable.Research in business and economics is a systematic, multi-step process designed to solve problems and establish empirical relationships. Defining the Target Universe/Population: Specifying whether the universe is finite ( is known and countable) or infinite ( is theoretically unlimited). Identifying the Sampling Unit: Selecting the elementary unit to be sampled (e.g., geographic region, household, firm, or individual). Establishing the Sampling Frame (Source List): Constructing or obtaining a comprehensive, accurate list of all sampling units in the population. Determining Sample Size (): Calculating an optimal sample size that balances statistical precision, confidence level, population variability, and cost. Selecting the Sampling Procedure: Deciding between probability and non-probability sampling designs. Under non-probability sampling, elements do not have a known or equal probability of selection. Selection depends on human judgment or convenience: Purposive / Judgment Sampling: Items are selected deliberately by the researcher based on personal expertise and belief that the sample represents the population. Limitation Highly vulnerable to researcher bias; sampling error cannot be calculated. Convenience Sampling: Selecting population units that are easily accessible (e.g., surveying students in a single cafeteria). Limitation Generates severely biased results that cannot be generalized to broader populations. Quota Sampling: Interviewers are given specific quotas to fill across non-overlapping categories (e.g., 50 males, 50 females) but selection within quotas is left to interviewer discretion. Every element in the population has a known, non-zero probability of being included in the sample, ensuring unbiased estimation and allowing formal mathematical calculation of sampling error. Simple Random Sampling (SRS): Each possible sample combination of size from a finite population has an equal probability of selection: Implemented using lottery draws or computerized random number generators (e.g., Tippett's random number tables). Systematic Random Sampling: Elements are selected at equal numeric intervals through an ordered sampling frame. Procedure: Calculate sampling interval . Select a random starting integer between and . The sample consists of elements: Critical Risk If the sampling frame possesses a hidden periodic structure or cycle that matches , the sample will suffer from severe systematic bias. Stratified Random Sampling: Used when a population is non-homogeneous. The population is divided into non-overlapping, internally homogeneous subgroups called strata (). Independent simple random samples are drawn from each stratum. Proportional Allocation: Stratum sample size is directly proportional to stratum population size : Optimum (Neyman) Allocation: Accounts for differences in both stratum size () and stratum variability (). Stratum sample size is computed as: (Allocates larger sample sizes to larger and more variable strata, minimizing the variance of the sample estimator for a fixed total sample size). Cluster Sampling: The population is divided into naturally occurring, internally heterogeneous subgroups called clusters (e.g., geographic blocks, corporate branches). A random sample of clusters is chosen, and either all elements within chosen clusters are examined (one-stage) or simple random samples are drawn within chosen clusters (two-stage). Trade-off: Highly cost-effective for geographically dispersed populations, but yields higher sampling error than SRS for a given sample size due to intra-cluster correlation. Area Sampling: A primary form of cluster sampling where clusters are defined by geographical subdivisions (e.g., counties, census tracts). Multi-Stage Sampling: Sequential random sampling across hierarchical levels in large-scale national surveys (e.g., Primary Stage: States Secondary Stage: Districts Tertiary Stage: Towns Final Stage: Households). Sequential Sampling: Sample size is not fixed prior to the survey; items are drawn sequentially until cumulative evidence satisfies a statistical decision rule under statistical quality control. Sampling Error: The random variation or difference between a sample statistic () and the true population parameter (): Sampling errors occur purely due to chance. The expected value of sampling error is zero. As sample size increases, sampling error decreases at the rate of . Non-Sampling (Systematic) Error: Errors caused by human mistake, flawed sampling frame, ambiguous survey questions, non-response bias, uncalibrated instruments, or incorrect data recording. Non-sampling errors do not decrease with larger sample sizes and can severely distort research conclusions. The sampling distribution of the sample mean is a probability distribution consisting of all possible sample means () calculated from all possible random samples of a specified size drawn from a given population . Expected Value (Unbiasedness): The mean of the sampling distribution of sample means () is strictly equal to the true population mean (): Standard Error of the Mean (): The standard deviation of the sampling distribution of sample means, measuring the dispersion of sample estimates around the population mean: When sampling is conducted without replacement from a finite population of size , and the sample size constitutes more than of the population (), the standard error formula must be multiplied by the Finite Population Correction (FPC) factor:Finite Population Correction (FPC) Impact of FPC: As the sample size approaches population size , , reflecting the fact that as , uncertainty vanishes and the sampling error approaches zero.Fundamental Theorem: The Central Limit Theorem The Central Limit Theorem is the foundational theorem of inferential statistics and classical econometrics. Statement: If random samples of size are selected from any population possessing a finite mean and a finite variance , as the sample size increases (), the sampling distribution of the sample mean approaches a normal distribution with mean and variance , regardless of the structural shape of the underlying population probability distribution. Using the CLT, any sample mean from a large sample () can be standardized into a standard normal random variable : Sample Space (): The set of all possible outcomes of a chance experiment. Event (): A specific subset of outcomes in . Axioms of Probability: for every event . . For mutually exclusive events : . A random variable taking distinct values with discrete PDF : A random variable defined over a continuous interval with PDF : Exception / Rule Fundamental Property: For any continuous random variable, the probability of assuming an exact single value is zero: . When two random variables and are observed simultaneously: Joint PDF : Discrete: Continuous: Marginal Probability Density Functions: Marginal PDF of : (discrete) or (continuous). Marginal PDF of : (discrete) or (continuous). Conditional Probability Density Functions: Statistical Independence: Random variables and are statistically independent if and only if their joint density equals the product of their marginal densities for all : Discrete: Continuous: for any constant . . (always holds, regardless of independence). If and are statistically independent: . Properties: If and are independent: . If and are independent, (note: converse is not generally true unless are bivariate normal). -th Central Moment: Skewness (): Measures lack of symmetry (3rd standardized moment): : Symmetric distribution. : Positively skewed (long right tail). : Negatively skewed (long left tail). Kurtosis (): Measures peakness and tail-heaviness (4th standardized moment): : Mesokurtic (Standard Normal Distribution). : Leptokurtic (Pied/slim peak, fat/heavy tails). : Platykurtic (Flat peak, thin tails). Numerical Problem 1: Stratified Sampling & Neyman Optimum Allocation Context: A business research institute needs to draw a sample of firms from a total population of companies categorized into three financial strata: Stratum 1 (Large-cap): , Stratum 2 (Mid-cap): , Stratum 3 (Small-cap): , Required: Compute the stratum sample sizes () under Proportional Allocation. Compute the stratum sample sizes () under Optimum (Neyman) Allocation. Provide the theoretical justification for why Neyman allocation differs from Proportional allocation. Part 1: Proportional Allocation Under proportional allocation, the proportion of elements sampled from each stratum equals the proportion of the population in that stratum: Stratum 1: Stratum 2: Stratum 3: Check: . Part 2: Optimum (Neyman) Allocation Under Neyman allocation, the sample size allocated to stratum is proportional to the product of stratum population size () and stratum standard deviation (): Step 1: Compute for each stratum: Stratum 1: Stratum 2: Stratum 3: Sum: Step 2: Compute for each stratum: Stratum 1: Stratum 2: Stratum 3: Check: . Part 3: Theoretical Justification Proportional allocation assigns sample size purely based on stratum size, ignoring internal variation. Neyman optimum allocation assigns a significantly larger sample size to Stratum 1 ( vs ) because Stratum 1 exhibits much higher internal variability ( vs ). By taking larger samples from more variable strata, Neyman allocation minimizes the overall variance of the stratified sample mean estimator for a fixed total sample size . Numerical Problem 2: Central Limit Theorem & Sampling Error Probability Analysis Context: An airline tracks the annual maintenance cost of commercial passenger jets. The population mean annual maintenance cost is with a population standard deviation of . The underlying distribution of maintenance costs across individual aircraft is strongly positively skewed. A simple random sample of aircraft is selected. Required: Describe the shape of the sampling distribution of the sample mean and state the governing statistical theorem. Calculate the standard error of the sample mean (). Compute the probability that the sample mean maintenance cost falls between and . Compute the probability that the sampling error exceeds in absolute magnitude. Part 1: Shape of the Sampling Distribution Although the underlying population distribution is positively skewed, the sample size exceeds 30 (). By the Central Limit Theorem (CLT), the sampling distribution of the sample mean is approximately normal: Part 2: Standard Error Calculation The standard error of the mean is . item.title: ACC 303 Notes Module 5
item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques Module: Module 5: Single-Equation Linear Regression Analysis (Nature & Two-Variable) Target Reading: Gujarati & Porter (5e) Intro & Ch. 1–5; Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) Ch. 13 Syllabus Focus: Methodology of econometrics, regression vs. causation vs. correlation, PRF vs. SRF, linearity in parameters, stochastic disturbance term rationale, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) derivation, 10 CLRM assumptions, Gauss-Markov BLUE proof, coefficient of determination (r^2), Classical Normal Linear Regression Model (CNLRM), Maximum Likelihood Estimation, hypothesis testing of regression parameters (t-test & 2-t rule), regression ANOVA (F = t^2), mean & individual prediction intervals, and Jarque-Bera normality test. This module covers Syllabus Topics 6, 7 & 8: The Nature of Regression, Two-Variable Regression Analysis (Estimation & Inference). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Introduction: Methodology of traditional econometrics, mathematical vs. econometric models, and the role of data. Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 1: The Nature of Regression Analysis (Modern interpretation, regression vs. correlation, cross-section vs. time-series vs. panel data). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 2: Two-Variable Regression Analysis: Some Basic Ideas (PRF, SRF, structural definition of linearity in variables vs. parameters). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 3: Two-Variable Regression Model: The Problem of Estimation (OLS derivation, 10 CLRM assumptions, Gauss-Markov Theorem/BLUE proof, ). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 4: Classical Normal Linear Regression Model (CNLRM) (Normality assumption of , Central Limit Theorem justification, Maximum Likelihood Estimation). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 5: Two-Variable Regression: Interval Estimation and Hypothesis Testing (Confidence intervals, -tests, ANOVA in regression, prediction intervals, Jarque-Bera normality test). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 13: Correlation and Linear Regression (Standard error of estimate, prediction/confidence intervals for ). Traditional econometric analysis follows a structured 8-step process designed to bridge economic theory with empirical measurement: Statement of Theory or Hypothesis: Formulating an economic proposition from economic theory. Example (Keynesian Consumption Theory): The marginal propensity to consume () is positive but less than unity: . Specification of the Mathematical Model: Expressing the theoretical hypothesis in exact, deterministic mathematical equations. Equation: Here is personal consumption expenditure, is gross domestic product (income), is the intercept (autonomous consumption), and is the slope coefficient (). Specification of the Econometric Model: Modifying the deterministic model to account for real-world inexactness by introducing a random, stochastic disturbance term (). Equation: The error term captures individual variations, omitted variables, measurement errors, and intrinsic human randomness. Obtaining Data: Collecting quantitative observational data on the dependent and explanatory variables (). Estimation of the Parameters of the Econometric Model: Applying statistical techniques—primarily Ordinary Least Squares (OLS)—to obtain numerical estimates () for the unknown parameters (). Estimated Model: Hypothesis Testing: Using statistical inference (-tests, -values, confidence intervals) to evaluate whether the estimated parameters align with theoretical predictions. For instance, testing versus . Forecasting or Prediction: Utilizing the validated model to forecast future values of the dependent variable () based on projected or known future values of the regressor (). Use of the Model for Control or Policy Purposes: Applying the estimated equation to manipulate policy variables () to achieve target macroeconomic outcomes (). Exam Pitfall / Exception Causation: Statistical regression does not establish physical or logical causation on its own. Causation must be justified by underlying economic or physical theory. A statistically significant regression relationship between two variables may reflect a genuine causal link, a mutual relationship driven by a third omitted factor, or a spurious correlation. Symmetry: Correlation treats and completely symmetrically. The correlation between and () is identical to the correlation between and (). In regression, the relationship is asymmetrical: is treated as a random/stochastic variable, while is treated as fixed in repeated sampling. Randomness: In correlation analysis, both variables are assumed to be random variables following a bivariate normal distribution. In regression analysis, only the dependent variable () needs to be random; the regressors () are conditioned upon as fixed numbers. Cross-Sectional Data: Data collected on one or more variables at a single point in time across multiple economic entities (e.g., households, firms, countries). Time Series Data: Data collected on one variable or a set of variables over successive time intervals (e.g., daily stock prices, quarterly GDP, annual inflation). Time series observations often exhibit temporal ordering and serial dependence. Pooled / Panel (Longitudinal) Data: A combination of cross-sectional and time-series features, where the same cross-sectional units (e.g., 50 states) are followed over multiple time periods (e.g., 20 years). Key Definition The Conditional Expectation Function (CEF) or Population Regression Function (PRF) is the locus of the conditional means across all sub-populations of : When the functional form is linear in parameters, the linear PRF is expressed as: where is the population intercept and is the population slope coefficient. In econometric theory, the term "linear regression" strictly refers to linearity in the parameters, not necessarily linearity in the variables: Linearity in the Variables: The conditional expectation is a straight-line function of . (Linear in variables and parameters) (Nonlinear in variable , but linear in parameters ) Linearity in the Parameters: The parameters () appear with an exponent of 1 and are not multiplied, divided, or transformed by other parameters. (Nonlinear in parameter ) (Nonlinear in parameter ) Key Definition Rule: All models linear in the parameters can be estimated using Classical Linear Regression Model (CLRM) theory and Ordinary Least Squares (OLS). Since individual observations deviate from their conditional mean , an individual observation is expressed as: where is the stochastic disturbance or error term: By taking conditional expectations on both sides: Gujarati identifies 7 explicit reasons why an error term is inherently necessary in regression models: Theoretical Ignorance: Economic theory rarely identifies all variables that influence a phenomenon. Unavailability of Data: Data on relevant variables (e.g., subjective consumer expectations) may be missing or unmeasurable. Core vs. Peripheral Variables: To maintain model parsimony, minor explanatory factors are left out and aggregated into . Intrinsic Randomness in Human Behavior: Human decisions exhibit inherent variability that cannot be explained even with full information. Poor Proxy Variables: When ideal theoretical variables cannot be measured, imperfect empirical proxies introduce measurement noise into . Principle of Parsimony (Occam's Razor): Models should be kept as simple as possible. Wrong Functional Form: Imperfect linear approximations of complex nonlinear relationships are absorbed by . In practice, the population parameters () are unknown because we only possess a finite random sample from the population. We estimate the PRF using the Sample Regression Function (SRF): Deterministic SRF Form: where is the estimator of , is the estimator of , and is the estimator of . Stochastic SRF Form: where is the sample residual (), serving as the sample counterpart to . To fit a sample regression line to a dataset of pairs , Carl Friedrich Gauss proposed minimizing the Residual Sum of Squares (RSS):Formula & Derivation: Derivation via Differential Calculus To minimize , take first-order partial derivatives with respect to and and set them equal to zero: Rearranging (1) and (2) yields the OLS Normal Equations: From Normal Equation 1, divide by : Substitute into Normal Equation 2: Using deviation notation where and : Thus, the OLS estimators are: Numerical properties hold automatically as a pure mathematical consequence of the least-squares minimization, regardless of how the underlying data were generated: Sum of Residuals is Zero: (and consequently the mean residual ). Sample Regression Line Passes Through Means: The fitted regression line always passes through . Mean of Estimated Equals Mean of Observed : . Residuals are Uncorrelated with : (or ). Residuals are Uncorrelated with Predicted : . To perform statistical inference and evaluate estimator precision, the CLRM imposes 10 fundamental assumptions on the Population Regression Function and error term : Assumption 1 (Linearity in Parameters): . The regression model is linear in parameters. Assumption 2 (Fixed Values or Independent of Disturbance): values are fixed in repeated sampling, or if is stochastic, . Assumption 3 (Zero Conditional Mean of Disturbance): . For any given , the mean of error terms is zero. Assumption 4 (Homoscedasticity or Constant Error Variance): for all . The variance of each conditional on is a constant positive finite value . Assumption 5 (No Autocorrelation / Serial Correlation): for all . Error terms are uncorrelated across observations. Assumption 6 (Number of Observations Parameters ): The sample size must exceed the number of parameters to be estimated ( in simple regression). Assumption 7 (Variability in Values): , meaning not all values in a sample are identical (). Assumption 8 (No Perfect Multicollinearity): There are no exact linear relationships among explanatory variables (extended to multiple regression). Assumption 9 (No Specification Bias): The regression model is correctly specified in terms of functional form and included variables. Assumption 10 (Normality of ): . The errors are normally and independently distributed (introduced in CNLRM). Formula & Derivation: Variances and Standard Errors Under CLRM Assumptions 1 through 7, the sampling variances and standard errors of and are: Since is unknown, it is estimated using the unbiased OLS sample variance estimator : where is the degrees of freedom (reflecting 2 linear restrictions imposed by estimating and ). The positive square root is called the Standard Error of the Estimate (). The theoretical justification for using OLS rests on the Gauss-Markov Theorem:Fundamental Theorem: Gauss-Markov Theorem Given the assumptions of the Classical Linear Regression Model (CLRM), the Ordinary Least Squares estimators are BLUE (Best Linear Unbiased Estimators) in the class of all linear unbiased estimators. To be BLUE, an estimator must satisfy three distinct criteria: Linear: It is a linear function of the random dependent variable . Unbiased: Its expected value equals the true population parameter: . Best (Efficient): It possesses the minimum variance among all linear unbiased estimators. Since and : For to hold identically for any , we must require: Evaluate : Therefore: Since (as it is a sum of squared terms): achieves its minimum strictly when for all , which implies and . Thus, OLS estimator has the minimum variance in the class of all linear unbiased estimators. To measure how well the estimated line fits the sample data, partition the total variation of around its mean :Squaring both sides and summing over all sample observations: Since (by Numerical Property 4): TSS (Total Sum of Squares): — Total variation of actual values around sample mean. ESS (Explained Sum of Squares): — Variation in explained by the regression line. RSS (Residual Sum of Squares): — Unexplained variation due to residual errors. Formula & Derivation The Coefficient of Determination () is the proportion of total variation in explained by regressor : Alternatively: Computational formula using sample covariance and variances: Range: . Relation to Pearson's : In a two-variable model, is the exact square of Pearson's sample correlation coefficient : The CNLRM adds Assumption 10 to the CLRM, specifying that each error term is normally distributed: By the Central Limit Theorem, represents the sum of a large number of independent, unobserved random variables (omitted factors, measurement noise, behavioral variations). Semilogarithmic Dummy Models (Halvorsen-Palmquist Correction): In , the exact percentage change in for vs. is: Key Definition Multicollinearity denotes the existence of exact or near linear relationships among the explanatory variables in a multiple regression model. Perfect Multicollinearity: (where ). OLS coefficients become mathematically indeterminate () and standard errors become infinite. Imperfect Multicollinearity: . Multicollinearity does not violate any core OLS assumption. Practical Consequences: Large Variances & Standard Errors: Variances inflate rapidly as correlation . Wider Confidence Intervals: Leading to frequent acceptance of false zero null hypotheses (Type II error). Insignificant -Ratios: Individual -statistics become small and statistically insignificant despite strong underlying relationships. High with Few Significant -Ratios: The "classic symptom" of multicollinearity. Extreme Sensitivity: Estimates and standard errors fluctuate wildly with small data additions or deletions. item.title: ACC 303 Notes Module 3
item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques Module: Module 3: Hypothesis Testing Foundations (Parametric & Nonparametric) Target Reading: Gujarati & Porter (5e) App. A (A.8); Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) Ch. 10, 11 & 15; Kothari (2e) Ch. 9 & 10 Syllabus Focus: 6-step hypothesis testing protocol, null vs. alternative hypotheses, Type I error, Type II error, statistical power (1 - beta), p-values, one-sample & two-sample Z/t tests, paired t-test vs. Sandler's A-test, two-variance F-test, Chi-square goodness-of-fit, test of independence in contingency tables, Yates' continuity correction, and measures of association (Phi, Cramer's V, Contingency C). Key Definition In statistical inference, a hypothesis is a quantitative claim or assertion about an unknown population parameter (e.g., population mean , population proportion , or population variance ). Hypothesis testing provides a formal, probability-based decision-making framework to evaluate whether empirical sample evidence supports or contradicts a specified hypothesis. Two competing hypotheses are always formulated: Null Hypothesis (): The baseline hypothesis being tested, representing a statement of "no effect", "no difference", or status quo. It is formulated for the explicit purpose of being rejected if sample evidence proves incompatible with it. The null hypothesis always contains an equality condition (, , or ). Alternative Hypothesis ( or ): The research hypothesis that is accepted if the sample data provide sufficient statistical proof that is false. It represents the claim the researcher seeks to establish (, , or ). In statistical literature, two complementary paradigms govern hypothesis testing: Neyman-Pearson Approach (Decision-Theoretic): Focuses on setting a predetermined level of significance (), establishing critical rejection regions prior to data collection, and balancing Type I () and Type II () errors to choose between two explicit decisions (Reject vs. Fail to Reject ). Fisherian Approach (Test-of-Significance): Measures the continuous strength of evidence against via the exact -value (observed significance level), leaving the final evaluation of evidence strength to the researcher without rigid binary decision boundaries. Hypothesis testing and confidence interval estimation are mathematically equivalent duals under classical normal theory: Confidence Interval Approach: Constructs a confidence interval for parameter . If the hypothesized value lies inside the interval , is not rejected at level . If falls outside the interval, is rejected at level . Test-of-Significance Approach: Computes a standardized test statistic under and compares it to a critical threshold derived from the sampling distribution under . Every formal test of hypothesis follows a rigorous 6-step protocol: Step 1: State and : Define population parameters and specify directional or non-directional claims. Step 2: Select Level of Significance (): Choose the maximum acceptable risk of committing a Type I error (typically or ). Step 3: Identify Test Statistic: Select the probability distribution () based on sample size , population variance knowledge, and data measurement scale. Step 4: Formulate Decision Rule: Establish critical values and rejection regions based on , degrees of freedom (), and test tail direction. Step 5: Collect Sample Data & Compute Test Statistic: Calculate the sample point estimates and evaluate the numerical test statistic or -value. Step 6: Make Statistical Decision & State Economic/Business Conclusion: Reject if test statistic falls in the rejection region (); otherwise, fail to reject . Contextualize the result in business terms. Key Definition The -value is the lowest significance level at which can be rejected. It represents the exact probability of obtaining a test statistic as extreme as, or more extreme than, the observed sample value, assuming is true. Decision Rule using -value: If (Statistically Significant Result). If (Statistically Insignificant Result). Strength of Evidence Guidelines: : Very strong evidence against . : Strong evidence against . : Weak/marginal evidence against . : Insufficient evidence against . In any hypothesis test, two types of classification errors can occur because decisions are made using sample data rather than complete population census:Key Definition Type I Error (): Rejecting when is true. . Controlled directly by setting the level of significance. Type II Error (): Failing to reject when is false. . Power of a Test (): The probability of correctly rejecting a false null hypothesis. Power measures the sensitivity of the test to detect a true underlying effect or parameter shift: Factors Influencing Test Power: Effect Size (): As the true parameter shifts further from , decreases and power () increases. Sample Size (): Increasing reduces standard error (), narrowing sampling distributions and dramatically boosting power. Significance Level (): Decreasing (e.g., ) widens the non-rejection region, increasing and reducing power. Population Variance (): Lower variance reduces overlap between sampling distributions under and , increasing power. Formula & Derivation When sampling from a normal population (or when by CLT) and the population standard deviation is known: Formula & Derivation When population standard deviation is unknown and estimated by sample standard deviation : Formula & Derivation When testing a binomial proportion under large-sample conditions ( and ): where is the sample proportion. Formula & Derivation When testing whether a population variance equals a hypothesized value in a normal population: Critical rejection boundaries at level for a two-tailed test are and . Formula & Derivation When population variances are unknown but assumed equal, sample variances and are combined into a weighted pooled variance : When equal variance assumption is violated: The effective degrees of freedom are calculated using the Satterthwaite approximation (rounded down to nearest integer): Formula & Derivation When observations are paired across two samples (e.g., before-and-after treatments on same subjects), extraneous subject-to-subject variation is eliminated by analyzing individual differences : Formula & Derivation Developed by Joseph Sandler (1955), Sandler's -test is a computationally simplified, mathematically exact substitute for the paired Student's -test when : Exact Relationship between and : Decision Rule for -Test: Because is inversely proportional to , is rejected if . Formula & Derivation To test , samples are combined to compute the pooled sample proportion : Formula & Derivation To test whether two independent normal populations have equal variances ( vs. ): By placing the larger sample variance in the numerator (), , requiring only upper-tail critical evaluation at level. Parametric Tests: Require stringent distributional assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity) and interval/ratio scale data. They possess higher statistical power when assumptions hold. Nonparametric (Distribution-Free) Tests: Require no assumptions regarding parent population distribution parameters. Applicable to nominal or ordinal data, robust against extreme outliers, but require larger sample sizes to achieve equal power. Asymmetry & Range: Non-negative continuous distribution (), positively skewed for small . Degrees of Freedom Convergence: As , the distribution approaches a normal distribution (). Additive Property: If are independent random variables with , then . Exam Pitfall / Exception Rule for Minimum Expected Frequencies: No category should have an expected frequency . No more than 20% of categories should have . If violated, adjacent categories must be merged. item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques Module: Module 4: Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) Target Reading: Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) Ch. 12; Kothari (2e) Ch. 11 Syllabus Focus: Fisher F-distribution, familywise Type I error inflation, ANOVA assumptions (normality, homoscedasticity, independence), One-Way ANOVA sum of squares partitioning (TSS = SST + SSE), shortcut raw score methods, Fisher's LSD post-hoc test, Two-Way ANOVA without interaction (Randomized Block Design), Two-Way ANOVA with interaction (Factorial Design), Latin Square Design, and ANOCOVA. Key Definition Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) is an inferential statistical technique developed by Sir Ronald A. Fisher to test the equality of three or more population means simultaneously. While Student's -test or the -test evaluates differences between two sample means, attempting to compare population means () through pairwise -tests leads to severe statistical distortions. Formula & Derivation: Familywise Type I Error Rate If a researcher wishes to compare independent treatment means (), the number of required pairwise comparisons is given by the combination formula: If each individual test is conducted at a nominal significance level of (meaning the probability of no Type I error per test is ), the overall familywise (or experimentwise) Type I error rate () across the 6 independent tests inflates according to: Thus, conducting multiple pairwise -tests dramatically increases the risk of falsely declaring a statistically significant difference when none exists. ANOVA solves this problem by conducting a single, omni-bus -test that controls the overall Type I error rate at the nominal level .For the -statistic in ANOVA to be strictly valid, three fundamental mathematical assumptions must be satisfied: Normality: The continuous dependent variable is normally distributed within each of the populations: Homogeneity of Variances (Homoscedasticity): The population variances are equal to a common variance : Independence of Errors: The observations are drawn independently within and across samples. There must be no serial correlation or systematic clustering among observations. Formula & Derivation: The -Distribution The -distribution is defined as the ratio of two independent chi-square () random variables, each divided by its respective degrees of freedom: where represents the numerator degrees of freedom and represents the denominator degrees of freedom. Key mathematical properties of the -distribution include: Non-negativity: Since is a ratio of squared quantities (variances), . The domain spans . Positive Skewness: The distribution is non-symmetric and positively skewed to the right. As and tend to infinity, approaches a normal distribution. Family of Curves: The exact shape of the -pdf depends uniquely on the parameter pair . Mathematical Equivalence to Student's : For a single numerator degree of freedom (), the square of a -distributed random variable with degrees of freedom is identically distributed as an -variable with degrees of freedom: Before running ANOVA or pooled two-sample -tests, the assumption of equal variances () can be directly evaluated using a two-variance -test: Null Hypothesis: (or ) Alternative Hypothesis: Test Statistic: where is conventionally designated as the larger sample variance () to place the computed ratio in the upper tail (). Degrees of Freedom: Numerator , Denominator . Decision Rule: For a two-tailed significance level , compare against . Reject if . In a One-Way ANOVA (or Completely Randomized Design - C.R. Design), experimental units or subjects are randomly assigned to mutually exclusive treatment groups or categories of a single independent factor. Let represent the -th observation in the -th treatment group, where and . The total sample size across all treatments is .The linear statistical model for One-Way ANOVA is expressed as: where: is the overall (grand) population mean. is the specific effect of treatment , subject to the restriction . is the random error term. The hypotheses tested are: The foundational principle of ANOVA is the algebraic decomposition of the total sum of squared deviations () into two orthogonal, non-overlapping components: Treatment Sum of Squares () and Error Sum of Squares ().Formula & Derivation: Proof of SS Partitioning Proof: Consider the identity for any individual observation relative to the grand mean and its group mean : Squaring both sides of the identity yields: Summing across all observations and all treatments : By definition of the sample mean, . Consequently, the cross-product term vanishes identically: Simplifying the remaining terms gives the fundamental ANOVA identity: Where: Total Sum of Squares (): Measures the total variation of all individual observations around the grand mean , with . Treatment Sum of Squares (): Measures the variation between treatment group means and the grand mean (between-group variation), with . Error Sum of Squares (): Measures the random variation within each treatment group (within-group / residual variation), with . Formula & Derivation: Mean Squares & Test Statistic Dividing each sum of squares by its corresponding degrees of freedom yields the variance estimates or Mean Squares (): Mean Square Treatments (): Under , . Under , . Mean Square Error (): is an unbiased estimator of the common population variance regardless of whether is true or false: . item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques Module: Module 2: Estimation Theory & Sample Size Determination Target Reading: Gujarati & Porter (5e) App. A (A.7); Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) Ch. 9; Kothari (2e) Ch. 8 Syllabus Focus: Point vs. interval estimation, BLUE properties (unbiasedness, efficiency, consistency, sufficiency), Gauss-Markov theorem foundations, confidence intervals for population means (sigma known vs. unknown t-distribution), finite population adjustments, population proportions, and sample size determination for means and proportions. In statistical inference, researchers utilize sample data to make generalizable statements or conclusions about unknown population parameters. Classical statistical inference comprises two fundamental branches: Estimation and Hypothesis Testing.Key Definition Point Estimator: A point estimator is a mathematical function, statistic, or rule derived from sample observations that is used to calculate a single numerical value estimating an unknown population parameter . Formally, an estimator is represented as a random variable , which varies across repeated random samples. Point Estimate: A point estimate is the specific numerical value generated by evaluating the point estimator formula using a concrete, realized sample of data. For example, if the point estimator for the population mean is the sample mean , and a sample of yields a value of , then is the point estimator and is the point estimate. Key Definition Interval Estimator: An interval estimator is a rule or formula that uses sample statistics to construct a random numerical interval around the estimator. This interval has a specified probability of enclosing the true, unobserved population parameter : where represents the lower confidence limit, represents the upper confidence limit, is the confidence coefficient (or confidence level), and () is the level of significance (the probability of committing a Type I error). Confidence Interval: Once a specific sample is drawn and numerical values are calculated for and (e.g., ), the interval is no longer random; it is fixed. Exam Pitfall / Exception Because population parameter is a fixed (though unknown) constant, it is mathematically incorrect to state that "there is a probability that the true population mean lies between and ." Once numerical limits are evaluated: The parameter either lies inside the fixed numerical interval or it does not. Therefore, the probability statement is strictly or . The confidence level refers to the long-run frequency property of the estimation methodology: If an infinite number of random samples of size were drawn from the same population and a confidence interval were constructed for each sample using the same formula, of those constructed random intervals would successfully contain the true population parameter , while would fail to enclose it due to sampling variability. To choose the optimal estimator among competing sample statistics, econometricians and mathematical statisticians evaluate estimators against four primary statistical criteria: Unbiasedness, Efficiency, Consistency, and Sufficiency. An estimator meeting these criteria is classified as a Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) under the Gauss-Markov Theorem.An estimator is said to be an unbiased estimator of a population parameter if the expected value (mean of the sampling distribution) of equals across repeated sampling of size : If , the estimator possesses a bias, defined mathematically as: Formula & Derivation: Proof that Sample Mean () is an Unbiased Estimator of Population Mean () Let be an independent and identically distributed (i.i.d.) random sample drawn from a population with mean and variance . The sample mean estimator is defined as: Taking the mathematical expectation operator on both sides: By the linearity property of expectations, constants can be factored out, and expectation distributes over sums: Since each is drawn from the population with mean : Thus, , proving that the sample mean is a strictly unbiased estimator of for any sample size . Express relative to the true population mean : Squaring both sides: Summing across all : Note that . Therefore: Now evaluate the expected value of the unadjusted sample variance : This proves that is biased downward in small samples by a factor of . To eliminate this bias, define the adjusted sample variance using degrees of freedom in the denominator: Taking its expectation: Hence, is an unbiased estimator of . An estimator is asymptotically unbiased if the limit of its expectation as sample size approaches infinity equals : For the unadjusted sample variance : Thus, while is biased in finite samples, it is asymptotically unbiased.If and are two competing unbiased estimators of parameter , is defined as more efficient than if its sampling variance is strictly smaller: An unbiased estimator that achieves the lowest possible variance among all unbiased estimators is called the most efficient or minimum-variance unbiased estimator (MVUE).When comparing biased and unbiased estimators, efficiency is generalized via Mean Squared Error: We expand by adding and subtracting : Since is a constant, , making the cross-product term drop out: The MSE criterion allows a researcher to accept a small amount of bias if it dramatically reduces sampling variance, achieving a lower overall .Consistency is a large-sample (asymptotic) property. An estimator is a consistent estimator of parameter if the probability distribution of collapses around as sample size increases indefinitely. Formally: In probability limit notation: An estimator is consistent if both its bias and its variance approach zero as : for all , so . , so . Since both conditions hold, is a consistent estimator of (demonstrating the Weak Law of Large Numbers). Unlike expected values (where for non-linear functions ), probability limits preserve non-linear transformations: If , then for any continuous function : For instance, if is a consistent estimator of , then is a consistent estimator of .An estimator is sufficient if it utilizes all the information regarding the parameter contained in the sample, such that no other estimator calculated from the same sample can provide additional information about . By the Neyman-Fisher Factorization Theorem, a statistic is sufficient for if and only if the joint probability density function can be factored into two non-negative functions: where does not depend on the parameter , and depends on only through the statistic .Under the assumptions of the Classical Linear Regression Model (CLRM), an estimator is a Best Linear Unbiased Estimator (BLUE) if: Linearity: It is a linear combination of the sample observations (e.g., ). Unbiasedness: Its expected value equals the true parameter (). Efficiency (Best): It possesses the minimum variance among the entire class of linear unbiased estimators. Because the entire confidence interval lies strictly above the required supermajority threshold (lower limit ), we conclude with confidence that the merger proposal will pass. item.title: ACC 301 Notes Step 13
item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 301 Intermediate Accounting Phase: Phase 4: Financial Statement Synthesis & Global Standards Target Reading: Weygandt, Kieso, and Warfield, Intermediate Accounting, 18th Edition — Chapters 22 & 23: Statement of Cash Flows and Full Disclosure (including IAS 1 & IAS 7) Syllabus Focus: Statement of cash flows purpose and definitions, operating, investing, and financing activity classifications, indirect vs. direct operating cash flow methods with all reconciliation adjustments, noncash investing/financing disclosures, free cash flow and cash coverage ratios, summary of significant accounting policies, subsequent events (Type 1 recognized vs. Type 2 nonrecognized), segment reporting (10% and 75% tests), and interim financial reporting. Key Definition The Statement of Cash Flows reports the cash receipts, cash payments, and net change in cash and cash equivalents resulting from a company's operating, investing, and financing activities during a specific period. It reconciles the beginning and ending balances of cash and cash equivalents. While the Income Statement measures profitability on an accrual basis and the Balance Sheet presents financial position at a single point in time, neither provides a comprehensive accounting of cash inflows and outflows. The Statement of Cash Flows bridges this gap, enabling investors and creditors to evaluate: Liquidity: The entity's ability to generate future positive net cash flows to meet short-term operational obligations. Solvency & Financial Flexibility: The entity's capacity to service long-term debt, pay dividends, and respond to unexpected opportunities or economic downturns. Quality of Earnings: The underlying reasons for differences between Net Income (accrual basis) and Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities (cash basis). Capital Allocation: The cash effects of both cash and noncash investing and financing transactions during the period. Cash: Includes currency on hand and demand deposits in financial institutions (e.g., checking, savings, and money market accounts). Cash Equivalents: Short-term, highly liquid investments that are both: Readily convertible to known amounts of cash. So near their maturity (typically three months or less from the date of acquisition) that they present an insignificant risk of changes in value due to interest rate fluctuations (e.g., Treasury bills, commercial paper, and 90-day certificates of deposit). Operating Activities: Include the cash effects of transactions and events that enter into the determination of Net Income. Cash Inflows: Cash receipts from sales of goods or services, collections on trade receivables, and receipts of interest revenue and dividend revenue. Cash Outflows: Cash payments to suppliers for inventory, to employees for wages/salaries, to government authorities for income taxes, to lenders for interest expense, and for other operating expenses. Investing Activities: Include making and collecting loans, and acquiring and disposing of investments (debt and equity securities) and long-lived tangible/intangible assets (Property, Plant, and Equipment). Cash Inflows: Principal collections on loans/notes receivable, proceeds from the sale of PP&E, and sales/redemptions of available-for-sale or held-to-maturity debt/equity investments. Cash Outflows: Cash spent to purchase PP&E and intangible assets, cash disbursed for loans/notes receivable, and cash paid to acquire debt or equity securities of other entities. Financing Activities: Include obtaining resources from owners, providing them with a return on/of their investment, and borrowing money from creditors and repaying amounts borrowed. Cash Inflows: Proceeds from issuing common or preferred stock and proceeds from issuing short-term or long-term debt (bonds, mortgage notes, bank loans). Cash Outflows: Payment of cash dividends to stockholders, repurchases of common stock (treasury stock transactions), and principal repayments/redemptions of short-term and long-term debt. Exam Pitfall / Exception Transactions that represent significant investing or financing activities but do not involve direct cash receipts or cash payments in the current period must be excluded from the body of the Statement of Cash Flows. To satisfy the Full Disclosure Principle, these transactions must be presented in a supplementary schedule at the bottom of the statement or disclosed in the notes: Acquisition of PP&E or intangibles by issuing stock, notes, or bonds payable. Conversion of convertible bonds or preferred stock into common stock. Nonmonetary asset exchanges (e.g., trading land for a building). Refinancing of long-term debt obligations. US GAAP (ASC 230) and IFRS (IAS 7) permit two alternative methods for determining and presenting Net Cash Flow Provided by (or Used in) Operating Activities: the Indirect Method and the Direct Method. The resulting net cash flow from operating activities is mathematically identical under both methods.The indirect method starts with accrual-basis Net Income and applies a series of adjustments to reconcile it to net operating cash flow. Add Back Noncash Expenses & Losses: Depreciation Expense Amortization of Intangible Assets & Lease Right-of-Use Assets Amortization of Bond Discount Impairment Losses on PP&E, Intangibles, or Goodwill Losses on Sale/Disposition of PP&E or Investments Increases in Deferred Tax Liabilities / Decreases in Deferred Tax Assets Bad Debt Expense (or increase in Allowance for Doubtful Accounts) Deduct Noncash Revenues & Gains: Amortization of Bond Premium Gains on Sale/Disposition of PP&E or Investments Equity in Net Income of Unconsolidated Investees (under Equity Method) Unrealized Holding Gains on Trading Securities Decreases in Deferred Tax Liabilities / Increases in Deferred Tax Assets Adjust for Changes in Operating Working Capital Accounts: Current Assets: Subtract increases in operating current assets (, , ) because cash outflows exceeded recognized expenses or recorded revenues exceeded cash collections. Add decreases in operating current assets because cash collections exceeded recorded revenues or recognized expenses exceeded cash outflows. Current Liabilities: Add increases in operating current liabilities (, , ) because expenses were recognized without immediate cash outflow. Subtract decreases in operating current liabilities because cash outflows exceeded recognized current-period expenses. Formula & Derivation: Master Formula for Indirect Operating Cash Flow The direct method adjusts each individual line item of the accrual-basis Income Statement to its direct cash equivalent.Formula & Derivation: Direct Method Conversion Formulas Cash Receipts from Customers: Cash Payments to Suppliers: Cash Payments for Operating Expenses: Cash Payments for Income Taxes: Exam Pitfall / Exception US GAAP Supplementary Reconciliation Requirement: If an entity elects the Direct Method, US GAAP mandates that it must provide a separate supplementary schedule reconciling Net Income to Net Cash Provided by Operating Activities (effectively reproducing the Indirect Method in the notes). Free Cash Flow measures an entity's discretionary cash flow available for investment in growth, debt retirement, share buybacks, or dividend expansions after maintaining existing operational capacity.Formula & Derivation: Free Cash Flow Capital Expenditures (CapEx): Cash outflows required to maintain competitive physical facilities and plant capacity. Cash Dividends: Preferred and common dividend distributions expected by equity capital providers. Formula & Derivation: Cash Coverage Ratios 1. Current Cash Debt Coverage Ratio (Short-Term Liquidity): 2. Cash Debt Coverage Ratio (Long-Term Solvency): Key Definition The Full Disclosure Principle requires that financial reports present all information of sufficient economic significance to influence the evaluation and decisions of an informed user. Main Body of Financial Statements: Formally recognized items that meet element definitions, are measurable with sufficient certainty, and are relevant and reliable. Notes to Financial Statements: Amplify, clarify, or explain recognized items, quantitative disaggregations, or unrecognized financial positions. Supplementary Information: Quantifiable data of high relevance but lower faithful representation (e.g., oil and gas reserve estimations). Summary of Significant Accounting Policies (Note 1 - ASC 235): Mandatory first note detailing selection among acceptable alternatives (e.g., inventory cost flow assumptions, depreciation methods, revenue recognition policies, investment valuation methods). Fair Value Measurement Disclosures (ASC 820 / IFRS 13): Valuation inputs prioritized across the Three-Level Fair Value Hierarchy (Level 1 observable active quotes through Level 3 unobservable models). Related-Party Transactions (ASC 850 / IAS 24): Disclosures required when one party exercises significant control or influence over another. Must disclose relationship nature, transaction descriptions, dollar amounts, and open balances. Subsequent Events (ASC 855 / IAS 10): Events occurring between the Balance Sheet date and the financial statement issuance date. Exam Pitfall / Exception Recognized vs. Nonrecognized Subsequent Events: Recognized Events: Provide additional evidence regarding conditions existing at the balance sheet date. Requires direct financial statement adjustment. Nonrecognized Events: Provide evidence regarding conditions that did not exist at the balance sheet date but arose subsequently. Requires note disclosure only. Conglomerate and diversified corporations must report financial information about operating segments to prevent consolidated totals from obscuring distinct risk and return profiles.Key Definition An Operating Segment is a component of a company that engages in business activities, whose operating results are regularly reviewed by the Chief Operating Decision Maker (CODM) to allocate resources and assess performance, and for which discrete financial information is available. Exam Pitfall / Exception Quantitative Materiality Thresholds (The 10% Tests): A segment is a reportable segment if it satisfies at least one of the following: 10% Revenue Test: Combined external and intersegment revenue of combined revenue of all operating segments. 10% Profit/Loss Test: Absolute operating profit or loss of the greater (in absolute amount) of: Combined operating profit of all profitable segments, or Combined operating loss of all loss-making segments. 10% Asset Test: Identifiable assets of combined identifiable assets of all operating segments. The 75% Overall Revenue Test: Total external revenue of all reportable segments must account for at least 75% of total consolidated revenue. Additional operating segments must be identified until this threshold is met. Interim reports cover reporting periods shorter than a full fiscal year (e.g., quarterly 10-Q reports). Discrete Approach: Views each interim period as a standalone, distinct accounting period. Integral Approach (US GAAP Preference): Views each interim period as an integral part of the full fiscal year. Accruals, deferrals, and estimated annual effective tax rates are allocated across quarters based on forecasted annual operations. Formula & Derivation: Interim Tax Expense For companies operating in Bangladesh, corporate reporting is governed by national statutory frameworks alongside International Accounting Standards (IAS/IFRS adopted as BRS/BFRS): The Companies Act, 1994 (Schedule XI): Part I: Prescribes the statutory format of the Balance Sheet (Statement of Financial Position), mandating asset and liability classifications. Part II: Prescribes statutory disclosure requirements for the Profit & Loss Account (Income Statement), including gross turnover, managerial remuneration, material expense disclosures, and auditor fees. Part III: Specifies audit and reporting rules for holding and subsidiary corporate structures. Securities and Exchange Rules, 1987 (Rule 12(2) & Schedules): Administered by the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) for publicly listed corporations. Mandates preparation of Cash Flow Statements in accordance with IAS 7 / BFRS. Requires annual submission of audited financial statements, quarterly interim reports, and a comprehensive Corporate Governance Compliance Report under BSEC Codes. Comprehensive Problem: Apex Synthetics Ltd. Cash Flow Construction Scenario Data: Apex Synthetics Ltd. presents the following comparative financial information for the years ended December 31, 2024, and December 31, 2025: Equipment costing with accumulated depreciation of was sold for cash, generating a loss. New equipment was purchased for cash. Land costing was acquired via direct cash purchase. Bonds payable with face value of were issued at par for cash. Common stock was issued for cash: ( shares at par). Declared and paid cash dividends during 2025: (). Cash Collections from Customers: Cash Paid to Suppliers: Cash Paid for Operating Expenses: Cash Paid for Interest: Cash Paid for Income Taxes: Interpretation: While Apex generated strong operational cash flow (), aggressive capital investment in productive capacity () created negative Free Cash Flow (), which was bridged through long-term debt and equity capital raises ( combined).

item.title: ACC 301 Notes Step 14
item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 301 Intermediate Accounting Phase: Phase 4: Financial Statement Synthesis & Global Standards Target Reading: Companies Act, 1994 (Schedule XI) & Securities and Exchange Rules, 1987 (Rule 12(2)) Syllabus Focus: Companies Act 1994 Schedule XI Part I statutory balance sheet format (Order of Permanence), Part II profit and loss disclosures (raw materials, turnover, managerial remuneration, auditor fees, plant capacity), Part III holding/subsidiary rules, BSEC Rule 12(2) compliance timeline and corporate governance code, and synthesis with IAS/IFRS. Key Definition In Bangladesh, while international standards (IAS/IFRS) are adopted by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of Bangladesh (ICAB), all registered corporate entities are legally bound by Section 185 and Schedule XI of the Companies Act, 1994. Schedule XI sets out the minimum statutory requirements for the layout and disclosure of corporate balance sheets and profit & loss accounts. Schedule XI is divided into three distinct operational parts: Part I: Prescribed Form and Contents of the Balance Sheet. Part II: Prescribed Requirements and Disclosures for the Profit and Loss Account. Part III: Detailed Statutory Rules for Holding and Subsidiary Company Accounts. Under Schedule XI, Part I, corporate balance sheets may be presented in either horizontal format or vertical (statement) format. The statute mandates the exact order of presentation and grouping of assets and liabilities.Exam Pitfall / Exception Under Schedule XI, the presentation order is opposite to US GAAP: Liabilities & Capital are presented first, beginning with permanent Share Capital down to short-term liabilities. Assets are presented starting with long-term Property, Plant, and Equipment down to current, liquid assets (Order of Permanence). Part II of Schedule XI outlines specific disclosures that must appear either on the face of the Profit & Loss Account or in accompanying statutory notes: Turnover & Sales: Total gross sales revenue, indicating quantities sold where practicable, disaggregated by major product categories. Raw Material Consumption: Total cost of raw materials consumed, disclosing quantities and major imported vs. indigenous categories. Managerial Remuneration: Specific disclosure of all remuneration, commissions, bonuses, and perquisites paid to managing directors, directors, and top corporate managers. Auditor's Remuneration: Detailed disaggregation of fees paid to statutory auditors: As auditors (Statutory audit fee). For taxation services. For other advisory and certification services. For reimbursement of out-of-pocket expenses. Industrial Capacity & Production: Licensed capacity. Installed capacity. Actual operational production during the fiscal period. Foreign Currency Transactions: Earnings in foreign exchange classified by export sales, royalties, and fees; expenditures in foreign currency classified by imports of raw materials, capital goods, and foreign travel. For publicly listed companies trading on the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) or Chittagong Stock Exchange (CSE), the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC) imposes strict compliance mandates under Rule 12(2): Mandatory Reporting Package: Listed entities must submit to the Commission and Stock Exchanges: Audited Balance Sheet. Audited Profit and Loss Account. Statement of Cash Flows (mandatory per IAS 7). Statement of Changes in Equity. Full explanatory notes. Statutory Submission Timeline: Complete audited packages must be furnished within 120 days (4 months) from the close of the financial year. Statutory Directors' Report Disclosures: Explanation of significant operational variations between quarterly and annual performance. Disclosure of all related-party transactions. Clear statement of internal accounting control efficiency and going concern validity. Corporate Governance Compliance Certificate from a professional practicing Chartered Accountant (CA) or Cost & Management Accountant (CMA).

item.title: ACC 301 Notes Step 11
item.description: Curriculum & Syllabus Context Course: ACC 301 Intermediate Accounting Phase: Phase 3: Liabilities & Owners' Equity Target Reading: Weygandt, Kieso, and Warfield, Intermediate Accounting, 18th Edition — Chapter 13: Long-Term Liabilities (including IFRS 9) Syllabus Focus: Nature and types of bonds payable, pricing and market yield mechanics, effective-interest amortization of discounts and premiums, bonds issued between interest dates, bond issue cost netting, early extinguishment gains/losses, long-term notes payable, installment mortgages, fair value option, and troubled-debt restructurings (ASC 470-60). Key Definition Long-term liabilities represent obligations that are not reasonably expected to be liquidated using current assets or through the creation of other current liabilities within one year or the normal operating cycle, whichever is longer. Long-term liabilities are primarily composed of bonds payable, long-term notes payable, mortgage obligations, and lease liabilities. A bond is a contractual financial instrument issued by a corporation or governmental entity that divides a large long-term borrowing into smaller, standardized denominations (typically face value per bond). The contract between the issuer and the bondholders is known as the bond indenture, which specifies the maturity date, coupon/stated interest rate, interest payment dates, covenants, call/conversion features, and collateral obligations. The market price of a bond is determined by the present value of all future cash flows, discounted at the prevailing market rate of interest (also called the effective rate or effective yield) on the issue date.A bond produces two distinct cash flow streams: Principal (Face Value, ): A single sum payable at maturity. Periodic Cash Interest Payments (): An ordinary annuity paid periodically (typically semiannually) based on the stated (coupon) interest rate (). Formula & Derivation: Bond Valuation (where is the number of interest compounding periods per year) The Bond Valuation Equation: where: Exam Pitfall / Exception The relationship between the stated coupon rate () and the market effective rate () determines the issuance price: Issued at Par (): The present value of future cash flows equals the face value. Issued at a Discount (): Investors demand a higher yield than the coupon rate. To provide the market yield, the bond sells for less than face value. The discount represents an additional borrowing cost realized over the bond's life. Issued at a Premium (): The coupon rate exceeds market yields, attracting high investor demand. The bond sells for more than face value. The premium represents a reduction of the net borrowing cost over the bond's life. Under US GAAP (ASC 835-30), the effective-interest method is the required method for amortizing bond discounts and premiums because it produces a constant interest rate applied to the carrying amount of the debt at the beginning of each period. The straight-line method is permitted only if the resulting amortization does not materially differ from the effective-interest method. Under IFRS (IFRS 9), the effective-interest method is mandatory without exception.Formula & Derivation: Core Effective-Interest Formulas For any period : Cash Interest Paid: Bond Interest Expense: Amortization Amount: Carrying Value: When bonds are issued between interest payment dates, buyers pay the issuer the purchase price of the bonds plus accrued interest from the last interest payment date to the date of issue. The buyer is reimbursed for this advance payment when the issuer pays the full periodic interest payment on the next interest date.Under ASC 835-30 and IFRS 9, bond issue costs (e.g., legal fees, accounting fees, printing costs, underwriting commissions) are netted against the initial carrying amount of the bonds payable rather than recorded as a deferred asset. The reduced initial carrying amount increases the effective-interest rate over the life of the debt.Extinguishment of debt occurs when a company reacquires its outstanding bonds or debt securities prior to maturity.Formula & Derivation: Early Extinguishment Gain/Loss Compute the Net Carrying Value (NCV) of the debt on the reacquisition date: Compute the Reacquisition Price: Total cash paid to extinguish the bonds (including call premiums and redemption expenses, but excluding accrued interest paid). Recognize the Gain or Loss on Extinguishment: Exam Pitfall / Exception Refunding: The replacement of an existing bond issue with a new bond issue. The gain or loss on the old issue is recognized immediately in income; it CANNOT be deferred or amortized over the life of the new debt. In-Substance Defeasance: An arrangement where a debtor places risk-free assets (e.g., U.S. Treasury securities) in an irrevocable trust solely for satisfying the debt service of an outstanding obligation. Under US GAAP (ASC 405-20), in-substance defeasance does not constitute an accounting derecognition/extinguishment unless the debtor is legally released from being the primary obligor. Like bonds, long-term notes payable are recorded at the present value of future cash flows (principal and interest) discounted at the market rate of interest. Notes Issued at Face Value: Stated interest rate equals market rate; present value equals face value. Zero-Interest-Bearing Notes: No stated cash interest payments; issued at a discount. The cash received equals the present value of the maturity payment discounted at the implicit interest rate. The discount is amortized to interest expense over the note term using the effective-interest method. Interest-Bearing Notes with Unreasonable Stated Rates: When the stated interest rate differs from the prevailing market rate, the note is recorded at present value, and a discount or premium is established and amortized. In arm's-length exchanges, the stated interest rate is presumed fair unless: No interest rate is stated. The stated interest rate is unreasonable. The face amount of the note is materially different from the current cash sales price of the property/services or the current fair value of the note. In such cases, the note is recorded at either the fair value of the property, goods, or services received, or the fair value (present value) of the note, determined by discounting cash flows using an imputed interest rate.A mortgage note payable is a promissory note secured by a document (mortgage) that pledges real property as collateral. Most mortgage notes require equal periodic installment payments consisting of both interest expense and principal reduction.Formula & Derivation: Installment Amortization Balance Sheet Presentation: Long-term debt is reported in a separate long-term liabilities section. Maturities Disclosure: US GAAP requires disclosure of the aggregate maturity amounts and sinking fund requirements for all long-term debt for each of the next five years following the balance sheet date. Off-Balance-Sheet Financing: Attempts to borrow funds or construct assets without recording liabilities on the balance sheet. Regulatory responses (like ASC 842) have brought previously hidden items (e.g., operating leases) onto the balance sheet as Right-of-Use assets and Lease Liabilities. Key Definition Companies may irrevocably elect the Fair Value Option for long-term financial liabilities on an instrument-by-instrument basis at initial recognition. The liability is revalued to fair value at each balance sheet date. Income Statement vs. OCI Allocation: General Market Risk Component: Changes in fair value attributable to changes in benchmark market interest rates are recognized in Net Income (Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss - Income). Instrument-Specific Credit Risk Component: Changes in fair value attributable to changes in the company's own credit risk/creditworthiness are recognized in Other Comprehensive Income (OCI) (Unrealized Holding Gain or Loss - Equity). Formula & Derivation: Solvency Ratios Debt to Assets Ratio: Measures the percentage of total assets funded by creditors: Times Interest Earned Ratio: Measures the company's ability to cover interest payments out of operating earnings: A troubled-debt restructuring (TDR) occurs when a creditor, for economic or legal reasons related to a debtor's financial difficulties, grants a concession to the debtor that it would not otherwise consider.Settlement involves transferring noncash assets (e.g., real estate, equipment) or issuing equity securities to satisfy the debt.Formula & Derivation: Settlement of Debt Debtor Accounting: Creditor Accounting: Modifications may include: reducing the stated interest rate, extending maturity dates, reducing face value, or forgiving accrued interest.Exam Pitfall / Exception Non-Symmetric Accounting Treatment (Debtor vs. Creditor) US GAAP prescribes highly non-symmetric accounting rules for debtors and creditors under term modifications: Debtor Accounting (Undiscounted Cash Flow Test) Compare pre-restructuring carrying amount to the total UNDISCOUNTED future cash flows. Case 1: No Gain (): No gain recognized. Do not adjust carrying amount. Calculate a new effective-interest rate that equates PV to carrying amount. Case 2: Gain (): Recognize Gain on Restructuring. Reduce carrying amount to total undiscounted future cash flows. The new effective-interest rate is 0% (no interest expense in future periods). Creditor Accounting (Discounted Expected Cash Flow Test) Compare pre-restructuring carrying amount with the PV of expected future cash flows DISCOUNTED at the loan's ORIGINAL effective-interest rate. The loss is charged to Bad Debt Expense and credited to Allowance for Doubtful Accounts. Numerical Problem 1: Bond Pricing, Effective-Interest Amortization, and Early Retirement Scenario: On January 1, 2025, Apex Corp. issued face value of 5-year, bonds. Interest is payable semiannually on June 30 and December 31. On the date of issuance, the market rate of interest for similar bonds was . On July 1, 2027 (after 2.5 years / 5 semiannual interest payments), Apex calls and extinguishes the entire bond issue at 101. Stated semiannual rate = Semiannual Cash Interest () = Market semiannual rate () = Total semiannual periods () = (Note: Interest Exp = Prev. Carrying Value 5%. Discount Amort = Interest Exp - Cash Paid). Carrying Value on July 1, 2027 = Unamortized Discount on July 1, 2027 = Reacquisition Price = Loss on Extinguishment: Numerical Problem 2: Troubled-Debt Restructuring (Non-Symmetric Debtor/Creditor Comparison) Scenario: On December 31, 2025, Metro Bank holds a note receivable from Titan Corp., issued at par. Titan is in severe financial distress. Metro Bank agrees to a modification of terms on December 31, 2025: Reduce principal from to . Extend maturity date for 3 years (due December 31, 2028). Reduce interest rate from to per year, payable annually on December 31. Total Undiscounted Future Cash Flows: New Principal = Annual Cash Interest = Total Undiscounted Cash Flows = Undiscounted Cash Flow Test: Pre-restructure Carrying Value = Since Undiscounted Cash Flows () < Carrying Value (), Titan recognizes a Gain on Restructuring: Debtor Carrying Value & Future Interest: New carrying value is adjusted to . Effective interest rate is 0%. Titan records interest expense over the next 3 years. Discounted Expected Cash Flows at Original Effective Rate (10%): Total PV of Restructured Cash Flows = Creditor Impairment Loss: Creditor Schedule for Future Years (Original Rate 10%): Year 2026: Cash Received = ; Interest Revenue = ; Increase in Allowance = .
