item.title: ACC 304 Cost Accounting I
item.description: I have created the mind map ACC 304 Logical Learning Path & Syllabus Map in your Studio panel. This mind map details a sequential, step-by-step reading flow that aligns your syllabus topics directly with the chapters of Srikant Datar and Madhav Rajan's Cost Accounting textbook.To ensure a seamless, logical progression that never requires you to jump ahead to a future chapter to understand a concept introduced early in your reading, the chapters have been reordered based on their conceptual dependencies. Syllabus Mapping: Topic 2 (Cost Accounting as a Discipline) & Topic 1 (Introduction - part). Core Concepts: Differences between financial, management, and cost accounting; organization structure of the management accountant; professional ethics; producing and service departments. Textbook Reading: Chapter 1: The Manager and Management Accounting. Logic: This serves as the necessary high-level overview. You must understand the strategic role of cost accounting and organizational structures before looking at cost mechanics. Syllabus Mapping: Topic 3 (Cost Concepts, Classification and Preparation of Cost Sheets) & Topic 1 (Introduction - part: Manufacturing vs. Non-manufacturing concerns). Core Concepts: Concepts of cost, expense, loss, and asset; classifications of direct/indirect and variable/fixed costs; inventoriable vs. period costs; flow of manufacturing costs through Work-in-Process and Finished Goods; and the preparation of the schedule of Cost of Goods Manufactured (COGM), Cost of Goods Sold (COGS), and the Income Statement. Textbook Reading: Chapter 2: An Introduction to Cost Terms and Purposes. Logic: This establishes the fundamental vocabulary (direct/indirect, fixed/variable) and provides the master financial template (COGM and COGS schedules) that you will use in every subsequent chapter. Syllabus Mapping: Topic 9 (Job Order and Batch Costing - part). Core Concepts: Job-costing and process-costing systems; normal costing and predetermined overhead rates; T-accounts and General Ledger transactions for tracing direct costs and allocating indirect costs. Textbook Reading: Chapter 4: Job Costing (specifically up to page 143 for basic job costing). Logic: Now that you know basic cost terms and flows, you learn how to apply them to track costs for a distinct, customized job or batch. Syllabus Mapping: Topic 4 (Costing and Control of Materials). Core Concepts: Inventory planning models including Economic Order Quantity (EOQ), safety stock, and reorder point; Material Requirements Planning (MRP) and Just-in-Time (JIT) purchasing/production impacts on inventory; materials requisition bookkeeping and simplified backflush costing systems. Textbook Reading: Chapter 21: Inventory Management, Just-in-Time, and Simplified Costing Methods (read in conjunction with material records in Chapter 4). Logic: Having covered basic costing systems, this step zooms in on the first major element of cost—Materials. You learn how to plan materials scientifically (EOQ) and how modern systems (JIT and Backflush Costing) simplify standard bookkeeping. Syllabus Mapping: Topic 6 (Costing and Control of Manufacturing Overhead) & Topic 9 (Job Costing - part: Spoilage, rework, and scrap). Core Concepts: Predetermined and actual overhead rates; variable and fixed overhead planning; variable/fixed overhead spending and efficiency variances; underallocated and overallocated overhead; absorption vs. variable costing methods; and production capacity levels (theoretical, practical, normal, and master-budget capacity). Textbook Readings: Chapter 8: Flexible Budgets, Overhead Cost Variances, and Management Control Chapter 9: Inventory Costing and Capacity Analysis Logic: This shifts focus to the most complex element of cost—Manufacturing Overhead. You learn how to plan it, analyze its variances (Chapter 8), choose how it is absorbed (variable vs. absorption costing), and manage capacity levels (Chapter 9). Syllabus Mapping: Topic 7 (Allocation of Manufacturing Overhead). Core Concepts: Allocating overhead of support (service) departments to operating (producing) departments; cost allocation methods (Direct method, Step-down method, and Reciprocal method); and single vs. dual-rate allocation methods. Textbook Reading: Chapter 16: Allocation of Support-Department Costs, Common Costs, and Revenues. Logic: Building on overhead control, this step tackles how to distribute indirect support costs (like Plant Administration or Materials Management) to producing departments before they are finally allocated to products. Syllabus Mapping: Topic 8 (Selling and Administrative Overhead). Core Concepts: Allocation of non-manufacturing costs; value-chain cost allocations across research, design, and distribution; and customer-level cost-hierarchy and profitability analysis. Textbook Readings: Chapter 14: Pricing Decisions and Cost Management (specifically sections on calculating full product costs across the value chain) Chapter 15: Cost Allocation, Customer-Profitability Analysis, and Sales-Variance Analysis (specifically customer-level cost-hierarchy and profitability) *Logic: This final step covers how to handle selling, administrative, and other value-chain period costs, allocating them to products for long-run pricing decisions (Chapter 14) or to customers to analyze service profitability (Chapter 15). While this reading flow covers the vast majority of your syllabus, a few specific topics represent uncovered gaps in the global textbook that you must supplement: Bangladesh Cost Accounting Standards (BCAS): Syllabus Mentions: BCAS 1 (Cost Concepts and Classifications), BCAS 4 (Indirect Costs), BCAS 5 (Indirect Cost Rate), BCAS 6 (Support Department Cost), and BCAS 7 (Job Order Costing). The Gap: Horngren's textbook does not cover these local national standards, which are specific to Bangladesh's regulatory environment. How to Fill It: Search the official publications of the Institute of Cost and Management Accountants of Bangladesh (ICMAB) for the text of these specific standards to read alongside their corresponding chapters (e.g., read BCAS 6 alongside Chapter 16). Integral and Non-Integral Accounting Systems: Syllabus Mention: "Preparation of financial statements of a manufacturing firm under integral and non-integral systems". The Gap: This terminology is typical of UK/Commonwealth cost accounting. Non-integral bookkeeping keeps cost ledgers completely separate from financial ledgers (requiring control accounts), while integral accounting combines them. Horngren does not explicitly use this terminology, natively assuming an integrated (integral) general ledger system. How to Fill It: Look up CIMA (Chartered Institute of Management Accountants) or UK-based textbook chapters specifically titled "Integrated and Non-Integrated Accounting Ledgers" to learn the specific double-entry journal postings for separating financial and cost accounts. Missing Syllabus Topic 5 (Labor Costing): Syllabus Mention: Your syllabus excerpt skips Topic 5 entirely (jumping from Topic 4 to Topic 6). The Gap: This missing topic is almost certainly "Costing and Control of Labor". How to Fill It: You can easily bridge this gap by studying Horngren's built-in coverage of labor. Focus on labor classifications, labor time tracking in job costing, and labor price/efficiency variances. Would you like me to generate a structured set of study notes for the first step (Discipline Foundations) to help you kick off this reading plan?

item.title: ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques
item.description: I have designed and dispatched a comprehensive, interactive Mind Map artifact (ACC 303 Advanced Statistical Techniques Learning Path) to your Studio panel. It maps your syllabus topics directly to your uploaded textbooks in a strictly linear, pedagogically sound sequence.Below is the structured, step-by-step reading roadmap, designed to build a continuous, logical progression from foundational statistics to advanced econometrics.Your uploaded syllabus document includes topics such as Leverage and Capital Structure, Working Capital Management, Capital Budgeting Decisions, and Dividend Policy. These topics belong to a parallel Financial Management curriculum (referencing Gitman or Horne & Wachowicz) and are not part of ACC 303: Advanced Statistical Techniques.The roadmap below is focused exclusively on the rigorous statistical and econometric requirements of ACC 303.Prerequisite: You must master how data is collected and how sample statistics represent a population before attempting to estimate parameters. Syllabus Topic 1: Sampling and Sampling Distributions Core Concepts: Population vs. Sample, Census vs. Sample Survey, Probability/Non-probability Sampling Methods, Sampling and Non-Sampling Errors, Sampling Distribution of the Mean, and the Central Limit Theorem. Sequential Reading Path: Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 1: What Is Statistics? (Focus on Population vs. Sample, and Levels of Measurement: Nominal, Ordinal, Interval, Ratio). Kothari (2e) — Chapter 1: Research Methodology (An Introduction) (Read "Meaning of Research" and "Census and Sample Survey" to understand raw data limitations). Kothari (2e) — Chapter 4: Sampling Design (Excellent for understanding different probability and non-probability sampling techniques, such as stratified, systematic, cluster, and purposive designs). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 8: Sampling, Sampling Methods, and the Central Limit Theorem (Focus on the mathematical definitions of Sampling Error, the Standard Error of the Mean, and how the Central Limit Theorem converts non-normal distributions into normal ones as sample size ). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Appendix A: Review of Some Statistical Concepts (Sections A.1 to A.6 for a mathematical review of probability density functions and theoretical probability distributions). Prerequisite: Understanding standard errors from Module 1 allows us to construct intervals around our sample statistics to estimate population parameters. Syllabus Topic 2: Estimation & Sample Size Core Concepts: Point vs. Interval Estimation (Mean and Proportions), Desirable Properties of Estimators (BLUE: Unbiasedness, Efficiency, Consistency, Sufficiency), and Mathematical Sample Size Determination. Sequential Reading Path: Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Appendix A (Section A.7): Statistical Inference: Estimation (Provides the mathematical criteria for picking a good estimator: Unbiasedness, Efficiency, Consistency, and Sufficiency). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 9: Estimation and Confidence Intervals (Read Sections on Point Estimates, Confidence Intervals for a Population Mean with known/unknown, Population Proportions, and Finite Population Correction Factors). Kothari (2e) — Chapter 8: Sampling Fundamentals (Estimation Section) (Study the derivation of Point and Interval estimates and the specific determination of sample size using the precision rate and confidence level approach). Prerequisite: Estimating intervals (Module 2) is the logical sister to testing a claim about a parameter. Parametric testing of means and variances must be mastered before studying multi-variable regressions. Syllabus Topics 3 & 4: Parametric Tests & Nonparametric Tests Core Concepts: Null/Alternative Hypotheses, Type I & II Errors, Significance Levels, One vs. Two-Tailed Tests, Power of a Test, One-Sample and Two-Sample tests (Independent/Dependent), Chi-square Goodness-of-Fit, and Independence of Attributes. Sequential Reading Path: Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Appendix A (Section A.8): Statistical Inference: Hypothesis Testing (Read to master the conceptual differences between the Confidence Interval and Test-of-Significance approaches, and the trade-offs between Type I () and Type II () errors). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 10: One-Sample Tests of Hypothesis (Follow the 6-Step procedure, p-values, known vs. unknown standard deviations, and calculating the probability of a Type II error). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 11: Two-Sample Tests of Hypothesis (Master the difference between independent sampling and paired/dependent/matched-pair samples). Kothari (2e) — Chapter 9: Testing of Hypotheses I (Read for testing specific parametric claims: difference between means, tests for proportions, and testing the equality of two normal variances using the F-test). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 15: Nonparametric Methods: Nominal Level Hypothesis Tests (Master Chi-Square tests for Goodness-of-Fit, Contingency Table Analysis for Independence, and the mathematical limitations of Chi-Square). Kothari (2e) — Chapter 10: Chi-Square Test (Reinforce with Yates' correction for continuity and conversion of to contingency coefficients). Prerequisite: ANOVA is the bridge between simple hypothesis testing and regression analysis, using variance partitions to test the equality of several means. Syllabus Topic 5: Analysis of Variance Core Concepts: Assumptions of ANOVA, One-way Classification, Two-way Classification (with and without Interaction), and the F-distribution. Sequential Reading Path: Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 12: Analysis of Variance (Focus on the F-distribution, setting up the One-Way ANOVA table, and the conceptual additions of blocking variables and interaction in Two-Way ANOVA). Kothari (2e) — Chapter 11: Analysis of Variance and Covariance (Provides an excellent mathematical walkthrough of the "Sum of Squares" partitioning and the shortcut coding methods). Prerequisite: With basic hypothesis testing and multi-mean comparisons (ANOVA) secured, you can now enter single-equation causal modeling. Syllabus Topics 6, 7 & 8: The Nature of Regression, Two-Variable Regression (Estimation & Inference) Core Concepts: Regression vs. Causation/Correlation, PRF and SRF, Linearity in variables/parameters, Stochastic Disturbance, Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), Gauss-Markov Theorem (BLUE), Coefficient of Determination (), Normality of errors (), Confidence Intervals/t-tests for regression coefficients (), and ANOVA in regression. Sequential Reading Path: Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Introduction (Read to understand the methodology of traditional econometrics, mathematical vs. econometric models, and the role of data). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 1: The Nature of Regression Analysis (Focus on modern interpretation, regression vs. correlation, and cross-section vs. time-series vs. panel data). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 2: Two-Variable Regression Analysis: Some Basic Ideas (PRF, SRF, and the structural definition of linearity in the parameters). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 3: Two-Variable Regression Model: The Problem of Estimation (OLS derivation, the 10 Classical Linear Regression Model assumptions, Gauss-Markov Theorem/BLUE, and ). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 4: Classical Normal Linear Regression Model (CNLRM) (Why the normality assumption of is required for hypothesis testing, and maximum likelihood estimation). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 5: Two-Variable Regression: Interval Estimation and Hypothesis Testing (Constructing confidence intervals for ; performing t-tests; mapping regression to ANOVA; and testing normality via Jarque-Bera). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 13: Correlation and Linear Regression (Reinforce OLS, assumptions, standard error of the estimate, and prediction/confidence intervals for ). Prerequisite: Having mastered the two-variable model under ideal conditions, you now generalize to multiple regressors and learn how to diagnose and correct violations of OLS assumptions. Syllabus Topics 9 & 10: Multiple Regression Analysis & Relaxing Classical Assumptions Core Concepts: Three-Variable Model, Partial Regression Coefficients, OLS Estimation, vs. Adjusted , overall significance testing (F-test), Multicollinearity, Heteroscedasticity, and Autocorrelation (Meaning, Detection, and Remedial measures). Sequential Reading Path: Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 7: Multiple Regression Analysis: The Problem of Estimation (The algebraic notation, interpretation of partial coefficients, and adjusted ). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 8: Multiple Regression Analysis: The Problem of Inference (t-tests for individual coefficients and the overall F-test using ANOVA in matrix/algebraic notation). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 14: Multiple Regression Analysis (Excellent practical introduction, focusing on global significance testing, dummy variables, and interaction models). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 10: Multicollinearity (What happens when regressors are correlated? Learn diagnostics like Tolerance/VIF and remedial measures like dropping variables). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 11: Heteroscedasticity (Non-constant error variance: examine consequences, detection via Park, Glejser, and White tests, and correction using Weighted Least Squares). Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Chapter 12: Autocorrelation (Correlated error terms: study time-series consequences, detection via Durbin-Watson d and Breusch-Godfrey tests, and Generalized Least Squares corrections). Lind, Marchal & Wathen (18e) — Chapter 18 (Section 18.6): Forecasting with Time Series Analysis (Reinforce the practical implementation of the Durbin-Watson statistic and autocorrelation detection). Software Training (STATA, SPSS, EViews): The syllabus indicates that students must learn these packages. Where it is covered: Gujarati & Porter (5e) — Appendix E provides concrete, side-by-side comparative outputs for EViews, MINITAB, Excel, and STATA. Additionally, Chapter 1 (Section 1.6) introduces the operational role of these software packages in modern empirical work. Research Design: While not explicitly a numbered topic in the ACC 303 syllabus, understanding the "Research Process" is highly recommended before starting econometrics. You can find this in Kothari — Chapters 2 and 3 (defining problems, establishing research blueprints, and understanding experimental vs. survey designs). What would you like to explore next? We can generate a customized quiz covering Module 1 to test your understanding of sampling distributions before you start reading, or we can dive deeper into the mathematical proofs of the Gauss-Markov Theorem.

item.title: ACC 302 Financial Management
item.description: This systematic, step-by-step reading roadmap organizes your studies for ACC 302: Financial Management. Standard finance textbooks often present topics in a chronological order that creates circular dependencies (such as introducing bond and stock valuation before the mathematical principles of the Time Value of Money, or presenting Cost of Capital before the Capital Asset Pricing Model).This learning path is designed with a strict non-linear progression to ensure all foundational concepts and mathematical tools are mastered before you proceed to more advanced, applied structures. Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 1: An Overview of Financial Management (Financial goals of the organisation; Financial management decisions; Agency relationships and resolving conflicts). Logical Dependency: Establishes the broad responsibilities of the financial manager (investment, financing, and asset management decisions) and the ultimate goal of the firm (maximizing shareholder wealth). Required Reading: Class Slides: CH-1_OVERVIEW OF FIN MGT.pdf (Full Slide Deck). Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 1: The Role of Managerial Finance (Sections 1.1: What is Finance/Goal of the Firm; 1.2: Managerial Finance Function; and 1.3: Organizational Forms, Taxation, and Principal-Agent Relationship). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 1: The Role of Financial Management (What is Financial Management?, The Goal of the Firm, Corporate Governance, and Organization of the Financial Management Function). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Implicit Foundational Prerequisite (Required for Topics 2, 3, 4, 6, and 7). Logical Dependency: You must master TVM now. Standard curricula often delay TVM, but you cannot mathematically evaluate bonds, stocks, projects, or cost of capital components without first understanding how to compound and discount cash flows through time. Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 5: Time Value of Money (Sections 5.1: Role of Time Value; 5.2: Single Amounts; 5.3: Annuities; 5.4: Mixed Streams; 5.5: Compounding Frequencies; and 5.6: Loan Amortization). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 3: The Time Value of Money (Simple Interest, Compound Interest, Compounding Frequency, and Amortizing a Loan). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Partial mapping to Topic 2: Risk and Returns and Topic 6: Capital Budgeting Decisions (Valuation of long-term debt and equity). Logical Dependency: Understanding how financial assets are priced in the market using TVM discounting must occur before studying required rates of return (Topic 2) and the Cost of Capital (Topic 3). Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 6: Interest Rates and Bond Valuation (Sections 6.1: Interest Rates; 6.2: Corporate Bonds; and 6.4: Bond Valuation). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 4: The Valuation of Long-Term Securities (Sections: Bond Valuation; Rates of Return or Yields). Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 7: Stock Valuation (Sections 7.1: Debt vs. Equity; 7.2: Features of Stock; 7.3: Common Stock Valuation; and 7.4: Decision Making and Stock Value). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 4: The Valuation of Long-Term Securities (Sections: Preferred Stock Valuation; Common Stock Valuation). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 2: Risk and Returns (Definition and types of return and risk; Measurement of returns and risk; Portfolio return and risk; The relationship between risk and rate of return; CAPM; Security Market Line; Capital Market Line). Logical Dependency: Establishes the relationship between risk and investors' required returns. The Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM) and Security Market Line (SML) developed here are the exact tools used to determine the Cost of Equity in the next phase. Required Reading: Class Slides: CH-2_RISK & RETURN.pdf (Full Slide Deck: Expected Return, Standard Deviation, Portfolio Risk, CAPM, and SML). Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 8: Risk and Return (Sections 8.1: Risk & Return Fundamentals; 8.2: Risk of a Single Asset; 8.3: Risk of a Portfolio; and 8.4: CAPM/SML). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 5: Risk and Return (Defining Risk & Return, Probability Distributions, Portfolio Risk/Diversification, CAPM, and SML) & Appendix A: Measuring Portfolio Risk. Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 3: Cost of Capital (Definition of Cost of Capital; Cost of specific sources of financing—Debt, Preference Capital, Retained Earnings, Newly Issued Common Shares; Weighted Average Cost of Capital—WACC; Marginal Cost of Capital—MCC; Combining MCC and Investment Opportunity Schedule). Logical Dependency: Blends the required returns of individual debt and equity components into a single composite rate (WACC). This serves as the "hurdle rate" that project returns must clear in Capital Budgeting. Required Reading: Class Slides: CH-3_COST OF CAPITAL.pdf (Full Slide Deck: Component Costs, WACC, and Hurdle Rates). Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 9: The Cost of Capital (Sections 9.1: Overview; 9.2: Cost of Long-Term Debt; 9.3: Cost of Preferred Stock; 9.4: Cost of Common Stock; and 9.5: WACC & Hurdle Rates). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 15: Required Returns and the Cost of Capital (Creation of Value, Overall Cost of Capital, CAPM Approach, and WACC). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 6: Capital Budgeting Decisions (Concept and importance of Capital Budgeting; Steps in Capital Budgeting; Project classifications; Cash flow estimation; Identifying the relevant cash flows; Capital Budgeting evaluation techniques—PBP, NPV, IRR, PI, MIRR; Capital rationing; Uncertainty in Capital Budgeting). Logical Dependency: Implements the core investment decision-making tools of the firm. It combines cash flow forecasting with TVM discounting at the project-specific hurdle rate determined in Phase 4. Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 10: Capital Budgeting Techniques (Sections 10.1: Overview; 10.2: Payback Period; 10.3: NPV; 10.4: IRR; and 10.5: NPV vs. IRR / MIRR). Chapter 11: Capital Budgeting Cash Flows (Sections 11.1: Project Cash Flows; 11.2: Initial Cash Flow; 11.3: Periodic Cash Flows; and 11.4: Terminal Cash Flow). Chapter 12: Risk and Refinements in Capital Budgeting (Sections 12.1: Assessing Risk; 12.3: RADRs; and 12.4: Unequal Lives/Capital Rationing). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 12: Capital Budgeting and Estimating Cash Flows. Chapter 13: Capital Budgeting Techniques & Appendix B: Replacement Chain Analysis. Chapter 14: Risk and Managerial (Real) Options in Capital Budgeting (Total Project Risk, Firm-Portfolio Approach, and Real Options). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 4: Leverage and Capital Structure (Concept and types of Leverage; Measurement of Leverage; Impacts of Leverage; Concept of Capital Structure; Capital Structure Theories; Optimal Capital Structure; Determination of Optimal Capital Structure; EBIT-EPS analysis). Logical Dependency: Once you know how to invest in assets (Phase 5), you must determine the optimal way to finance them. Capital structure choices alter the firm’s financial risk, which feeds back into the cost of equity (levering/unlevering beta) and WACC. Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 13: Capital Structure (Sections 13.1: Financial Leverage and Its Effects; 13.2: Irrelevance in Perfect Markets; 13.3: M&M and Taxes; 13.4: Trading Off Benefits and Costs; and 13.5: Agency/Asymmetric Info). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 16: Operating and Financial Leverage (Operating/Financial Leverage, EBIT-EPS Indifference Analysis, and Total Firm Risk). Chapter 17: Capital Structure Determination (Net Operating Income Approach, Traditional Approach, M&M, Taxes/Imperfections, Signaling, and Checklist) & Appendix A: Adjusting Beta for Financial Leverage. Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 7: Dividend Policy (Basics of dividend and dividend policy; Mechanics of dividend policy; Types of dividend policy; Theories of dividend policy; Factors influencing dividend policy; Stock Dividend, Stock Repurchase, and Stock Split). Logical Dependency: Evaluates the trade-off between distributing cash to shareholders versus retaining it within the firm. Retained earnings directly affect the common equity component weight of future WACC and the firm's capital structure. Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 14: Payout Policy (Sections 14.1: Basics; 14.2: Payout Irrelevance vs. Relevance; 14.3: Establishing Policy; 14.4: Three Payout Policies; 14.5: Stock Dividends; and 14.6: Stock Splits). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 18: Dividend Policy (Passive vs. Active, Stability Factors, Stock Dividends/Splits, and Stock Repurchases). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 5: Working Capital Management (Working capital terminology; Requirements for working capital finance; Determining Cash Conversion Cycle; Working Capital estimation; Working Capital investment and financing policy; Cash, Credit, and Inventory Management). Logical Dependency: Shifts focus from long-term corporate strategy to day-to-day liquidity. Effective working capital management maintains the short-term solvency required for the firm to survive and pursue its long-term strategic investments. Required Reading: Smart & Zutter (16e): Chapter 15: Working Capital and Current Assets Management (Sections 15.1: Net Working Capital Fundamentals; 15.2: Cash Conversion Cycle; 15.3: Inventory Management; 15.4: Accounts Receivable Management; and 15.5: Receipts/Disbursements). Chapter 16: Current Liabilities Management (Sections 16.1: Spontaneous Liabilities; 16.2: Unsecured Short-Term Loans; and 16.3: Secured Short-Term Loans). Van Horne (13th ed): Chapter 8: Overview of Working Capital Management (Working Capital Issues, Financing Current Assets, and Combining Decisions). Chapter 9: Cash and Marketable Securities Management (Motives for Holding Cash, Speeding Collections, Slowing Disbursements, and Marketable Securities Portfolio). Chapter 10: Accounts Receivable and Inventory Management (Credit & Collection Policies, Credit Applicant Analysis, and Inventory Control EOQ/Safety Stock). Chapter 11: Short-Term Financing (Spontaneous Financing, Unsecured/Secured negotiated short-term loans, and Factoring Receivables). Syllabus Topic Alignment: Topic 8: Financial Management Practice in Bangladesh (Goals and objectives of public and private sector enterprises; Techniques of Public Financial Management; Organizations and management structures; Control measures; Problems and prospects; Case studies). Logical Dependency: Contextualizes international textbook theories within the local regulatory, private, and public financial environment of Bangladesh. Syllabus Topic Gap: Neither textbook covers the local regulatory landscape of Bangladesh, the structure of Bangladeshi public/private sector organizations, nor the specific local techniques for Public Financial Management (PFM). Recommended Search Keywords & local sources to fill this gap: Search Query: "Public Financial Management (PFM) Reform Strategy Bangladesh" (Refer to Ministry of Finance, GOB publications). Search Query: "Corporate Governance Guidelines Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC)". Search Query: "State-Owned Enterprises (SOEs) financial management Bangladesh". Bangladesh Case Studies: Focus on financial restructurings, dividend payouts, or capital budgeting decisions of local publicly listed conglomerates on the Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE). I have created a comprehensive ACC 302 Logical Learning Path mind map in your Studio panel. It visually diagrams these non-linear connections, prerequisite bridges (such as the TVM-to-Valuation and CAPM-to-Cost-of-Capital links), and syllabus-to-textbook mappings to help you navigate your semester smoothly.Would you like me to construct a targeted study guide focusing specifically on how the Hamada Equation is used to adjust beta for financial leverage across our textbooks and class slides?

item.title: ACC 301 Intermediate Accounting
item.description: To help you navigate your ACC 301: Intermediate Accounting course with maximum efficiency, I have designed a highly structured, sequential reading flow. An interactive Mind Map has been created in your Studio panel, visually charting this exact conceptual journey.This roadmap is built on a pedagogical dependency philosophy: it ensures you master foundational concepts (theory, cycle mechanics, and the mathematics of interest) before you are introduced to the complex asset, liability, and equity structures that rely on them.For example, although Syllabus Topic 1 (Receivables) appears first in your syllabus, it requires discounting and evaluating interest-bearing and zero-interest-bearing notes. This cannot be understood without the time value of money. Therefore, Chapter 5 (Time Value of Money) has been positioned as a strict prerequisite before you open Chapter 6 (Receivables). Similarly, a comprehensive study of financial statements (Syllabus Topic 8) is placed at the end as a synthesis capstone.Before diving into specific accounting topics, you must master the reporting environment, the database structure of accounting, and basic financial statement layouts. Step 1: The Core Framework Textbook Reading: Chapter 1: The Environment and Conceptual Framework of Financial Reporting Syllabus Focus: Foundations of accounting assumptions, qualitative characteristics (relevance, faithful representation), elements, and principles (historical cost, revenue/expense recognition). Prerequisite for: All subsequent chapters. Step 2: The Accounting Cycle Mechanics Textbook Reading: Chapter 2: The Accounting Information System Syllabus Focus: Debits and credits, journalizing, ledger posting, trial balances, adjusting entries, and the closing process. Prerequisite for: Practical implementation of all ledger accounts. Step 3: Basic Financial Statement Structures Textbook Reading: Chapter 3: Sections 3.1 to 3.3 (Income Statement & Stockholders' Equity) & Chapter 4: Section 4.1 (Balance Sheet Overview) Syllabus Focus: Prepares you for Syllabus Topic 8 by introducing what a Statement of Comprehensive Income, Statement of Stockholders' Equity, and Statement of Financial Position look like before you begin auditing or adjusting their individual sub-accounts. Step 4: The Mathematics of Interest (Crucial Prerequisite) Textbook Reading: Chapter 5: Accounting and the Time Value of Money Syllabus Focus: Compound interest, future/present value of single sums, and annuities (ordinary and annuity due). Prerequisite for: Strictly required to calculate notes receivable discounting (Syllabus Topic 1) and bond valuations (Syllabus Topic 6). With your foundations and mathematical tools in place, you can logically transition into asset accounting, moving from highly liquid assets to tangible and intangible long-lived assets. Step 5: Receivables & Note Discounting Syllabus Topic: Topic 1: Accounting for Receivables Textbook Reading: Chapter 6: Cash and Receivables Direct Alignment: Accounts and Notes Receivable, discounting interest/non-interest-bearing notes, direct write-off vs. allowance methods, and recovery of written-off receivables. Step 6: Inventory Costing & Estimation Syllabus Topic: Topic 2: Accounting for Inventories Textbook Reading: Chapter 7: Valuation of Inventories: A Cost-Basis Approach & Chapter 8: Inventories: Additional Valuation Issues Direct Alignment: Perpetual/periodic systems, FIFO, LIFO, Average Cost, LIFO reserve/liquidation, inventory errors, LCNRV and LCM valuation, and estimation via the Gross Profit and Retail Inventory methods. Standards Covered: IAS 2: Inventories (integrated via IFRS Insights). Step 7: Tangible Long-Lived Assets (PP&E) Syllabus Topic: Topic 4: Accounting for Property, Plant and Equipment (Part 1) Textbook Reading: Chapter 9: Acquisition and Disposition of PPE & Chapter 10: Depreciation, Impairments, and Depletion Direct Alignment: Determining cost of fixed assets, capitalization of interest, subsequent expenditures, disposal gains/losses, depreciation methods, impairments, and depletion of natural resources. Standards Covered: IAS 16: Property, Plant and Equipment (integrated via IFRS Insights). Step 8: Intangible Assets & Goodwill Syllabus Topic: Topic 4 (Part 2): Accounting for Intangible Assets Textbook Reading: Chapter 11: Intangible Assets Direct Alignment: Characteristics of intangibles, valuation and amortization of patents, copyrights, franchises, and recording/impairment of goodwill. Step 9: Temporary Marketable Investments Syllabus Topic: Topic 3: Accounting for Temporary Investments Textbook Reading: Chapter 16: Investments (specifically Trading and Available-for-Sale Debt & Equity securities) Direct Alignment: Nature of temporary investments, fair value adjustments, marketable equity/debt securities, disposition, and financial statement disclosures. This phase progresses from short-term operational obligations to long-term financing structures, concluding with the residual ownership interests of the company. Step 10: Current & Contingent Liabilities Syllabus Topic: Topic 5: Accounting for Current and Contingent Liabilities Textbook Reading: Chapter 12: Current Liabilities and Contingencies Direct Alignment: Accounts and notes payable, payroll liabilities, unearned revenues, current maturities of long-term debt, and contingent liabilities. Standards Covered: IAS 37: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets (integrated via IFRS Insights). Step 11: Long-Term Liabilities (Debt Financing) Syllabus Topic: Topic 6: Accounting for Long term Liabilities Textbook Reading: Chapter 13: Long-Term Liabilities Direct Alignment: Bond issuance, trading, premium/discount amortization (effective-interest method), bond retirements, long-term notes payable, and balance sheet reporting. Step 12: Owners' Equity & Dividends Syllabus Topic: Topic 7: Owners' Equity Textbook Reading: Chapter 14: Stockholders' Equity Direct Alignment: Nature and classifications of capital stock, common/preferred stock issuance, treasury stock transactions, cash and property dividends, stock dividends, stock splits, and presentation of equity on the balance sheet. The final step integrates all individual accounts into complete corporate reporting packages, satisfying the ultimate reporting objectives of the course. Step 13: Financial Statement Presentation & Cash Flows Syllabus Topic: Topic 8: Preparation of Financial Statements for Companies Textbook Reading: Chapter 22: Statement of Cash Flows & Chapter 23: Full Disclosure in Financial Reporting Direct Alignment: Preparation and classification of the cash flow statement using the direct and indirect methods, full disclosure notes, segment reporting, and interim statements. Standards Covered: IAS 1: Presentation of Financial Statements and IAS 7: Cash Flow Statement. Upon a rigorous mapping of the ACC 301 Syllabus against the Kieso, Weygandt, and Warfield textbook, I have detected two major uncovered gaps. Because this textbook is globally focused (US GAAP/IFRS), it does not cover the specific national laws of Bangladesh mandated by your university's syllabus: Syllabus Gap 1: Schedule XI of the Companies Act, 1994 (Bangladesh) What is missing: The textbook teaches statement structures under US GAAP and IAS 1, but does not cover the legal presentation formats and disclosure requirements of Schedule XI Parts I, II, and III of the Companies Act, 1994. How to bridge it: Conduct an independent web search to find corporate templates from the Registrar of Joint Stock Companies and Firms (RJSC) in Bangladesh. Suggested Search Queries: "Companies Act 1994 Bangladesh Schedule XI financial statement format pdf" "Bangladesh Companies Act 1994 Statement of Financial Position Schedule XI" Syllabus Gap 2: Securities and Exchange Rules, 1987 (Rule 12(2) & Schedules) What is missing: The textbook's discussion of corporate governance and reporting does not contain the statutory requirements of Rule 12(2) and Parts I, II, III, and IV of the Securities and Exchange Rules, 1987 of Bangladesh. How to bridge it: Look up the official manuals published by the Bangladesh Securities and Exchange Commission (BSEC). Suggested Search Queries: "Securities and Exchange Rules 1987 Bangladesh Rule 12(2) pdf" "BSEC corporate governance report requirements Bangladesh" For a quick hierarchical view (matching the generated interactive Mind Map), here is the course structure:# ACC 301 Intermediate Accounting Logical Path ## Foundations of Accounting Theory & Procedures ### 1. Conceptual Framework #### Chapter 1 (FASB Framework, Qualitative Characteristics, Assumptions/Principles) ### 2. Information Systems #### Chapter 2 (Accounting Cycle, Debits/Credits, Adjusting & Closing Entries) ### 3. Basic Financial Layouts #### Chapter 3.1-3.3 (Income Statement) & Chapter 4.1 (Balance Sheet Overview) ### 4. Mathematical Tools #### Chapter 5 (Time Value of Money, Single Sums, Annuities) Prerequisite for Notes/Bonds ## Asset Valuation & Cost Allocation ### 5. Receivables (Syllabus Topic 1) #### Chapter 6 (Accounts Receivable, Valuation, Note Discounting) ### 6. Inventories (Syllabus Topic 2) #### Chapters 7 & 8 (Cost flow, LCNRV, LCM, Gross Profit & Retail Methods, IAS 2) ### 7. Property, Plant & Equipment (Syllabus Topic 4 - Part 1) #### Chapters 9 & 10 (Acquisition, Interest Capitalization, Depreciation, Depletion, IAS 16) ### 8. Intangible Assets (Syllabus Topic 4 - Part 2) #### Chapter 11 (Amortization, Patents, Copyrights, Goodwill recording/impairments) ### 9. Temporary Investments (Syllabus Topic 3) #### Chapter 16 (Debt/Equity Marketable Securities, Fair Value Adjustments) ## Liabilities & Owners' Equity ### 10. Current & Contingent Liabilities (Syllabus Topic 5) #### Chapter 12 (Payables, Payroll, Unearned Revenue, Contingencies, IAS 37) ### 11. Long-Term Liabilities (Syllabus Topic 6) #### Chapter 13 (Bonds Payable, Discount/Premium Amortization, Notes Payable) ### 12. Owners' Equity (Syllabus Topic 7) #### Chapter 14 (Corporate Capital, Common/Preferred Stock, Treasury Stock, Dividends) ## Statement Synthesis & Global Standards ### 13. Financial Statements & Disclosures (Syllabus Topic 8) #### Chapters 22 & 23 (Cash Flow Statement, IAS 1, IAS 7, Disclosures, Segment/Interim) ## Uncovered National Gaps ### 14. Bangladesh Corporate Law (Syllabus Topic 8 Gaps) #### Companies Act 1994 (Schedule XI Parts I, II, III Financial Statement Formats) #### Securities & Exchange Rules 1987 (Rule 12(2) & Parts I, II, III, IV Governance Report) What would you like to explore next? We can dive into Chapter 5 to master the present value calculations needed for receivables and bonds, or I can help you draft a study guide focusing on the valuation and amortization of Intangibles (IAS 38 vs. US GAAP).

item.title: PYQ ACC 302
item.description: Institution: University of Chittagong | Department: Department of Accounting Program: BBA 5th Semester Standard Instructions: Answer any FIVE questions sequentially/serially. Time: 4 Hours | Total Marks: 75Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 (a) "Investment, financing and dividend decisions are all interrelated." Comment. [03] (c) Explain why the following statements appearing in the objectives of two well-known listed companies are not necessarily contradictory? [04] "We never confuse why we exist - to create the maximum possible returns to our shareholders." "In everything the company does, it is committed to creating wealth always with integrity, for our employees, customers, suppliers and the community in which we operate." (d) Why do managers and other agents of the shareholders, such as employees sometimes have different objectives? [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) What are the possible alternative financial goals of the organization? Which one do you recommend and why? [06] (b) Point out the decisions that are made by financial manager. Explain. [05] (c) What do you mean by agency costs? How can this costs be minimized? [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (a) "The profit maximization is not an operationally feasible criterion." Do you agree? Illustrate your views. Assuming wealth maximization to be the objective of financial management, show how the financing, investment and dividend decisions of a company can help to attain this objective. [07] (b) Why is it necessary for business students who do not plan to major in finance to understand the basics of finance? [04] (c) What do you mean by agency problem? What are some mechanisms that encourage managers to act in the best interests of stockholders? [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) Define financial management. Why is it necessary for business students who do not plan to major in finance to understand the basics of finance? [05] (b) "The ultimate goal of a business firm is to maximize wealth, not to maximize profit." Explain the statement logically. [05] (c) What do you mean by agency problem? What are some mechanisms that encourage managers to act in the best interests of stockholders? [05] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 (a) Explain the following statement: "Most investors are risk averse." [03] (b) "An asset held as part of a portfolio is generally less risky than the same asset held in isolation." Do you agree with this statement? Why or why not? [03] (c) BSCCL stock has an expected return of 10 percent, a beta coefficient of 0.9, and a standard deviation of expected returns of 35 percent. BSC stock has an expected return of 12.5 percent, a beta coefficient of 1.2, and a standard deviation of expected returns of 25 percent. The risk-free rate is 6 percent, and the market risk premium is 5 percent. Required: i. Calculate each stock's coefficient of variation. ii. Which stock is riskier for diversified investors? iii. Calculate each stock's required rate of return. iv. On the basis of the two stocks' expected and required returns, which stock would be most attractive to a diversified investor? v. Calculate the required return of a portfolio that has Tk. 7,500 invested in BSCCL stock and Tk. 2,500 invested in BSC stock. vi. If the market risk premium increased to 6 percent, which of the two stocks would have the largest increase in their required return? [09] (a) Scenario: Assume that there are three stocks in a portfolio - stock-1, stock-2, and stock-3. The expected return vector of this portfolio is and the weighting vector of this portfolio is where, The variances of stock-1, stock-2, and stock-3 are 12%, 7%, and 9% respectively and the correlation coefficients between stock-1 and stock-2, stock-1 and stock-3, and stock-2 and stock-3 are 0.2, -0.6, and -0.3. Required: - i. Compute portfolio return (use vector multiplication). [02] - ii. Compute portfolio risk (use vector multiplication). [07] - iii. Compute minimum and maximum portfolio return. [02] (c) How can investors be classified in terms of their risk preference? [05] (c) An investor purchases one European call option on a stock that is currently trading at $40 per share. The option has a strike price of $35 and a premium of $5, and it expires in three months. Required: Determine the payoff and profit or loss at expiration for various possible stock prices: $30, $35, $40, $45, and $50 and plot the results in the graph. [05] (d) A stock is currently trading at $50. A European call option with a strike price of $55 expiring in 6 months is trading at $4.50, and a European put option with the same strike price and expiration is trading at $9.00. The risk-free interest rate for 6 months is 2% (continuously compounded). Required: Verify whether put-call parity holds and explain the relationship between the call and put prices. [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) Explain why you agree or disagree with this statement "Most investors are risk-averse". [03] (b) Data: Consider the following information for Stocks A, B, and C. The returns on the three stocks are positively correlated, but they are not perfectly correlated. (That is, each of the correlation coefficients is between 0 and 1.) Fund Dhaka Ltd has one-third of its funds invested in each of the three stocks. The risk-free rate is 5.5%, and the market is in equilibrium. (That is, required returns equal expected returns.)Requirements: - i. What is the market risk premium ()? - ii. What is the beta of Fund Dhaka Ltd? - iii. What is the required return of Fund Dhaka Ltd? - iv. Would you expect the standard deviation of Fund Dhaka Ltd to be less than 15%, equal to 15%, or greater than 15%? Explain. [08] (c) A mutual fund manager has a Tk. 20 million portfolio with a beta of 1.7. The risk-free rate is 4.5%, and the market risk premium is 7%. The manager expects to receive an additional Tk. 5 million, which she plans to invest in a number of stocks. After investing the additional funds, she wants the fund's required return to be 15%. Required: What should be the average beta of the new stocks added to the portfolio? [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (a) Explain the concept of systematic and unsystematic risk. How can an investor mitigate unsystematic risk? [04] (b) Explain the Capital Market Line (CML) and its significance in the context of the Capital Asset Pricing Model (CAPM). [04] (c) Data: Stocks A and B have the following probability distributions of expected future returns: Required: - I. Calculate the expected rate of return, , for Stock B (.) - II. Calculate the standard deviation of expected returns for Stock A (That for Stock B is 20.35 percent.) Now calculate the coefficient of variation for Stock B. Is it possible that most investors might regard Stock B as being less risky than Stock A? Explain. [07] (i) Business risk and its determinants [03] (iii) Stand-alone and portfolio risk and their measures [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) Define risk. Distinguish between business risk and financial risk. [04] (b) In general, can the riskiness of a portfolio be reduced to zero by increasing the number of stocks in the portfolio? Explain. [03] (c) Data: Intex corporation is considering three possible capital projects for the next year. Each project has a 1-year life and project returns depend on next year's state of the economy. The estimated rates of return are shown in the table: Also assume that Intex Corporation is going to invest one-third of its available funds in each project. Intex Corporation will create a portfolio of three equally weighted projects.Required: - i. Find each project's expected rate of return, variance and standard deviation. - ii. What is the expected rate of return, variance and standard deviation of the three projects' portfolio? [08]Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 (b) A firm's equity beta is 0.9. The risk-free rate is 4% and the expected market return is 11%. Calculate the cost of equity. [02] (c) A firm's stock is currently being traded at $40. The expected dividend next year is $2.50 and dividends are expected to grow at 5% per year indefinitely. Estimate the cost of equity capital. [02] (a) A two-year bond has a face value of $1,000 and a coupon rate of 8% paid annually. The probability of default each year is 4%. If default occurs, the recovery value is $500. The bond is issued at par. Required: Estimate the expected cost of debt. [05] (b) A project is fully financed by equity and has the same business risk as three pure-play comparable firms that are also all-equity financed. The equity betas of the comparable firms are 1.1, 1.3, and 1.6, respectively. The risk-free rate is 4% and the market risk premium is 8%. Required: Estimate the appropriate discount rate for the project. [05] (b) A company issues a $1,000 par bond, paying a 10% annual coupon semiannually for 6 years. The required annual rate of return is 12%. Required: Determine the bond value. [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) General Electric Company (GEC) uses only debt and common equity. It can borrow unlimited amounts at an interest rate of as long as it finances at its target capital structure, which calls for 35% debt and 65% common equity. Its last dividend () was Tk 2.20, its expected constant growth rate is 6%, and its common stock sells for Tk 26. GEC's tax rate is 40%. Two projects are available: Project A has a rate of return of 12% and Project B's return is 11%. These two projects are equally risky and about as risky as the firm's existing assets. Requirements: i. What is its cost of common equity? ii. What is the WACC? iii. Which projects should GEC accept? [08] (b) The KR Company's EPS was TK 6.50 in 2024, up from TK 4.42 in 2019. The company pays out 40% of its earnings as dividends, and its common stock sells for TK 36.00. Requirements: i. Calculate the past growth rate in earnings. (Hint: This is a 5-year growth period.) ii. The last dividend was . Calculate the next expected dividend, , assuming that the past growth rate continues. iii. What is KR's cost of retained earnings, ? [07] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (a) Discuss why the cost of capital is considered the minimum required rate of return on an investment. How does it influence a firm's investment decisions? [03] (b) Explain the impact of a company's capital structure on its overall cost of capital. How does the mix of debt and equity financing influence this cost? [03] (c) Longstreet Communications Inc. (LCI) has the following capital structure, which it considers to be optimal: debt = 25%, preferred stock = 15%, and common stock = 60%. LCI's tax rate is 40%, and investors expect earnings and dividends to grow at a constant rate of 6% in the future. LCI paid a dividend of D_0$), and its stock currently sells at a price of $60 per share. Ten-year Treasury bonds yield 6%, the market risk premium is 5%, and LCI's beta is 1.3. The following terms would apply to new security offerings. Preferred: New preferred could be sold to the public at a price of $100 per share, with a dividend of $9. Flotation costs of $5 per share would be incurred. Debt: Debt could be sold at an interest rate of 9%. Common: New common equity will be raised only by retaining earnings. Required: I. Find the component costs of debt, preferred stock, and common stock. II. What is the WACC? [09] (v) Weighted average cost of capital [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) Which method of calculating the cost of equity shares would be most appropriate for the following firms: i. A profitable firm that has never paid a dividend, but has had steady growth in earnings. ii. An electricity company that has paid a dividend every year for the last eighty years. [04] (b) Two firm, F-1 and F-2. The firm F-1 has no debt and is totally financed by equity capital. The firm F-2 has Tk 2,000,000 outstanding debt and pays an interest rate of 10%. The firm's net income after-taxes are calculated using three tax rates, 0, 25 and 50 percent and the resulting values of net incomes are compared. Assume that the earnings before interest and taxes of both firms is Tk 1,000,000 each. Required: Calculate cost of debt. [07] (c) Robi is currently selling for Tk 60 a share. The firm is expected to earn Tk 5.40 per share this year and to pay a year-end dividend of Tk 3.60. Required: i. If investors require a 9 percent return, what rate of growth must be expected for Robi? ii. If Robi reinvests retained earnings in projects whose average return is equal to the stock's expected rate of return, what will be next year's EPS? [Hint: g = (1-Payout rate)(ROE).] [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 (a) A firm operates in a perfect capital market where the Modigliani-Miller (MM) assumptions hold and there are no taxes. The firm's overall cost of capital (cost of assets) is 12 percent. The firm is financed with $4 million of debt and $6 million of equity. The cost of debt is 7 percent. Required: Find the cost of equity. [02] (b) An investor owns 1% of an unlevered firm worth $5,000,000. The firm decides to remain unlevered, but the investor wants leverage equivalent to a firm with 40% debt. Required: How can the investor create homemade leverage? [03] (c) A firm is financed with both debt and equity. The market value of debt is $5 million and the market value of equity is also $5 million. The required rate of return on equity is 14 percent, while the cost of debt is 8 percent. The corporate tax rate is 30 percent. In addition, investors face personal taxes: interest income is taxed at 40 percent, whereas equity income is taxed at 20 percent. Required: Find the firm's weighted average cost of capital (WACC) considering both corporate and personal taxes. [05] (d) A firm generates an annual EBIT of $1,200,000. The required return on assets for an unlevered firm is 10 percent. The corporate tax rate is 30 percent. The firm plans to issue permanent debt of $4,000,000. In addition to corporate taxes, investors face personal taxes: Personal tax rate on interest income = 35% Personal tax rate on equity income = 15% Required: i. Find the value of the unlevered firm. [02] ii. Find the value of the levered firm considering both corporate and personal taxes. [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) Explain this statement "Using financial leverage has both good and bad effects". [03] (b) Explain what asymmetric information means, and how signals affect capital structure decisions. [04] (c) A company currently has assets of Tk 5 million. The firm is 100 percent equity financed. The company currently has net income of Tk 1.5 million, and it pays out 40 percent of its net income as dividends. Both net income and dividends are expected to grow at a constant rate of 6 percent per year. There are 200,000 shares of stock outstanding, and it is estimated that the current cost of capital is 13.40 percent. The company is considering a recapitalization where it will issue Tk 1.5 million in debt and use the proceeds to repurchase stock. Investment bankers have estimated that if the company goes through with the recapitalization, its before-tax cost of debt will be 11 percent, and the cost of equity will rise to 14.5 percent. The company has a 40 percent federal tax rate. Requirements: i. What is the current share price of the stock (before the recapitalization)? ii. Assuming that the company maintains the same payout ratio, what will be its stock price following the recapitalization? [08] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (a) Define optimal capital structure. Briefly outline the four primary factors that influence the capital structure decisions. [05] (b) Briefly explain the (i) MM theory; (ii) Trade-off theory; and (iii) the Signaling theory. [05] (c) The Weaver Watch Company sells watches for $25, the fixed costs are $140,000, and variable costs are $15 per watch. Required: i) What is the breakeven point? Illustrate by means of a chart. ii) What would happen to the breakeven point if the selling price was raised to $31? What is the significance of this analysis? [05] (ii) Operating leverage [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) Required: Write short notes on: i. Optimal Capital Structure ii. EBIT-EPS analysis [05] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 (b) To avoid the problem of shortage and surplus of funds, what is required in Financial management? Name the concept and explain four points of importance. [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) Delineate the alternative current asset financing policies with suitable diagram. [05] (b) What is cash conversion cycle? Define its three components. [03] (c) Christie Corporation is trying to determine the effect of its inventory turnover ratio and days sales outstanding (DSO) on its cash flow cycle. Christie's 2023 sales (all on credit) were $150,000; and it earned a net profit of 6%, or $9,000. It turned over its inventory 6 times during the year, and its DSO was 36.5 days. The firm had fixed assets totaling $35,000. Christie's payables deferral period is 40 days. Requirements: i. Calculate Christie's cash conversion cycle. ii. Assuming Christie holds negligible amounts of cash and marketable securities, calculate its total assets turnover and ROA. iii. Suppose Christie's managers believe that the inventory turnover can be raised to 7.3 times. What would Christie's cash conversion cycle, total assets turnover, and ROA have been if the inventory turnover had been 7.3 for 2023? [07] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (a) Discuss the operating cycle and the cash conversion cycle. How do these cycles affect a company's liquidity and working capital requirements? [03] (b) Compare and contrast aggressive, conservative, and moderate working capital policies. What are the risks and benefits associated with each policy? [04] (c) Data: The board of directors of Aravind mills limited request you to prepare a statement showing the working capital requirements for a level of activity of 30,000 units of output for the year. The cost structure for the company's product for the above-mentioned activity level is given below. Additional Information: I. Past experience indicates that raw materials are held in stock, on an average for 2 months. II. Work in progress (100% complete in regard to materials and 50% for labour and overheads) will be half a month's production. III. Finished goods are in stock on an average for 1 month. IV. Credit allowed to suppliers: 1 month. V. Credit allowed to debtors: 2 months. VI. A minimum cash balance of Rs 25,000 is expected to be maintained. Required: Prepare a statement of working capital requirements. [08]Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) Define working capital and working capital management. Discuss the significance of working capital management policy in case of a manufacturing enterprise. [06] (b) Data: From the following information extracted from the books of Zahin Textile Ltd compute the operating cycle in days and the amount of working capital required: [09]Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 A firm is evaluating a proposal to install a new production machine to expand its operations. The project requires careful estimation of cash flows considering depreciation tax shield and interest tax shield. Project Information: Cost of new machine: USD 10,000,000 Installation and transportation cost: USD 1,000,000 Total initial investment: USD 11,000,000 The machine will be depreciated using the straight-line method over 5 years to a salvage value of USD 1,000,000. The project life is 5 years. Expected annual sales revenue: USD 6,000,000 Annual operating costs (excluding depreciation and interest): USD 3,000,000 Corporate tax rate: 30% The project will be financed as follows: 40% debt and 60% equity Loan amount will carry an interest rate of 10% per year The loan will be repaid in equal principal installments over 5 years Expected salvage value at the end of Year 5: USD 1,200,000 Working capital requirement: USD 500,000 (required at the beginning and fully recovered at the end of Year 5) Required rate of return (WACC): 12% Required: - i. Estimate the initial cash flows of the project. **[01]** - ii. Estimate the operating cash flows of the project. **[05]** - iii. Estimate the terminal cash flows of the project. **[03]** - iv. Based on the NPV, should the company accept the project? Justify your answer. **[06]** Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) If two mutually exclusive projects were being compared, would a high cost of capital favor the longer-term or the shorter-term project? Why? If the cost of capital declined, would that lead firms to invest more in longer-term projects or shorter-term projects? Would a decline (or an increase) in the WACC cause changes in the IRR ranking of mutually exclusive projects? Explain. [04] (b) An electric utility is considering a new power plant in Chattogram. Power from the plant would be sold in the Hathazari area, where it is badly needed. Because the firm has received a permit, the plant would be legal, but it would cause some air pollution. The company could spend an additional Tk 40 million at Year 0 to mitigate the environmental problem, but it would not be required to do so. The plant without mitigation would cost Tk 240 million, and the expected cash inflows would be Tk 80 million per year for 5 years. If the firm does invest in mitigation, the annual inflows would be Tk 84 million. Unemployment in the area where the plant would be built is high, and the plant would provide about 350 good jobs. The risk-adjusted WACC is 17%. Requirements: i. Calculate the NPV and IRR with and without mitigation. ii. How should the environmental effects be dealt with when evaluating this project? iii. Should this project be undertaken? If so, should the firm do the mitigation? Why or why not? [11] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (a) Explain the concept of mutually exclusive projects. How should a firm decide between two mutually exclusive projects? [03] (b) Why is NPV considered a superior method for evaluating capital investment projects? [03] (c) Data: Mr. Solaiman is responsible for considering two investment projects for his firm, each of which requires an up-front expenditure of Tk 25 million. You estimate that the cost of capital is 10% and that the investments will produce the following after-tax cash flows (in millions of taka): Required: - I. What is the regular payback period for each of the projects? - II. What is the discounted payback period for each of the projects? - III. If the two projects are independent and the cost of capital is 10%, which project or projects should the firm undertake? - IV. If the two projects are mutually exclusive and the cost of capital is 5%, which project should the firm undertake? - V. If the two projects are mutually exclusive and the cost of capital is 15%, which project should the firm undertake? - VI. What is the crossover rate? [09]Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) What is profitability index? Which one is the superior ranking criterion, profitability index (PI) or net present value (NPV)? Explain. [04] (b) Data: Edelman Engineering is considering including two pieces of equipment, a truck and an overhead pulley system, in this year's capital budget. The projects are independent. The cash outlay for the truck is $17,100, and that for the pulley system is $22,430. The firm's cost of capital is 14%. After-tax cash flows, including depreciation, are as follows: Required: Calculate the IRR, the NPV, and the MIRR for each project, and indicate the correct accept/reject decision for each. [07] (c) Explain why, if two mutually exclusive projects are being compared, the short term project might have the higher ranking under the NPV criterion if the cost of capital is high, but the long-term project might be deemed better if the cost of capital is low. Would changes in the cost of capital ever cause a change in the IRR ranking of two such projects? [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2025 (a) A company has reported earnings per share of $4.00 and maintains a dividend payout ratio of 40 percent. The company's return on equity is 15 percent, and the required rate of return on the stock is 12 percent. The company is expected to experience high growth for the next four years, after which it will settle into a stable growth rate of 5 percent indefinitely. Required: Estimate the intrinsic value of the stock using the two-stage dividend discount model, where the high-growth rate is derived from the firm's sustainable growth rate. [04] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2024 (a) Would it ever be rational for a firm to borrow money in order to pay cash dividends? [02] (b) What is the difference between a stock dividend and a stock split? As a stockholder, would you prefer to see your company declare a 100% stock dividend or a two-for-one split? Assume that either action is feasible. [03] (c) Data: Clifton Inc. is prepared to report the following 2024 income statement (shown in thousands of dollars): Prior to reporting this income statement, the company wants to determine its annual dividend. The company has 320,000 shares of common stock outstanding, and its stock trades at Tk 37 per share.Requirements: - i. The company had a 25% dividend payout ratio in 2023. If Brooks wants to maintain this payout ratio in 2024, what will be its per-share dividend in 2024? - ii. If the company maintains this 25% payout ratio, what will be the current dividend yield on the company's stock? - iii. The company reported net income of Tk 1.35 million in 2023. Assume that the number of shares outstanding has remained constant. What was the company's per-share dividend in 2023? - iv. As an alternative to maintaining the same dividend payout ratio, Brooks is considering maintaining the same per-share dividend in 2024 that it paid in 2023. If it chooses this policy, what will be the company's dividend payout ratio in 2024? [10]Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 | BBA 5th Semester 2023 (iv) Factors influencing dividend policy [03] Tracking Ref: Course Code ACC 302 / FCC 209 | BBA 5th Semester 2021 (a) Explain the logic of the residual dividend model, the steps a firm would take to implement it, and why it is more likely to be used to establish a long-run payout target than to set the actual year-by-year payout ratio. [05] (b) The Well Corporation expects next year's net income to be Tk 150 million. The firm's debt ratio is currently 40 percent. Well has Tk 120 million of profitable investment opportunities, and it wishes to maintain its existing debt ratio. Required: According to the residual dividend model, how large should Well's dividend payout ratio be next year? Assume the firm uses only debt and common equity in its capital structure. What was last year's dividend per share?
