item.description: Session: 2020-2021 & 2021-2022 Year of Examinations: 2021 & 20221st Semester BCC 101 - Introduction to Business BCC 102 - Basic Accounting BCC 103 - Business Mathematics BCC 104 - Principles of Management BCC 105 - Business Communication 2nd Semester BCC 106 - Principles of Marketing BCC 107 - Microeconomics BCC 108 - Business Statistics BCC 109 - Business Law BCC 110 - Information Technology in Business 3rd Semester BCC 201 - Business Finance BCC 202 - Human Resource Management BCC 203 - Principles of Banking BCC 204 - Macroeconomics BCC 205 - Theory & Practices of Taxation 4th Semester BCC 206 - Insurance & Risk Management BCC 207 - Business Ethics BCC 208 - Entrepreneurship Development BCC 209 - Organizational Behavior BCC 210 - Bangladesh Studies and Economic Development 5th Semester ACC 301 - Intermediate Accounting ACC 302 - Financial Management ACC 303 - Advanced Statistical Techniques ACC 304 - Cost Accounting-I ACC 305 - Auditing and Assurance 6th Semester ACC 306 - Advanced Financial Accounting-I ACC 307 - Management Accounting ACC 308 - Cost Accounting-II ACC 309 - Public Finance and Taxation ACC 310 - Operations Research 7th Semester ACC 401 - Advanced Financial Accounting-II ACC 402 - Corporate Accounting ACC 403 - Investment Analysis and Portfolio Management ACC 404 - Advanced Auditing and Assurance ACC 405 - Accounting Information System 8th Semester ACC 406 - Economics of Securities Market ACC 407 - Financial Statement Analysis ACC 408 - Research Methodology ACC 409 - Strategic Management ACC 410 - Accounting for Specialized Institutions ACC 411 - Internship Marks: 100 | Credit: 3.00 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Course Objectives: The main objective of this course is to acquaint the students with accounting for receivables, inventories, temporary investments, current and contingent liabilities, fixed assets, bonds & long-term notes and owners' equity. This course would also expose the students to the preparation of company accounts.Course Contents: Accounting for Receivables: Nature and Composition of Receivables - Accounts Receivable & Notes Receivable - Discounting - Interest and No-interest Bearing Notes Receivable - Un-collectible Accounts Receivable - Methods of Determining Un-collectible Accounts Receivable - Allowances for Doubtful Debts - Methods of Accounting for Un-collectibles - Recovery of Receivables Written off Earlier. Accounting for Inventories: Nature of Inventories - Classes of Inventories, Inventory Systems - Impact of Inflation on Inventory - Inventory Costing – Cost Allocation Methods - Inventory Errors - Estimation and Valuation Procedures of Inventories - Gross Profit Method - Retail Inventory Method, FIFO, LIFO - Average Cost - Recording Inventory - Presentation of Inventories in the Financial Statement - and IAS 2: Inventories. Accounting for Temporary Investments: Nature of Temporary Investments - Accounting for Changes in Market Value - Marketable Equity and Debt Securities - Disposition of Marketable Securities - Disclosure of Marketable securities in Financial Statements. Accounting for Properties, Plant and Equipment: Acquisition, Utilization & Retirement - Categories of Fixed Assets - Determining Cost of Fixed Assets - Disposal of Fixed Assets - Gains and Losses from Disposal - Depreciation and Its Methods - Causes and Objects of Depreciation - Depreciation & Valuation - Depreciation & Cash flow, Depletion of Resources - Accounting for intangible assets - Valuation and Amortization of Intangibles - Presentation and disclosure of Fixed Assets in the Financial Statements, IAS 16: Property, Plant and Equipment. Accounting for Current and Contingent Liabilities: Definition - Classification and measurement of liabilities - Accounting for current liabilities - Notes payable, Accounts payable, liability for payroll - unearned revenue - current maturity of long-term Debt - Contingent liabilities and its state of circumstances - Measurement, Presentation and disclosure of current and contingent liabilities in the financial statements. IAS 37: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets. Accounting for Long term Liabilities: Nature and types of Bonds - Bond Issuance - Bond Trading - Accounting for Bond Issues - Accounting for Bond Retirements – Accounting for other long-term Notes payable - Valuation of Bonds and long term Notes - Reporting of Bonds and long-term Notes on the Financial Statements. Owners' Equity: Capital Stock, Retained Earnings and Dividend: Nature and classifications of capital stock - Accounting for common stock issues - Accounting for Treasury stock - Preferred Stock - Factors affecting retained earnings - Statement of retained earnings - Addition to or deductions from owners' equity - Types of dividend - Accounting for cash dividend - Recording Stock dividend and Stock splits - Stockholders' Equity Presentation. Preparation of Financial Statements for Companies: Definition, Nature, objectives and components of financial statements - Statement of Comprehensive Income - Retained Earnings - Changes in equity - Statement of Financial Position - Disclosure - interpretation and requirements as to Statement of Financial Position and Statement of Comprehensive Income as explained in Part I, Part II and Part III in Schedule XI of Companies Act, 1994 - Requirements as to Statement of Financial Position - Statement of Comprehensive Income - cash flow statement - Corporate governance report and interpretation as explained in Rule 12(2) and schedule Parts I, II, III and IV of the Securities and Exchange Rules, 1987 - IAS 1: Presentation of Financial Statements and IFRS 9 - preparation of cash flow statement IAS 7: Cash Flow Statement. Basic Texts: Weygandt, Kieso and Kimmel, Intermediate Accounting. Smith and Skousen, Intermediate Accounting. Reference Books: R. H. Hermanson, J. E. Edwards and M. W. Maher, Accounting Principles. Horngren, Harrison and Bamber, Accounting. P. E. Fess & C. R. Niswonger, Accounting Principles. Companies Act, 1994. Securities & Exchange Rules, 1987. IAS / IFRS Issued by International Accounting Standards Board (IASB). Marks: 100 | Credit: 3.00 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Course Objective: This course provides an understanding of the finance function and responsibilities of the financial manager. This course also develops concepts and tools for use in effective investment and financial decision-making and problem-solving. This course covers risk-return analysis, cost of capital, capital structure, leverage, capital budgeting decisions, and dividend policy.Course Contents: An Overview of Financial Management: Financial goals of the organization; Financial management Decisions; Agency Relationships and Resolving Conflicts. Risk and Returns: Definition and Types of Return and Risk; Measurement of Returns and Risk; Adjusted Rate of Return; Portfolio Return and Risk; The Relationship between Risk and Rate of Return; CAPM; Security Market Line; Capital Market Line. Cost of Capital: Definition of Cost of Capital; Cost of Specific Sources of Financing – Debt, Preference Capital, Retained Earnings, Newly Issued Common Shares of External Equity - Weighted Average Cost of Capital (WACC) - Marginal Cost of Capital (MCC) - Combining MCC and Investment Opportunity Schedule. Leverage and Capital Structure: Concept and types of Leverage; Measurement of Leverage; Impacts of Leverage. Concept of Capital Structure; Capital Structure Theories, Optimal Capital Structure; Determination of Optimal Capital Structure. EBIT-EPS analysis. (Ref: Gitman). Working Capital Management: Working capital Terminology, The Requirements for Working Capital Finance, Determining Cash Conversion Cycle, Working Capital Estimation, Working Capital Investment and Financing Policy, Cash Management, Credit Management, Inventory Management. Capital Budgeting Decisions: Concept and Importance of Capital Budgeting, Steps in Capital Budgeting; Project Classifications; Cash Flow Estimation; Identifying the Relevant Cash Flows; Capital Budgeting/Projects Evaluation; Capital Budgeting Evaluation Techniques; Capital Rationing; Uncertainty in Capital Budgeting. Dividend Policy: Basics of Dividend and Dividend Policy; The Mechanics of Dividend Policy; Types of Dividend Policy; Theories of Dividend Policy; Factors Influencing Dividend Policy; Stock Dividend, Stock Repurchase and Stock Split. (Ref: Gitman). Financial Management Practice in Bangladesh: Goals and Objectives of Financial Management of Public and Private Sector Enterprises – Technique of Public Financial Management - Organizations and Management Structures – Control Measures – Problems and Prospects. Case Studies. Basic Texts: Eugene F. Brigham, Fundamentals of Financial Management. Lawrence J. Gitman and Chad J. Zutter, Principles of Managerial Finance (13th edition), Prentice Hall. Reference Books: Foundations of Financial Management – Block, Hirt, and Danielsen. Fundamentals of Financial Management – Horne and Wachowicz. Marks: 100 | Credit: 3.00 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Course Objective: This course is designed to understand the statistical processes of data analysis and the application of econometric tools and techniques for solving different kinds of economic, business and socio-economic problems, policy formulations and implications. The main focus of the course is to study different techniques to estimate different models and parameters, testing of hypotheses and uses of the estimates of parameters. Students will also learn the use of software packages like SPSS, STATA and EViews.By the end of the course, students should be able to: Describe and construct a sampling distribution. Learn how to test hypotheses using parametric and nonparametric methods. Learn how to use analysis of variance. Use two-variable regression analysis and multiple regression analysis. Apply regression analysis to business problems. Course Contents: Sampling and Sampling Distributions: Definition of population, Sample, Census, sampling, Types of sampling, methods of sampling, sampling and Non-sampling errors, Definition and applications of sampling distributions and central limit theorem. Estimation: a) Point and interval estimation: Point estimation for a mean, interval estimation for a mean and proportion. b) Choosing an appropriate sample size. Parametric Tests: Procedure of Testing Hypothesis - Null Hypothesis - Alternative Hypothesis - Type I and Type II Errors - Level of Significance - Degree of Freedom - One Tailed and Two Tailed Tests - Power of Test - Tests About Mean - Tests about the Difference between Two Means - Tests about the Difference between Two Means with Dependent Samples - Tests about the Correlation Co-efficient - Tests of Equality of Two Variances - Tests for proportion. Nonparametric Tests: Chi-square test - Limitations of Chi-square - Contingency Table Analysis - Goodness-of-Fit Test - Independence of attributes. Analysis of Variance: Assumptions in Analysis of Variance - Computation of Analysis of Variance (One-way and Two-way Classification of data). The Nature of Regression Analysis: The Modern Interpretation of Regression, Statistical versus Deterministic Relationships, Regression versus Causation, Regression versus Correlation, The Nature and Sources of Data for Economic Analysis. Two-Variable Regression Analysis: The Concept of Population Regression Function (PRF), The Meaning of Term Linear, Stochastic Specification of PRF, The Significance of the Stochastic Disturbance Term, The Sample Regression Function (SRF), The Method of Ordinary Least Squares (OLS), The Classical Linear Regression Model: The Assumptions Underlying the method of Least Squares, Precision of Standard Errors of Least-Squares Estimates, The Coefficient of Determination, : A Measure of "Goodness of Fit", The Normality Assumption for . Two-Variable Regression: Interval Estimation and Hypothesis Testing: Confidence Intervals for Regression Coefficients and , Hypothesis Testing: General Comments, Hypothesis Testing: The Confidence-Interval Approach, Hypothesis Testing: The Test-of-Significance Approach, Hypothesis Testing: Some Practical Aspects, Regression Analysis and Analysis of Variance, Reporting the results of Regression Analysis, Evaluating the Results of Regression Analysis. Multiple Regression Analysis: The Three-Variable Model: Notation and Assumptions, Interpretation of Multiple Regression Equation, The Meaning of Partial Coefficients, OLS Estimation of the Partial Regression Coefficients, The Multiple Coefficient of Determination and the Multiple Coefficient of Correlation , and the Adjusted , Hypothesis Testing in Multiple Regression: General Comments, Hypothesis Testing about Individual Regression Coefficients, Testing the Overall Significance of the Sample Regression. Relaxing the Assumptions of the Classical Model: Multicollinearity: Meaning, Detection and Remedial Measures; Heteroscedasticity: Meaning, Detection and Remedial Measures; Autocorrelation: Meaning, Detection and Remedial Measures. Basic Texts: Lind, Marchal & Wathen, Statistical Techniques in Business and Economics. Damodar N. Gujarati and Dawn C. Porter, Basic Econometrics, 5th Edition. Reference Books: Lind, Mason, & Marchal, Basic Statistics for Business and Economics. Richard Levin & David S. Rubin, Statistics for Management. M.K. Roy and J. C. Paul, Business Statistics. R. Carter Hill, William E. Griffiths, Guay C. Lim, Principles of Econometrics, 5th Edition. Jeffrey M. Wooldridge, Introductory Econometrics: A Modern Approach, Latest Edition. Marks: 100 | Credit: 3.00 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Course Objectives: To introduce Cost Accounting as a separate branch of Accounting. To give an idea about measurement, analysis, accumulation and control of various elements of cost. To give an elementary knowledge about preparation of cost sheets. To give sufficient knowledge about preparation of financial statements of a manufacturing firm under integral and non-integral systems. Course Contents: Introduction: Manufacturing concerns; Definitions; Characteristics; Manufacturing activity; Manufacturing vs. non-manufacturing concerns; Organization structure; Producing departments and service departments; Chart of accounts; Financial statements of a manufacturing concern. Cost Accounting as a Discipline: Definition and objectives of Cost Accounting; Limitations of financial accounting; Importance of cost accounting; Cost accounting vs. financial accounting; Cost accounting vs. management accounting; Evolution of cost accounting; Cost accounting standards; Relationship of cost accounting with mathematics, economics and statistics; Methods and techniques of cost accounting; Characteristics of an ideal cost accounting system; Installation of a cost accounting system; Modern trends in cost accounting. Cost Concepts, Classification and Preparation of Cost Sheets: Concept of cost; Cost, expense, loss and asset; Classification of costs; Cost centers and cost unit; Cost object; Cost accounting cycle; Factory cost flow; Statement of cost of goods manufactured and sold; Statement of comprehensive income; BCAS 1: Cost Concepts and Classifications. Costing and Control of Materials: a) Purchasing and storing materials; Classification of materials; Accounting for materials; Inventory planning and controlling: EOQ, Safety stock and Reorder point; Material control methods; Impact of JIT on inventory accounting; Materials Requirement Planning System (MRP); Materials requisition, Materials requisition journal; Issuing materials to production. b) IAS 2 Inventories: Objectives; Scope and definitions; Measurement: Cost of inventories, Cost formulae (Specific identification methods: FIFO, Weighted average, Retail method), Net Realizable Value (NRV); Recognition as an expense; Disclosure. Costing and Control of Labor: Productivity and labor cost; Classification of labor; Labor cost records; Accounting for labor; Incentive wage plan (Straight piece work plan, 100 percent bonus plan and Group bonus plan) and Other methods (Taylor's differential piece rate, Merrick differential piece rate, Gantt task bonus system, Emerson efficiency system, Premium bonus plans, Halsey scheme, Halsey weir scheme, Rowan scheme, Barth scheme, Accelerating premium bonus etc.); Computation of total payroll and allocation of payroll costs; Special problems relating to accounting for labor: Idle time, Overtime and Fringe benefit; Labor turnover and control of labor turnover, Learning curve theory. Costing and Control of Manufacturing Overhead: Definition; Classification of overheads; Actual and predetermined factory overhead; Actual vs. normal costing; Predetermined overhead rates; Departmental vs. plant wide overhead rates; Production capacity; Analysis and disposition of under applied and over applied overhead; BCAS 4: Indirect Costs. Allocation of Manufacturing Overhead: Primary allocation of overhead: Producing department and servicing department; Bases of allocation; Secondary allocation: Service department cost; Need for cost allocation; Guidelines for cost allocation; Cost allocation methods: Direct method; Step method; Reciprocal method; Single and dual rate methods; BCAS 5: Indirect Cost Rate; BCAS 6: Support Department Cost. Selling and Administrative Overhead: Definition, Classification, Allocation, Accounting Treatment. Job Order and Batch Costing: Job Order Costing: Introduction, Main features, Advantages and disadvantages; Job costing procedure; Completing a job cost sheet; Cost control in job order system; Spoiled goods; Defective goods; Scrap materials and waste materials in a job order cost system; Batch costing: Economic Batch Quantity; BCAS 7: Job Order Costing. Text Books: Horngren, C. T., G. Foster and S. M. Datar, Cost Accounting: A Managerial Emphasis, New Delhi, Prentice-Hall India Ltd. Polimeni, Ralph S., Frank J. Fabozzi, and Arthur H. Adelberg, Cost Accounting: Concepts and Applications for Managerial Decision Making (New York: McGraw-Hill, Inc.). Reference Books: Barfield, J. T., C. A. Raiborn, and M. R. Kinney, Cost Accounting: Traditions and Innovations, Cincinnati, OH: South-Western. Usry, Milton F. and Hammer, Cost Accounting: Planning & Control (Cincinnati, Ohio: South-Western Publishing Co.). Marks: 100 | Credit: 3.00 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Course Objective: The objectives of the course are to impart knowledge among the students about the introductory concepts, conceptual framework of auditing, engagement procedures, auditing process, and audit reporting with special reference to ISAs. In addition, the course will deal with important aspects of legal, ethical, and professional responsibilities for conducting audits.Course Contents: An Introduction to Auditing and Assurance Services: Nature, definition, objectives and scope of an audit, Types of audit and auditors, The need for an audit, Definition and types of assurance services, Demand for auditing and assurance, Relationships among auditing, attestation, and assurance services, Generally Accepted Auditing Standards (GAAS). ISA 200: Overall Objectives of the Independent Auditor and the Conduct of an Audit in Accordance with International Standards on Auditing. Accepting Professional Engagement and Managing Assignments: 2.1. Explain the matters to be considered and the procedures that an audit firm/professional accountant should carry out before accepting a specified new client/engagement or continuing with an existing engagement, including: i) client acceptance; ii) engagement acceptance (new and existing engagements); iii) establish whether the preconditions for an audit are present; iv) agreeing the terms of engagement. 2.2. Recognise the key issues that underlie the agreement of the scope and terms of an engagement with a client. ISA 210: Agreeing the Terms of Audit Engagements. Basic Auditing Concepts: Risk Assessment, Materiality and Evidence: 3.1. Risk Assessment and Materiality: Fundamental concepts in conducting an audit: Materiality, audit risk and evidence; Form and components, use and limitations of the audit risk model, auditor’s risk assessment process, material misstatement, audit tests, risk assessment, concept of materiality in an audit. 3.2. Audit Evidence and Audit Documentation: Basic concepts and nature of audit evidence, sources and reliability of the types of evidence, assertions about the classes of transactions, account balances and disclosures, audit procedures and audit documentation. ISA 315 (Revised): Identifying and Assessing the Risks of Material Misstatement through Understanding the Entity and Its Environment; ISA 320: Materiality in Planning and Performing an Audit; ISA 330: The Auditor’s Responses to Assessed Risks; ISA 230: Audit Documentation; ISA 500: Audit Evidence. Planning the Audit and Understanding Internal Control: Audit Planning & Types of Audit Test: Concept and objective of audit planning, Factors of audit planning, Planning Procedures, Knowledge about the client's business, Overall audit strategy, Audit Programme, Audit Engagement Letter, Types of Audit test, Purposes and types of analytical procedures. Internal Control: Concept of internal control and accounting system, need, objectives, categories of internal control, principles of internal control, internal audit, evaluation of internal control, internal control questionnaire, and limitations of internal control. ISA 300: Planning an Audit of Financial Statements; ISA 265: Communicating Deficiencies in Internal Control to Those Charged with Governance and Management. Auditing Business Processes: Audit testing methodology, An overview and application to tests of controls, an application to substantive tests of account balance, audit sampling, Detailed audit processes of Assets, Liabilities, Income, Expenses and all types of transactions, Cash books including auditing the revenue and collection process, auditing the purchase and payment process, auditing the human resource management process, auditing the inventory management process, financing process, auditing cash, investments, fixed assets, liabilities and equities. ISA 505: External Confirmations; ISA 510: Initial Audit Engagements—Opening Balances; ISA 520: Analytical Procedures; ISA 530: Audit Sampling. Auditor’s Legal, Ethical and Professional Responsibilities: The fundamental principles of professional ethics; Threats and safeguards; professional ethical responsibilities; ICAB Code of Ethics, IFAC Code of Ethics; statutory responsibilities and rights; appointment, remuneration, resignation, removal, powers, duties, qualifications and disqualifications etc. of auditor under Companies Act, 1994; Audit regulation in Bangladesh under Financial Reporting Act (FRA), 2015 and other statutes; key responsibilities derived from International Standards on Auditing (ISAs); auditor's responsibilities defined by case laws arising from alleged negligence and related exposure and consequences. Audit Reporting: Meaning and concept of audit report, distinction between report and certificate; key concepts; opinion, true and fair view, materiality and statutory requirements; basic elements of the auditor's report; types of audit reports, qualifications in audit reports; circumstances giving rise to modified reports; limitations on scope and disagreements with management; auditor's responsibility before and after the date of the auditor's reports; management representation and other special purpose audit reporting. ISA 700 (Revised): Forming an Opinion and Reporting on Financial Statements; ISA 701: Communicating Key Audit Matters in the Independent Auditor's Report; ISA 705 (Revised): Modifications to the Opinion in the Independent Auditor's Report; ISA 706 (Revised): Emphasis of Matter Paragraphs and Other Matter Paragraphs in the Independent Auditor's Report. Basic Texts: Dr. Monjur Morshed Mahmud & Dr. Md. Salim Uddin, Contemporary Auditing and Assurance. Handbook of International Quality Control, Auditing, Review, Other Assurance, and Related Services Pronouncements, 2020 Edition, Volumes I, II, and III, Published by International Auditing and Assurance Standards Board (IAASB). William F. Messier, Steven M. Glover, Douglas F. Prawitt, Auditing and Assurance Services: A Systematic Approach, Fifth Edition. Reference Books: Taylor, Auditing: Integrated Concepts and Procedures. Study Manual on Auditing, Published by ICAB. IFAC Handbook of Auditing & Ethics Pronouncements: Latest Version. IFAC Code of Ethics for Professional Accountants: Latest Version. Institute of Chartered Accountants in England & Wales (ICAEW), 2007, Audit & Assurance Study Manual.

item.title: 4th Semester Final 2025
item.description:
(a) Construct your own definition of 'risk' and justify the conceptual boundary between risk and uncertainty.
(b) Justify the necessity of risk management in contemporary business operations. Identify at least four common organisational risks and outline the sequential stages of an effective risk management framework.
(c) Contrast pure risk with speculative risk using real-life scenarios. Show how the element of loss operates differently in each category. For each of the following risk situations, design an appropriate risk management strategy (single or combination) and defend your choice:
(a) Rahim, a 45-year-old bank manager, has a sedentary lifestyle and his father died of a heart attack at age 55.
(b) A private investment fund notices unusual volatility in the stock market that threatens its portfolio value.
(c) A software development firm discovers critical security loopholes in its client database system.
(d) A small business owner fears bankruptcy because of mounting personal loan obligations.
(e) A garment export company has three factories located in coastal areas frequently hit by cyclones and tidal surges.
(a) Explain the interrelationship between loss frequency and loss severity in risk assessment. Use examples to show how a change in one can impact the other.
(b) How can quantitative methods like probability distributions and statistical analysis be used to assess loss frequency and severity? Illustrate with an example.
(c) Discuss how changes in economic conditions such as inflation and interest rates affect the demand for insurance among individuals and organisations.
(a) Distinguish between insurance and gambling. Illustrate your answer with suitable examples, and explain why insurance is generally regarded as a socially beneficial practice, whereas gambling is not.
(b) Explain the principle of utmost good faith in insurance contracts. Why is this principle essential for maintaining trust and fairness between the insurer and the insured?
(c) Discuss the significance of the principle of "insurable interest" in insurance contracts. Illustrate your answer with suitable examples.
(d) Discuss the purpose and importance of reinsurance in the insurance industry. Explain how reinsurance enables insurance companies to manage their risk exposure effectively.
(a) Craft a precise definition of life insurance and highlight its primary mission. Show how life insurance serves as a tool for intergenerational financial security.
(b) Contrast term life, whole life, and universal life insurance on parameters such as premium structure, cash value, and suitability for different life stages.
(c) Identify the pressing challenges confronting the life insurance industry today and examine recent trends including insurtech innovations and evolving consumer expectations.
(a) Explain the concept of marine insurance and discuss its significance in international trade. Illustrate your answer with suitable examples.
(b) Discuss the key elements of a marine insurance policy. Define the following types of marine insurance policies: i. Time Policy ii. Unvalued Policy iii. Floating Policy iv. Blanket Policy v. Block Policy
(a) Enumerate and briefly characterise the diverse life insurance product categories currently operated and administered by Jiban Bima Corporation.
(b) Compose a concise analytical note on the establishment, mandate, and key functions of the Insurance Development and Regulatory Authority (IDRA) of Bangladesh.
(c) Propose a set of actionable policy measures and strategic initiatives that the Government of Bangladesh ought to adopt in order to enhance the public appeal and penetration of the insurance business.
(a) Define ethics. Identify the relationship between ethics and law.
(b) Briefly explain the importance of business ethics.
(c) Point out the relevance of globalisation for business ethics.
(a) Explain the key components of an ethical decision in business. How do individual factors, such as moral development, personal values, and cognitive biases, influence ethical decision-making?
(b) Define Sustainability and explain how the Triple Bottom Line (TBL) framework shifts the goal of a corporation from purely economic value to an extended set of social and environmental goals.
(c) A Bangladeshi tea estate owner finds that using a specific pesticide increases yield by 30% but is contaminating into local water sources used by villagers. Using the TBL framework, argue why the owner should or should not continue using the pesticide. Consider the economic benefits, social impacts, and environmental consequences in your answer.
(a) Discuss the ethical issues that arise in the firm-employee relationship. How does globalisation create additional ethical challenges for companies employing people in developing countries?
(b) Outline the core rights and duties of employees in an organisation. How does workplace discrimination violate these rights?
(c) FoodGiant is a large food and beverage company. In developing countries, it advertises sugary foods and drinks to children using cartoon characters, free toys, and school programmes. However, in developed countries, the company promotes its own products as healthy choices. At the same time, workers in FoodGiant's factories work 12 hours a day without extra pay for overtime. Employees who try to form a labour union often lose their jobs. Required: i. Identify the ethical issues related to FoodGiant's treatment of consumers and employees. ii. Explain why the company's marketing practices in developing countries can be considered a double standard. iii. Discuss whether FoodGiant's actions are socially responsible. Support your answer with reasons.
(a) Define business ethics management. Explain its components.
(b) Briefly explain the different types of ethical codes.
(c) Identify the reasons for social accounting by the organisations.
(a) How does the government function as a stakeholder in business ethics? What ethical issues typically arise in the relationship between business and government, particularly in developing economies?
(b) What is meant by 'corporate citizenship'? Discuss the relationship between viewing a business as a "key player in the regulatory game" versus a "passive rule-follower". How should corporations engage with government in an ethical manner?
(c) MegaPort Ltd. is a large port infrastructure company seeking a major government contract in a South Asian country. Company representatives paid government officials a fee to accelerate the approval process, although illegal under international anti-bribery laws. This is a common local practice. The company argues that without such payments, it cannot compete with the local firms who routinely engage in such practices. Also, it claims that the project will bring thousands of jobs and local people. Required: Analyze the ethical dimensions of MegaPort Ltd.'s conduct using the concepts of government as stakeholder, corporate citizenship, and globalisation of business-government relations. Is the 'common local practice' argument ethically valid? What systemic changes in both corporate governance and regulatory frameworks would help prevent such ethical violations?
(a) Explain the Agency Relationship between shareholders (principals) and managers (agents), identifying the roles of conflict of interest and informational asymmetry.
(b) A large multinational company seeks a hostile takeover of a traditional Bangladeshi food brand without the board's approval. Evaluate the potential impact of this takeover on employee welfare and local community identity.
(c) In a major Bangladeshi pharmaceutical firm, the CEO sold a significant volume of personal shares in the company one week before the public announcement of a failed drug trial that caused the stock price to fall by 35%. The information about the drug trial failure was known internally months before the announcement. Minority shareholders suffered major losses. Regulators launched an investigation, but the CEO argued the sale was 'planned in advance' for personal financial reasons. Required: Analyze the above case from the perspectives of (i) ethical issues in corporate governance, (ii) shareholder rights. What governance reforms should the company implement to prevent such a situation?
(a) Distinguish between Consequentialist and Non-consequentialist ethical theories. Provide one business example for each to illustrate their application.
(b) Compare and contrast egoism, Utilitarianism, and ethics of duties. Which theory do you consider most applicable to modern business decision-making and why?
(c) Nadia is the operations director of a garment factory in Chittagong. Year-end profits are strong. She faces a choice: (1) distribute a substantial bonus to all 500 workers, improving their living standards but reducing investor dividends; or (2) pay higher dividends to shareholders to retain investment for planned expansion, which may create 200 new jobs next year but provides nothing to current workers now. Some senior managers suggest a third path: allocate funds to improve safety equipment, which satisfies no one immediately but reduces accident risk in future periods. Required: Apply at least two ethical theories to evaluate each of Nadia's three options. Which course of action is most ethically defensible? Justify your reasoning.
(a) Passion works as a driving force for a successful entrepreneur. Elucidate the statement by defining Entrepreneur and Entrepreneurship.
(b) Define execution intelligence. How would you relate it with an entrepreneur?
(c) Mention some attributes of firms that pursue high levels of corporate entrepreneurship.
(d) In 1978, Ayesha Abed helped establish Aarong in Bangladesh to create sustainable income opportunities for rural artisans, especially women. At that time, many artisans struggled to find reliable markets for their handcrafted products and often faced delayed payments. Ayesha Abed recognized this problem and transformed it into an entrepreneurial opportunity by connecting rural producers with urban consumers through Aarong. Her success demonstrates several key entrepreneurial qualities. First, she showed vision by identifying an unmet market need. Second, she displayed leadership by organising thousands of artisans into a productive network. Third, she exhibited social responsibility, ensuring fair prices and employment opportunities for disadvantaged women. Finally, her perseverance and innovation helped Aarong grow from a small outlet into one of Bangladesh's leading lifestyle retail brands. Today, Aarong supports tens of thousands of artisans and serves as a successful example of how entrepreneurial qualities can create both business success and positive social impact in Bangladesh. Required: i) Which entrepreneurial quality was most important in establishing Aarong? Why? ii) How did leadership contribute to Aarong's success? iii) In what way did Aarong create social value in Bangladesh?
(a) How can finding a gap in the marketplace create a business opportunity for an entrepreneur to pursue?
(b) How does creativity contribute to the opportunity recognition process?
(c) Point out some traits that help an entrepreneur in successful opportunity recognition.
(d) In many areas of coastal Bangladesh, especially in districts such as Satkhira and Khulna, people face severe shortages of safe drinking water due to salinity in groundwater. During the dry season, families often travel long distances to collect fresh water, which consumes time and affects health and productivity. Recognising this problem, Drinkwell introduced community-based water purification systems that convert saline and contaminated water into safe drinking water. The company installs purification plants in villages and operates them through local entrepreneurs. Residents can purchase clean water at an affordable price while local operators earn income from managing the facilities. This solution addressed a significant social problem while creating a sustainable business opportunity. As a result, thousands of people gained access to safe drinking water, waterborne diseases were reduced, and local employment opportunities were created. The case demonstrates how identifying a community problem can lead to innovative entrepreneurial ventures that generate both social and economic value. Required: i) What problem did Drinkwell identify in coastal Bangladesh? ii) Why can this case be considered an entrepreneurial opportunity? iii) What innovation did the company introduce?
(a) What is the best time for a firm to develop its business model?
(b) Pathao, one of Bangladesh's leading digital platforms, emerged in 2015 as a motorcycle-based ride-sharing service at a time when Dhaka's traffic congestion was among the worst in the world. Traditional transportation—taxis, rickshaws, and buses—struggled to offer reliability or speed. Pathao introduced a disruptive business model built on smartphone connectivity, real-time matching, and a gig-based rider network. Instead of owning vehicles, Pathao empowered thousands of freelance bikers to join the platform, drastically lowering operational costs and enabling rapid scale-up. Pathao further expanded into food delivery, courier services, and digital payments through Pathao Pay, creating a multi-sided digital ecosystem. Each service disrupted a separate traditional sector: restaurant deliveries, parcel logistics, and even cash-based transactions. Its pricing transparency, quick service, and user-friendly app attracted a large urban young population, while conventional transport operators and courier companies faced declining demand and competitive pressure. By leveraging local market insights—such as acceptance of mobile payments and the widespread use of affordable smartphones—Pathao adapted global ride-sharing concepts to Bangladeshi realities. The company's disruptive approach not only redefined urban mobility but also generated income opportunities for tens of thousands of riders and delivery agents, reshaping Bangladesh's digital economy. Required: i) What made Pathao's business model disruptive in Bangladesh? ii) Which traditional industries were most affected by Pathao's expansion? iii) What local factors enabled Pathao's success in the Bangladeshi market?
(c) Briefly point out the main contents of a business plan.
(d) In 2022, three graduates from Chattogram noticed that many farmers in rural Bangladesh struggled to sell fresh vegetables at fair prices because of multiple intermediaries. At the same time, urban consumers often paid high prices for vegetables that were not always fresh. Seeing this gap, the entrepreneurs developed a business plan for Aamra Fresh Agro, a startup that would connect farmers directly with consumers through a mobile app and delivery network. The business plan included a market analysis showing increasing demand for safe and fresh food in major cities such as Dhaka and Chattogram. The founders estimated an initial investment of BDT 15 lakh for app development, cold-storage facilities, and delivery vehicles. Revenue would come from a commission on each sale and subscription packages for regular customers. The plan identified potential risks, including transportation delays, seasonal fluctuations in production, and competition from established online grocery platforms. To address these challenges, the entrepreneurs planned partnerships with local farmer cooperatives and logistics providers. They also projected that the business would break even within three years if monthly sales grew by 10%. After presenting the business plan to investors, the startup secured seed funding and launched operations. Within the first year, it supplied fresh vegetables to more than 2,000 households and increased participating farmers' incomes by approximately 20%. Required: i) What were the main sources of revenue for Aamra Fresh Agro? ii) What risks were identified in the business plan?
(a) What are the prerequisites for building a strong ethical culture in a firm?
(b) Define the concept liability of newness. What can a new venture do to overcome the liability of newness?
(c) Why does having relevant industry experience help the founder of a firm to be successful?
(d) FreshBrew is a mobile coffee truck business started by college friends Mia and Arif. They noticed many commuters near their city's business district lacked quick access to quality coffee. After securing a small investor, they launched the truck and hired an assistant manager. Although they had a great product, the business struggled. Customers sometimes waited too long, and social media feedback was slow. Mia realised that they needed more help with operations and marketing to grow. They also felt inexperienced running a business and had no credible reputation with suppliers yet. Mia and Arif invited two industry advisors with café experience to join their team to help with training and supplier contracts. Required: i. What concept explains FreshBrew's early struggles because the founders lacked experience and reputation? ii. Why might adding industry advisors help FreshBrew? iii. What is the benefit of having more than one founder or team member?
(a) Define acquisition with an example. Why do acquisitions fail sometimes?
(b) What challenges do second-generation entrepreneurs face when taking over established family business?
(c) Amena Akter, a resident of Cumilla, started a small online clothing business in 2019. She sold traditional Bangladeshi dresses through social media and initially operated from her home with a small amount of personal savings. Her products gained popularity among local customers, and she planned to expand her business by opening a boutique and hiring employees. However, Amena faced several challenges common to many women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh. One major challenge was limited access to finance. Banks often required collateral and lengthy documentation, which made it difficult for her to obtain a business loan. She also encountered social barriers, as some family and community members believed that women should prioritise household responsibilities over business activities. Another challenge was balancing family and business commitments. As a mother of two children, Amena had to manage household duties while handling customer orders, supplier negotiations, and marketing activities. Additionally, she faced difficulties in building professional networks, which are often crucial for obtaining business information and opportunities. The COVID-19 pandemic further disrupted her business by reducing customer demand and creating supply-chain problems. Despite these obstacles, Amena adapted by increasing her online marketing efforts, offering home delivery services, and participating in entrepreneurship training programmes organised by local support organisations. Today, her business employs six women and serves customers across Bangladesh. Amena's story demonstrates both the significant challenges faced by women entrepreneurs and their ability to overcome barriers through resilience, innovation, and determination. Required: i) What financial challenge did Amena face? ii) What social barrier affected her business growth? iii) How did family responsibilities impact her entrepreneurship? iv) What strategies helped her overcome challenges?
(a) Identify the keys to effective new product development. Explain the common reasons new products fail.
(b) Explain the difference between internal growth strategies and external growth strategies.
(c) Explain "licensing" and how it can be used as a growth strategy.
(a) Explain why most new ventures need to raise money at some point during their early life?
(b) Identify the three steps involved in properly preparing to raise debt or equity financing.
(c) Explain why an initial public offering is an important milestone for a firm.
(d) Explain the advantages of leasing for an entrepreneurial firm.
(a) Define organisational behaviour. What is the importance of interpersonal skills in the workplace?
(b) Describe the major behavioural science disciplines that contribute to Organisational Behaviour.
(c) Why might the same Organisational Behaviour concept succeed in one organisation but fail in another? Analyze using any two challenges and two opportunities managers face in applying Organisational Behaviour concepts.
(a) A software company needs to hire for a programming role, while a construction company needs to hire for a heavy equipment operator role. Analyse which type of ability (intellectual or physical) is more critical for each role and why.
(b) What are biographical characteristics? Identify and explain how they affect Organisational Behaviour.
(c) What causes job satisfaction? Compare the relative importance of pay versus the work itself.
(a) What are the three components of attitude? How can managers use an understanding of attitudes to predict employee behaviour?
(b) What is Emotional Labour? Distinguish between surface acting and deep acting with examples from a customer service job.
(c) GreenMart Superstore employs a large team of cashiers and customer service representatives. In the past six months, management noticed rising absenteeism, customer complaints, and employee turnover. Exit interviews revealed employees felt unappreciated, emotionally exhausted, and dissatisfied with their work. Several employees stated they had to 'fake smiles' all day despite dealing with rude customers and heavy workloads. Required: i. Which major job attitudes—job satisfaction, organisational commitment, or employee engagement—seem most affected at GreenMart? Explain with reference to the case. ii. How can the concept of Emotional Intelligence (EI) help GreenMart's supervisors reduce employee burnout and improve morale?
(a) Briefly describe the Big Five Personality Model. Which trait do you think is most important for a manager in Bangladesh's business environment? Justify your answer.
(b) What is perception? Explain any three common perceptual shortcuts (biases) that managers should be aware of when evaluating employees.
(c) What is the link between perception and individual decision making? How can organisational constraints affect decisions?
(a) What is a group? Explain the stages of group development in your own words.
(b) What is the difference between a work group and a work team? What are the key characteristics of an effective team?
(c) BDCom Networks formed a cross-functional project team to develop a new billing system. The team consists of members from IT, Finance, and Customer Service departments. In the first few weeks, members were polite but uncertain about roles. By the second month, open conflicts arose over who should lead. Members from different departments argued about priorities, and the project fell behind schedule. Required: i. At which stage of group development is this team currently? Justify your answer using evidence from the case. ii. As the team leader, suggest two specific actions you would take to move the team to the 'Norming' or 'Performing' stage.
(a) Why is leadership important in organisations? Briefly distinguish between charismatic leadership and transformational leadership.
(b) Define power. What are the five bases of power explored in the text? Which base of power is most sustainable in the long run, and why?
(c) Mr. X was recently promoted to Factory Manager at DynaFab Ltd. He noticed that several senior workers ignored his instructions but quickly obeyed orders from the previous manager, who had worked at DynaFab for 20 years. Mr. X relies mostly on his formal authority (position) to gain compliance, but the results have been poor. Workers seem to respect only those they consider experienced and trustworthy. Required: i. Which type of power is Mr. X relying on, and which power bases does the previous manager likely possess? Use the case to support your answer. ii. What advice would you give Mr. X to build a more effective power base and gain genuine influence over his team?
(a) Define conflict. Explain the five stages of the conflict process as described in the textbook.
(b) What is organisational change? What are the most common reasons employees resist change? Suggest two ways managers can overcome resistance.
(c) MegaBank recently merged with a smaller bank. Following the merger, employees experienced role ambiguity, fear of job loss, increased workloads, and poor communication from management. Many employees began reporting headaches, insomnia, and reduced concentration. Absenteeism rose by 30%. A group of senior tellers refused to adopt the new software system, causing operational delays. Required: i. Identify at least two sources of stress (organisational and personal) that MegaBank employees are experiencing. What consequences of stress are visible in this case? ii. As an HR consultant, recommend one individual-level and one organisational-level strategy to help MegaBank manage stress effectively during this change.
(a) Write a brief on the history of Bangladesh mentioning Pakistan movement and the birth of Pakistan, language movement (1948-1952), Juktafront election of 1954, six points programme of 1966, mass upsurge of 1969, election of 1970 and birth of Bangladesh in 1971.
(b) What do you know about the constitution of Bangladesh? Discuss the features of constitution-1972 of people's republic of Bangladesh.
(c) Discuss the judiciary system of Bangladesh.
(a) Discuss the characteristics of Bangladesh economy. What are the reasons for underdevelopment of Bangladesh?
(b) Mention the main cottage industries in Bangladesh. What role small and cottage industries can play for a developing country like Bangladesh?
(c) What are the features of the population of Bangladesh? Discuss the impact of overpopulation on the Bangladesh economy.
(a) Is economic development means economic growth? How can you measure the Human Development Index (HDI)? Briefly discuss the factors that determine economic growth.
(b) Explain the Kuznets hypothesis of economic growth and income distribution. What are the causes of increase in income inequality with economic development?
(c) What do you mean by sustainable development? Briefly discuss the sustainable development goals.
(a) What is poverty? Discuss the poverty alleviation programme of different organisations in Bangladesh.
(b) Write a brief on the 8th five-year plan of Bangladesh.
(c) What do you mean by micro credit? Do you think that microcredit programme can reduce poverty in Bangladesh? Discuss the major activities of NGOs.
(a) What drives economic development according to Schumpeter? Discuss the salient features of Schumpeter model of economic development.
(b) What is the big push theory? Why is big push needed in a less developed country?
(c) Discuss the theories of balanced and unbalanced growth. Which model do you support to be applicable for developing countries like Bangladesh?
(a) How capital formation can be a measure of economic development of Bangladesh? Discuss the sources of capital formation.
(b) Discuss the theory of demographic transition in economic development with criticism. Bangladesh in what part of this theory?
(c) "A strong agricultural economy brings social progress" – Do you agree? Explain your view.
(a) Give a comparison between developed and developing countries. What lessons do you learn from developed countries for Bangladesh?
(b) Discuss the traditional theory of free trade with regard to its effects on a country's development.
(c) What measures encourage economic integration among developing countries? Discuss the benefits from and problems of economic integration.

item.title: Solutions
item.description: Definition of Risk and the Boundary with Uncertainty Risk: Risk is the uncertainty concerning the occurrence of a loss. It can also be defined in a specific sense as the relative variation of actual loss from expected loss. Boundary: The conceptual boundary lies in the measurability of probability. Risk applies to situations where the probabilities of possible outcomes are known or can be estimated with accuracy (e.g., mortality rates). Uncertainty applies to situations where such probabilities cannot be calculated or estimated (e.g., the probability of a home being hit by a meteorite). Necessity of Risk Management and Effective Framework Necessity: It is essential to ensure the survival of the firm, maintain stability of earnings, and meet legal obligations. It reduces the "cost of risk," which maximizes business value by lowering expected losses and reducing the fear associated with catastrophic events. Common Organisational Risks: (1) Price Risk (fluctuations in commodity/currency prices); (2) Credit Risk (customer default); (3) Liability Risk (lawsuits); and (4) Property Risk (damage to assets). Framework Stages: Identify all significant loss exposures. Measure and Analyze the frequency and severity of these exposures. Select Techniques: Choose a combination of Risk Control (avoidance, prevention) and Risk Financing (retention, transfer/insurance). Implement and Monitor the program for ongoing suitability. Pure Risk vs. Speculative Risk Pure Risk: Only the possibilities of loss or no loss exist (e.g., a dwelling fire). The element of loss is absolute; society is generally harmed because wealth is destroyed without offsetting gains. Speculative Risk: Either profit or loss is possible (e.g., investing in the stock market). Here, the element of loss can be socially beneficial; for instance, a firm failing due to a new competitor’s cheaper technology still results in lower costs for society. Rahim (Sedentary lifestyle/Family history): Loss Prevention combined with Life Insurance. Defense: Prevention (lifestyle changes/medical check-ups) reduces the high-frequency/high-severity health hazard, while Life Insurance transfers the catastrophic financial impact of premature death to an insurer. Investment Fund (Market volatility): Hedging with Financial Derivatives. Defense: Volatility is a speculative price risk; hedging (e.g., put options) provides an offsetting profit when market values decline, protecting the portfolio's net value. Software Firm (Security loopholes): Loss Prevention and Cyber Liability Insurance. Defense: Prevention ("hardening" networks) lowers the probability of a breach, while specialized insurance handles the potentially ruinous legal liability and restoration costs associated with data theft. Small Business Owner (Bankruptcy fear): Incorporation. Defense: Incorporation is a non-insurance transfer that limits the owner’s legal liability, shielding personal assets from business creditors. Garment Company (Coastal factories): Separation and Specialized Property Insurance. Defense: Separation (multiple locations) ensures that a single event does not destroy all capacity. Specialized catastrophe insurance provides recovery funds for the unavoidable high-severity losses caused by cyclones. Loss Frequency vs. Loss Severity Relationship: They generally share an inverse relationship. Frequency is the number of losses in a period; Severity is the size of each loss. High-frequency losses are usually low-severity (e.g., shoplifting), while low-frequency events often have high severity (e.g., plane crashes). A change in frequency (via loss prevention) can reduce total annual losses even if the severity of a single hit remains high. Quantitative Assessment Methods Methods: Probability distributions (like the normal distribution) use historical data to find the mean (expected loss) and standard deviation (risk/variability). Example: An actuary analyzing 10,000 homes knows that if 1% burn annually, the expected loss is 100 homes. Using the Law of Large Numbers, as the sample size increases, objective risk (variation) decreases, making predictions more accurate. Economic Conditions (Inflation and Interest Rates) Inflation: Increases the demand for higher policy limits as the cost of repairing property or paying medical claims rises. Interest Rates: Rising rates can lower premiums through cash flow underwriting (where investment income offsets underwriting losses). However, they also create interest rate risk for insurers' bond portfolios, which may eventually lead to a "hard" market with higher premiums. Insurance vs. Gambling Difference: Insurance handles already existing pure risk; gambling creates a new speculative risk. Social Benefit: Insurance is socially beneficial because it provides financial stability, enhances credit, and serves as a source of investment funds. Gambling is unproductive as the winner's gain comes solely at the loser's expense without restoring the loser's position. Principle of Utmost Good Faith Definition: It requires all parties to a contract to act with total honesty and disclose all material facts. Importance: It is essential for trust because insurers cannot personally verify every detail of an applicant’s life or property; it prevents adverse selection and ensures fairness in premium pricing. Principle of Insurable Interest Significance: The insured must be in a position to lose financially if the event occurs; this prevents insurance from becoming a wagering contract. Examples: A person has an insurable interest in their own home; a bank in a mortgaged property; or a business partner in the life of another partner. Reinsurance Purpose: Reinsurance is the transfer of insurance from a primary insurer (ceding company) to another insurer (reinsurer). Importance: It allows companies to increase underwriting capacity, stabilize profits, and protect against catastrophic losses (clash losses) that exceed their retention limits. Life Insurance and Intergenerational Security Definition: A contract where the insurer, in exchange for a premium, pays a fixed sum upon the death of the insured or at the end of a specified period. Mission: To provide protection against the financial consequences of premature death and to provide income for old age. Intergenerational Tool: It provides intergenerational security by ensuring that a family head’s unfulfilled financial obligations (e.g., child education, mortgage) are met, allowing wealth and opportunity to persist despite the breadwinner's death. Term vs. Whole Life vs. Universal Life Term: Level or decreasing death benefit; no cash value; lowest premium; suitable for young families with limited income or temporary needs. Whole Life: Lifetime protection; guaranteed cash values; fixed level premiums; suitable for lifelong estate planning. Universal Life: Separates protection and savings; flexible premiums; cash value earns interest (market-linked with a guaranteed minimum); suitable for those needing adjustable benefits. Challenges and Trends Challenges: Volatile interest rates, market saturation in developed regions, and rising management expenses. Trends: Insurtech (digital marketing/underwriting), Unit-Linked Insurance Plans (ULIPs) which shift investment risk to the policyholder, and a shift toward micro-life insurance for low-income segments. Marine Insurance in International Trade Concept: Covers losses incident to a marine adventure, including damage to ships (Hull), goods (Cargo), and loss of earnings (Freight). Significance: It is the backbone of global trade, providing indemnity against "perils of the sea" (collision, sinking, piracy). Example: Insuring a shipment of computers from one port to another. Types of Marine Insurance Policies i. Time Policy: Covers the risk for a specific period of time rather than a specific voyage. ii. Unvalued Policy: The value of the property is not fixed at inception; the claim is based on the market value at the time of loss. iii. Floating Policy: Covers multiple shipments under one sum; details of each shipment are declared later. iv. Blanket Policy: Covers varied property in a particular time and place for a fixed premium, often with a year-end adjustment based on actual risk. v. Block Policy: Provides very broad "all-risk" coverage for specific trade inventories (e.g., jewelers' block) whether on premises or in transit. Jiban Bima Corporation (JBC) Product Categories JBC operates diverse schemes including Whole Life, Endowment (the most popular), Double Endowment, Marriage Endowment, Educational Annuity, Limited Payment Endowment, and Money Back Policies. Note on IDRA Bangladesh Establishment: Created by the Insurance Regulatory and Development Authority Act, 1999. Mandate: To regulate the insurance industry to ensure solvency, fair play, and the protection of policyholders' interests. Key Functions: Licensing new insurers, approving product pricing/wording, monitoring solvency margins, and regulating market conduct to prevent fraud. Proposed Government Policy Measures Strategic Initiatives: Implement mandatory insurance for high-risk public sectors like commercial transport and industrial construction. Promote Microinsurance by supporting NGOs and Self-Help Groups to reach the low-income population. Develop Public-Private Partnerships for catastrophe and agricultural crop insurance to manage national-level disaster risks. Enforce stricter transparency norms and corporate governance to restore public trust and ensure prompt claim settlements. Launch nationwide insurance awareness campaigns focusing on the "Risk and Safety" (Yogakshema) benefits of coverage. Definition of Ethics & Relationship with Law Definition of Ethics: Ethics is the study of business situations, activities, and decisions where issues of right and wrong are addressed. Relationship between Ethics and Law: Ethics begins where the law ends, covering "grey areas" where legal rules are silent or values are in conflict. Importance of Business Ethics It is crucial for mitigating potential harm to stakeholders, restoring public trust, and addressing the increasing power and influence of business in society. Relevance of Globalisation Globalisation deterritorializes economic activities, allowing them to escape the control of national governments and necessitating global ethical standards. Ethical Decision Components and Individual Factors Key Components of an Ethical Decision: An ethical decision is characterized by choice, significant effects on others, and the perception of the issue as ethically relevant by at least one party. Influence of Individual Factors: Factors such as cognitive moral development determine an individual's reasoning process, while personal values and cognitive biases shape what they perceive as "preferable" conduct. Sustainability and TBL Sustainability: Meeting present needs without compromising future generations. The Triple Bottom Line (TBL): Shifts corporate goals from purely economic value to a balanced focus on People, Planet, and Profit. Tea Estate Case Under the TBL framework, the owner should not continue using the pesticide; while it offers a 30% economic gain, it fails the environmental pillar (water contamination) and the social pillar (harm to villager health). Firm-Employee Relationship & Globalisation Firm-Employee Relationship: Ethical issues include discrimination, privacy breaches, and the struggle for fair wages. Globalisation: Complicates this by creating a "race to the bottom" where multinationals exploit lower standards in developing countries. Employee Rights and Duties Core Rights and Duties: Core rights include freedom from discrimination, privacy, and fair wages, while duties include complying with contracts and respecting employer property. Workplace Discrimination: Violates these rights by denying equal opportunity based on irrelevant characteristics. FoodGiant Case: i. Ethical Issues: Targeted marketing to vulnerable children (consumers) and exploitative working hours without overtime pay or union rights (employees). ii. Double Standard: The company promotes "healthy choices" in developed markets while exploiting lack of regulation to sell sugary products to children in developing ones. iii. Social Responsibility: These actions are not socially responsible because they fail to respect the long-term well-being of stakeholders for short-term gain. Business Ethics Management Definition: This is the formal or informal attempt to manage ethical issues through specific policies and programmes. Components: Include codes of ethics, reporting channels, and risk analysis. Types of Ethical Codes These include corporate codes of conduct, professional codes, and industry-wide codes. Reasons for Social Accounting Organizations engage in this to respond to stakeholder pressure, enhance transparency, and improve internal accountability. Government as Stakeholder Function: Government defines the "licence to operate" for businesses. Ethical Issues: In developing economies, issues like "state capture"—where private firms influence regulation through illicit payments—are common. Corporate Citizenship and Engagement Corporate Citizenship: This views the firm as a political actor governing citizens' rights. Roles: A "key player" actively shapes the regulatory game to its advantage, while a "passive rule-follower" merely complies with existing laws. MegaPort Ltd. Case: Analysis: Bribery to accelerate approvals is ethically invalid; it violates the principles of fair competition and corporate integrity. Systemic Changes: Stricter transparency, independent auditing, and international enforcement are required to prevent such ethical violations. Agency Relationship Shareholders are principals who hire managers as agents. Conflict arises from diverging interests (e.g., profit vs. high pay), while informational asymmetry leaves shareholders with less knowledge than managers. Hostile Takeovers These can devastate employee welfare through layoffs and erode local community identity by relocating traditional brands. Pharma CEO Share Sale: Analysis: This is a case of insider trading, violating shareholder rights to fairness and information. Governance Reforms: Should include mandatory "blackout" periods for executive trading and stricter internal controls. Ethical Theories Consequentialist theories (e.g., Utilitarianism) judge actions by their outcomes. Non-consequentialist theories (e.g., Ethics of Duties) focus on underlying principles. Egoism vs. Utilitarianism vs. Duties Egoism: Focuses on self-interest. Utilitarianism: Seeks the "greatest good for the greatest number". Utilitarianism is most common in business due to its alignment with cost-benefit analysis. Ethics of Duties: Focuses on universal moral laws. Nadia’s Factory Choice: Distributing a bonus is defensible via Feminist Ethics (prioritizing relationships/care), while investing in safety equipment is most defensible via Ethics of Duty (treating workers as ends in themselves by ensuring long-term safety). Definitions and Passion: An entrepreneur is a person who creates a new venture and undertakes the risk of starting an enterprise by putting an idea into practice. Entrepreneurship is the process of pursuing opportunities and turning an idea into a business without regard to resources currently controlled. Passion is the number one characteristic of successful entrepreneurs, acting as the driving force that sustains the business through tough times. Execution Intelligence: It is the ability to fashion a solid idea into a viable business by developing a business model, assembling a team, and managing finances. It relates to an entrepreneur as the factor that often determines start-up success through translating creativity and imagination into measurable results. Attributes of Corporate Entrepreneurship: Include being proactive, innovative, and risk-taking. Aarong Case: i) Vision was most important, as she identified an unmet market need by connecting rural artisans with reliable markets. ii) Leadership allowed for organizing thousands of artisans into a productive network. iii) Aarong created social value by ensuring fair prices and employment opportunities for disadvantaged rural women. Marketplace Gap: Gaps in the marketplace are business opportunities created when products or services that consumers need aren't available at all or in a specific location. Entrepreneurs create value by identifying these underserved niches within larger markets. Creativity in Opportunity Recognition: Creativity is the process of generating novel or useful ideas. It allows entrepreneurs to recognize opportunity gaps—the difference between what's available and what's possible—and turn them into business concepts. Traits for Opportunity Recognition: Prior industry experience, cognitive factors such as entrepreneurial alertness, social networks, and creativity. Drinkwell Case: i) Drinkwell identified severe shortages of safe drinking water caused by salinity in groundwater in coastal districts. ii) This is an entrepreneurial opportunity because it addressed a major social and health problem while creating a sustainable business model where local operators earn income. iii) The company introduced community-based water purification systems that convert contaminated water into affordable, safe drinking water through plants operated by local entrepreneurs. Best Time for Business Model: The best time for a firm to develop its business model is following the initial validation of the business idea but prior to fleshing out the operational details of the company. Pathao Case: i) Pathao's business model was disruptive because it used a gig-based rider network and real-time matching via smartphone connectivity to lower costs and scale rapidly without owning vehicles. ii) Affected industries included taxis, rickshaws, buses, restaurant deliveries, parcel logistics, and cash-based transactions. iii) Local factors included Dhaka's extreme traffic congestion, widespread affordable smartphone use, and the local acceptance of mobile payments. Main Contents of a Business Plan: Executive Summary, Industry Analysis, Company Description, Market Analysis, The Economics of the Business, Marketing Plan, Design and Development Plan, Operations Plan, Management Team and Company Structure, Overall Schedule, and Financial Projections. Aamra Fresh Agro Case: i) Revenue sources were commissions on each sale and subscription packages for regular customers. ii) Identified risks included transportation delays, seasonal fluctuations in production, and competition from established online grocery platforms. Ethical Culture Prerequisites: Prerequisites for a strong ethical culture include leaders leading by example, establishing a formal code of conduct, and implementing ethics training programs. Liability of Newness: Liability of newness refers to the fact that new companies often falter because the people involved can't adjust quickly enough to their new roles and the firm lacks a track record of success. A new venture can overcome this by assembling a talented management team and recruiting high-quality advisors to gain legitimacy. Industry Experience: Relevant industry experience provides founders with better-established professional networks, more applicable marketing and management skills, and a deeper understanding of industry subtleties. FreshBrew Case: i. Liability of newness explains their struggles, as they lacked the experience and reputation needed with suppliers and customers. ii. Industry advisors help FreshBrew with specialized tasks like training and negotiating supplier contracts while providing legitimacy. iii. A benefit of multiple founders is that a team provides greater resources, a broader diversity of viewpoints, and psychological support compared to a sole individual. Acquisition: Acquisition is the outright purchase of one firm by another, such as Walmart buying Moosejaw. They fail sometimes due to a clash of corporate cultures, incompatible business processes, and increased business complexity. Second-Generation Challenges: Challenges for second-generation entrepreneurs include non-participating family members, family emotions, family versus business conflicts, defining authority, and the "fair to all" approach to profit-sharing. Amena Akter Case: i) Amena faced the financial challenge of limited access to finance due to bank requirements for collateral and lengthy documentation. ii) The social barrier was the belief that women should prioritize household responsibilities over business. iii) Family responsibilities required her to balance household duties and childcare with supplier negotiations and marketing. iv) Strategies included increasing online marketing, offering home delivery services, and participating in entrepreneurship training programs. New Product Development: Keys to effective NPD include finding an unfilled need, developing products that add value, getting quality and pricing right, and focusing on a specific target market. Common reasons for failure are overestimating market potential, poor design, inadequate feasibility analysis, bad timing, and poor service. Internal vs. External Growth: Internal growth strategies rely on efforts generated within the firm itself, such as new product development or geographic expansion. External growth strategies rely on third-party relationships, including mergers, acquisitions, strategic alliances, joint ventures, and licensing. Licensing as a Growth Strategy: Licensing is granting permission for another firm to use proprietary rights to a product or process in exchange for royalties. As a growth strategy, it enables firms to expand their reach and earn income with low capital investment by leveraging others' manufacturing or distribution capabilities. Need for Capital: New ventures need to raise money to manage cash flow challenges (lag between spending and sales), fund capital investments (equipment/facilities), and support lengthy product development cycles. Steps to Raise Financing: Three steps for raising debt or equity: 1. Determine precisely how much money is needed; 2. Determine the most appropriate type of financing; 3. Develop a strategy for engaging potential investors or bankers. IPO as a Milestone: An IPO is a milestone because it raises equity capital, increases public profile, provides a liquidity event for investors, and creates currency (stock) for future acquisitions. Advantages of Leasing: Advantages of leasing include the ability to acquire assets with little or no down payment, which preserves cash for other operational needs. Introduction to OB and Interpersonal Skills: Definition of OB: A field of study investigating the impact that individuals, groups, and structure have on behavior within organisations to apply such knowledge toward improving effectiveness. Importance of Interpersonal Skills: Determines managerial effectiveness and career advancement. Helps organisations attract and retain high-performing employees. Strongly associated with employee job satisfaction and reduced stress/turnover. Major Contributing Disciplines: Psychology: Focuses on individual behavior (learning, personality, emotions, perception). Social Psychology: Blends psychology and sociology to focus on influence and change. Sociology: Studies people in relation to their social environment or culture. Anthropology: Studies societies to learn about fundamental values and national cultures. Concept Success vs. Failure (Analysis): Challenge 1: Continuing Globalization: Concepts must adapt to differing cultural norms (e.g., what motivates in one culture may not in another). Challenge 2: Workforce Diversity: Managers must adapt to heterogeneous characteristics (age, gender, race) that shape distinct preferences for rewards and communication. Opportunity 1: Positive Work Environments: Using OB to develop human strengths and foster vitality. Opportunity 2: Big Data/AI: Leveraging data to define objectives and test theories for more effective decision-making. Software vs. Construction Ability Analysis: Programming (Software): Requires Intellectual Ability—mental capacities for thinking, reasoning, and problem-solving (e.g., number aptitude, verbal comprehension). Heavy Equipment Operator (Construction): Requires Physical Ability—capacity for tasks demanding stamina, dexterity, and strength. Biographical Characteristics: Objective personal characteristics—such as age, gender, race, and ethnicity—easily obtained from personnel records. Effect on OB: They represent "surface-level diversity" that may activate stereotypes or influence turnover, absenteeism, and perceived fairness. Causes of Job Satisfaction: Intrinsic Factors: Interesting work, training, variety, autonomy, and social support. Pay vs. Work Itself: Pay correlates with satisfaction only up to a point of financial comfort. The intrinsic nature of the work itself is a much stronger long-term predictor of satisfaction. Components of Attitude and Predicting Behaviour: Three Components of Attitude: Cognitive (The belief or opinion segment), Affective (The emotional or feeling segment), Behavioral (The intention to behave in a certain way). Predicting Behaviour: Managers use attitudes (like job satisfaction) as the best single predictors of outcomes like performance, absenteeism, and turnover. Emotional Labour: An employee’s expression of organizationally desired emotions during interpersonal transactions. Surface Acting: Hiding inner feelings and forgoing emotional expressions (e.g., a cashier smiling despite being berated by a rude customer). Deep Acting: Trying to modify inner true feelings based on display rules (e.g., a customer service rep empathizing with a caller’s frustration to feel genuine care). GreenMart Case Analysis: i. Affected Attitudes: Job Satisfaction (dissatisfied/unappreciated) and Employee Engagement (checked out/emotional exhaustion). ii. Role of Emotional Intelligence (EI): EI helps supervisors detect and manage emotional cues. High EI can improve morale and reduce burnout by facilitating better teamwork and reducing counterproductive behaviors. Big Five Personality Model: Traits: Conscientiousness (Responsible, dependable), Emotional Stability (Calm, secure), Extroversion (Sociable, assertive), Openness to Experience (Creative, curious), Agreeableness (Cooperative, trusting). Manager in Bangladesh: Conscientiousness is the best overall predictor of job performance. However, in a collectivist culture like Bangladesh, Agreeableness may be more important for fostering organizational commitment and team harmony. Perception and Shortcuts: Perception is how individuals organize and interpret sensory impressions to give meaning to their environment. Halo/Horns Effect: Drawing a general impression based on a single characteristic. Contrast Effect: Evaluation affected by comparisons with recently encountered people. Stereotyping: Judging someone based on the perception of the group they belong to. Perception/Decision-Making Link: Decisions are choices among alternatives; perception determines which data are screened and interpreted as "relevant". Organizational Constraints: Performance evaluation systems, reward systems, formal regulations, and time constraints all limit choices and bias decisions.
