Technical aspects encompass the technological frameworks, digital architectures, production mechanisms, and data systems that empower contemporary ventures to create, deliver, and capture value.High-speed broadband, ubiquitous smartphone penetration, and cloud computing architectures serve as the backbone of modern entrepreneurship. These technologies lower administrative costs, allow startups to scale operational capacity on demand, and dismantle geographic boundaries, enabling micro-multinationals to run efficiently from day one.Integrated digital commerce platforms paired with localized payment gateways create an automated transaction environment. In developing financial landscapes, the expansion of Mobile Financial Services (MFS) and secure digital payment systems mitigates transaction friction, enhances cash flow velocity, and builds consumer trust during distant transactions.The accessibility of Computer-Aided Design (CAD) software, 3D printing, and automated, small-scale machinery allows entrepreneurs to engage in rapid prototyping and flexible production. Startups can bypass the heavy capital expenditures historically demanded by large-scale manufacturing facilities, achieving cost-effective customization and shorter time-to-market.Modern computational tools enable small businesses to harvest and interpret granular consumer behavior data. By deploying Customer Relationship Management (CRM) engines and AI-driven market analytics, entrepreneurs optimize supply chains, predict shifting demand trends, and execute highly targeted digital marketing campaigns with superior return on ad spend.The entrepreneurship cycle constitutes a continuous, iterative progression through which a venture moves from an abstract concept to an established market entity. It is governed by four foundational principles:The cycle initiates not merely with an idea, but with the systematic identification of a commercially viable opportunity. This involves matching an unaddressed market problem, inefficiency, or consumer pain point with a scalable, value-driven solution.Entrepreneurs must assemble, coordinate, and leverage critical human, financial, and physical assets. A core principle here is financial boot-strapping and strategic resource-leveraging—controlling necessary resources without necessarily owning them outright during the initial stages to minimize overhead.This phase demands converting the value proposition into an operational business structure. It encompasses drafting a flexible business model, establishing compliance with legal and regulatory frameworks, and launching a Minimum Viable Product (MVP) to test true consumer demand.The final principle dictates that the cycle is never static. Based on market signals, competitive countermoves, and financial indicators, the management team must continuously iterate, pivot, or scale operations. Profits are systematically re-invested into organizational learning and capability development to sustain competitive advantage or prepare for a successful harvest/exit.

item.title: ED 2019 Exam Q1
item.description: Definitions of an Entrepreneur: According to Joseph Schumpeter (1934): "Entrepreneurs are innovators who use the process of shattering the status quo of existing products and services, to set up new products, new methods of production, to open new markets, or to reorganize an industry." According to Richard Cantillon (1755): "An entrepreneur is an agent who buys factors of production at certain prices in order to combine them into a product with a view to selling it at uncertain prices in the future, thereby assuming the inherent operational risks." Definitions of Entrepreneurship: According to Howard Stevenson (Harvard Business School): "Entrepreneurship is the pursuit of opportunity without regard to resources currently controlled." According to Robert D. Hisrich: "Entrepreneurship is the process of creating something new with value by devoting the necessary time and effort, assuming the accompanying financial, psychic, and social risks, and receiving the resulting rewards of monetary and personal satisfaction." Successful entrepreneurs exhibit a distinct blend of psychological traits, technical skills, and behavioral characteristics that enable them to navigate market uncertainties. The primary qualities include: Passion for the Business: This is the ultimate driving force behind any entrepreneurial venture. It sustains the entrepreneur through periods of financial hardship, operational bottlenecks, and skepticism from external stakeholders. Product/Customer Focus: A successful entrepreneur understands that a business exists to satisfy customer needs. They exhibit a keen focus on product quality, utility, and superior customer experience over purely financial or administrative tasks. Tenacity Despite Failure: Because entrepreneurs try new things, the failure rate is naturally high. Tenacity means having the resilience to treat setbacks, rejections, and commercial failures as critical learning opportunities rather than terminal endpoints. Execution Intelligence: The ability to convert a conceptual idea into a viable corporate reality. This involves strategic planning, resource mobilization, assembling a functional team, and managing day-to-day operations effectively. Calculated Risk-Taking: Contrary to the popular myth that entrepreneurs are reckless gamblers, successful entrepreneurs systematically evaluate risks, mitigate potential downsides, and avoid situations with absolute uncertainty. Creativity and Innovativeness: The capacity to look at traditional problems and formulate novel, value-adding solutions, whether through a unique business model, resource utilization, or process optimization. Entrepreneurship development acts as a catalyst for socio-economic transformation in a developing country like Bangladesh. Its core significance can be understood through the following dimensions: Employment Generation: Bangladesh faces a high youth unemployment and underemployment rate. Entrepreneurship development shifts the population paradigm from "job seekers" to "job creators," providing employment opportunities across urban and rural landscapes. Poverty Alleviation and Economic Growth: The growth of Micro, Small, and Medium Enterprises (MSMEs) distributes wealth directly to the grassroots level. It increases the per capita income, expanding the country's Gross Domestic Product (GDP). Resource Mobilization: Entrepreneurs utilize local, unexploited resources, such as agricultural products, native craftsmanship (e.g., Nakshi Kantha, Jamdani), and indigenous raw materials, converting them into high-value commercial goods. Export Promotion and Import Substitution: Developing entrepreneurial ventures reduces the country's reliance on foreign goods by creating domestic alternatives. Simultaneously, innovative startups expand the nation's export portfolio beyond traditional Readymade Garments (RMG). Reduction of Regional Disparity: Industrial concentration is heavily skewed toward major metropolitan hubs like Dhaka and Chittagong. Developing localized rural entrepreneurship helps decentralize economic power and modernizes agrarian areas. At the individual level, aspiring and nascent entrepreneurs face several distinct bottlenecks that hinder their growth and sustainability: Lack of Managerial Knowledge and Formal Training: Many individuals possess creative ideas but lack technical expertise in basic business fundamentals such as accounting, inventory management, regulatory compliance, and marketing. Fear of Failure and High Risk Aversion: Social structures often place a heavy stigma on failure. This creates psychological barriers, discouraging individuals from leaving secure corporate or public service jobs to pursue risky business concepts. Collateral and Credit Access Constraints: Financial institutions typically demand hard assets as collateral before issuing credit. Young or first-generation entrepreneurs often lack individual personal wealth, leading to critical capital shortages at start-up. Societal and Familial Skepticism: In many developing contexts, formal entrepreneurial paths are viewed with skepticism compared to stable, institutional employment. A lack of initial emotional and financial backing from family members causes severe psychological strain. Susceptibility to Entrepreneurial Stress: The "liability of newness" subjects individual founders to intense personal stress, long operational hours, and role ambiguities, frequently leading to burnout before the firm stabilizes.

item.description:
(a) Define entrepreneur, corporate entrepreneurship, and entrepreneurship. [03]
(b) Discuss the qualities of a successful entrepreneur. [04]
(c) Explain the steps of the entrepreneurial process. [08]
(a) Define Entrepreneurship. "Entrepreneurs Are Born, Not Made"—is it a myth or reality? Explain. [04]
(b) Briefly explain the steps of the entrepreneurial process. [05]
(c) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Arif Hossain (Sylhet, Bangladesh) Arif Hossain, from Sylhet, Bangladesh, grew up in a modest farming family. Despite financial struggles, his parents emphasized the importance of education. After completing his business administration degree, Arif developed an interest in entrepreneurship, seeing it as a way to solve local challenges. Returning to his hometown, Arif noticed farmers struggled to sell their products due to limited market access while urban consumers sought high-quality organic food. He saw an opportunity to create a business connecting farmers to urban markets and promoting organic farming. This led to Green Harvest, a company designed to support farmers and meet the growing demand for organic products. Arif began by researching organic farming and the needs of farmers and consumers. He designed a business model in which farmers received training and resources like seeds and organic fertilizers in exchange for selling their products to Green Harvest. Arif set up a processing and packaging unit to ensure quality, marketing the products through social media and partnerships with urban grocery stores. In the beginning, Arif faced resistance. Farmers were skeptical about organic farming due to fears of reduced yields, while consumers questioned the authenticity of organic products. Arif tackled these challenges by offering workshops for farmers and sharing the transparency of farming practices with consumers. Within a year, Green Harvest gained recognition. More farmers joined the network, demand grew, and the business expanded, employing over 50 people. Green Harvest benefited farmers, consumers, and the environment, showing how entrepreneurship can create economic and social change. [2+2+2=06] Required:
i. Explain why educated people like Arif Hossain choose to start their businesses.
ii. How did Green Harvest affect farms and the farming business?
iii. What entrepreneurial traits did Arif exhibit?
(a) Define Entrepreneur and Entrepreneurship. "All you need is money to be an entrepreneur." Is it a myth or reality? Explain. [05]
(b) Do you agree with the notion that entrepreneurs are born and not made? Explain your answer. [04]
(c) Briefly explain the skills and abilities required to execute a business idea effectively. [06]
(a) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Rajesh & GreenFields Rajesh grew up in a rural village in Uttarpradesh, India where traditional customs and social hierarchies dictated life choices and opportunities. As a member of a marginalized community, Rajesh faced discrimination and limited access to education and economic resources. Unable to sustain itself in the middle of severe caste discrimination, Rajesh's family shifted to a village in a nearby state. Unable to enter mainstream job-oriented occupations, Rajesh decided to become an entrepreneur. At that time, the state government was promoting organic farming to foster healthier ecosystems by avoiding synthetic pesticides, herbicides, and fertilizers, which help to reduce chemical pollution. Conventional farmers were facing several challenges in adopting organic farming. Rajesh established a social enterprise called "GreenFields" dedicated to promoting organic farming techniques and empowering local farmers. His sufferings in early life led to his commitment to social justice, environmental sustainability, and community empowerment. His enterprise aimed to provide training, resources, and market access to smallholder farmers while promoting ecological resilience and food security. At the initial stage, Rajesh faced severe problems in financing GreenFields. Gradually he learnt the preparation of a financial plan that outlines sources of funding, budget allocation, and financial milestones for achieving profitability. Required:
i. What are the different entrepreneurial schools of thought? [04]
ii. Explain Rajesh's entrepreneurial journey using the macro views of entrepreneurial schools of thought. [04]
(b) Complete the following table: What are the generational differences in entrepreneurial activity? Which generation group are you in? Do you think your generation has a better opportunity to become entrepreneurs than the generations of the pre-internet world?
(c) What are the components of a university-based entrepreneurship ecosystem? Are you studying in an entrepreneurial university? Explain your answer. [03]
(a) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Sarah's Renewable Energy Startup Sarah is a driven and ambitious individual with a passion for innovation and problem-solving. With a background in engineering and a keen interest in sustainability, Sarah aspires to launch her renewable energy startup to address environmental challenges and promote clean energy solutions. Sarah begins her entrepreneurial journey by conducting market research, developing a business plan, and seeking funding for her startup. Along the way, she encounters numerous challenges, including funding rejections, technical setbacks, and market uncertainties. Despite these obstacles, Sarah demonstrates resilience, perseverance, and adaptability, leveraging her psychological characteristics to navigate challenges and pursue her entrepreneurial vision. She embraces experimentation and iteration, viewing failures as learning opportunities for refining her ideas and approaches. She embraces ambiguity and uncertainty, adapting her strategies and approaches in response to changing market dynamics and emerging challenges. She cultivates self-awareness, recognizing her strengths, weaknesses, and limitations, and seeking feedback and support from mentors and peers. Required:
i. What are the key psychological characteristics and traits exhibited by Sarah that contribute to her entrepreneurial success? [2.5]
ii. How can entrepreneurs cultivate and strengthen their psychological characteristics for entrepreneurial success? [2.5]
(b) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Innovation at Google Creativity has several different manifestations in Google. And one of the obvious loci of creativity at Google is called Google Labs, where a number of new ideas are incubated, a process whereby Google welcomes users' thoughts about new ideas. Based on those comments, they can determine whether to develop the ideas further or start on new ones. It was in these labs that many creative ideas, such as Google Maps and Google Glass, were developed. Google also has the belief that ideas come from anywhere. So, on top of Google platforms, developers from around the world are invited to work with the Google App Engine, Android and the Google Web Toolkit. They are given the opportunity to create, even though they are not themselves Google employees. Another aspect of the priority given by Google to creativity is the company's adherence to a '20% time philosophy', which encourages employees to allocate 20% of their worktime to developing side-projects and to working cross-functionally with other teams. Googlers are thus more empowered to think freely and implement new ideas and thoughts of benefit to the organisation as a whole. Required:
i. From the above case, discuss the characteristics of firms with higher entrepreneurial intensity. [2.5]
ii. How does Google differ from a conservative firm? [2.5]
(c) What are the four specific areas of risk that entrepreneurs face? How can an entrepreneur deal with stress? [05]
(a) Define the term: 'corporate entrepreneurship'. Name some organizations with high entrepreneurial intensity. [3]
(b) Do entrepreneurs suffer more from mental disorders than other people? Answer the question considering the dark side of entrepreneurship. [4]
(c) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Islam's Generational Shift Islam is a successful first-generation entrepreneur who migrated from a remote village of Sonagazi, Noakhali to Chittagong City. He started out as a mechanic in Chittagong and dreamed of building a better future for his next generation. Islam was thrifty and disciplined. Although in a low-status occupation, he was very proud of how hard he worked. He took a few attempts with calculated risk and that paid off until he could open his own garage and he now runs a successful franchise business of several dozen oil and lube operations, where he trains other mechanics. Islam is a classical entrepreneur, but how should he teach his children? Does he encourage them to follow his lead and create financial success as entrepreneurs? The chances are he won't. Fewer than one in five do. Instead, Islam wants his children to have a 'better' life. He encourages them to spend many years at university. He wants his children to become physicians, lawyers, accountants, executives and so on. But in encouraging them so, Islam essentially discourages his children from becoming entrepreneurs. He unknowingly has them postpone their entry into the labor market until they have finished the finest education. And, of course, he encourages them to reject his lifestyle of thrift and the self-imposed environment of scarcity and instead to be consumers of material goods. Islam defines 'better' as having better 'stuff': finer homes, new cars, quality clothing and costly foods. What he doesn't include are the elements that were the foundation stones of his own success: hard work, risk taking and perseverance. Islam does not realize that being well educated but having a materialistic mentality has certain economic drawbacks. What Islam's well-educated children often learn by the time they are adults is to be the grand consumers of material goods. And at the same time, they are also underperformers as entrepreneurs. They are the opposite of their father; the blue-collar, successful business owner. They are part of the high-consuming, self-employment-postponing generation, and what's worse they still live at home enjoying the old man's wealth! [8] Required:
i. In your own experience, what are the social and cultural reasons that Islam's children are underachievers?
ii. Do you know people who are like Islam's children? Are you like them?
iii. What would you recommend 'to kick some sense' into their heads?
(b) How does cultural diversity affect entrepreneurship development? Explain your answer from a theoretical background. [4]

(e) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Tariq's Solar Cold Storage Tariq, a young entrepreneur from Rangpur, noticed that farmers in his area lose a large portion of their vegetable harvest due to lack of proper storage facilities. Most rely on selling produce immediately after harvest, often at low prices. Inspired by renewable energy solutions, Tariq proposes building solar-powered cold storage units that allow farmers to preserve vegetables longer and sell when prices are higher. He prepares a feasibility analysis. In the product/service test, farmers show interest but worry about rental costs. For the market feasibility, he finds many small farmers but limited awareness of solar technology. Organizational feasibility looks promising since an NGO is willing to provide technical support. Financial feasibility remains challenging because the upfront investment is high, though microfinance institutions show partial interest. Tariq wonders: Should he launch this idea now, or refine it further before scaling? [06] Required:
i. Which part of Tariq's feasibility analysis seems most critical to decide before launching? Why?
ii. How could Tariq use low-cost experiments to test farmers' willingness to pay?
iii. What "fatal flaw" could still threaten this business, even if everything looks feasible?

(b) Imagine, after graduation, you want to start a restaurant at your university campus. What factors should you consider in conducting a market feasibility analysis for your business? How can you assess the financial feasibility? [06]

The Gym will have the following advantages, among others: Privacy and comfort, developing a supportive community, tailored workouts and classes, fostering self-esteem to the female students, safety concerns, reducing gender stereotypes in society, health and hygiene support. Required:

(d) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: EcoPack Bangladesh Rafiq, a young entrepreneur from Dhaka, noticed the growing problem of plastic waste in urban areas. He decided to launch EcoPack Bangladesh, a startup producing biodegradable packaging materials for local restaurants and e-commerce businesses. After conducting preliminary market research, Rafiq identified that many small businesses were willing to pay slightly more for eco-friendly packaging if it helped them appeal to environmentally conscious customers. Rafiq drafted a business plan outlining his mission, target market, and value proposition. He included a marketing strategy focusing on social media campaigns and partnerships with eco-conscious brands. Operationally, he planned to source raw materials from a supplier and establish a small production facility near Dhaka. The financial section projected initial investment requirements of BDT 15 lacs, break-even within 18 months, and a net profit margin of 12% by year two. To secure funding Rafiq prepared an executive summary highlighting both environmental impact and potential financial returns. However, potential challenges included competition from imported packaging products, fluctuating raw material costs, and convincing traditional businesses to switch from plastic. [06] Required:
i. Identify the key components of Rafiq's business plan.
ii. How does Ecopack's value proposition address a market need in Bangladesh?
iii. How can a strong business plan help Rafiq secure funding from investors?

(a) What is the best time for a firm to develop its business model? [02]
(b) Describe the key aspects of standard business models and disruptive business models. [06]
(a) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: TOMS Shoes - A Business with Purpose TOMS Shoes, founded by Blake Mycoskie in 2006, is a prime example of a business with a strong social mission. The idea for TOMS originated during a trip to Argentina, where Blake noticed that many children were walking barefoot, leading to health risks and infections. Moved by the children's plight, Blake decided to create a company that would sell shoes and give back to those in need. The result was TOMS Shoes, a brand that adopted the "One for One" business model: for every pair of shoes sold, TOMS would donate a pair to a child in need. This business model combined commerce with a meaningful social impact, setting TOMS apart from traditional footwear companies. The "One for One" model quickly captured the attention of socially-conscious consumers who wanted to make a difference through their purchases. TOMS provided an opportunity for people to contribute to a greater cause without having to make additional charitable donations. As a result, TOMS became an instant success, with its shoes meeting a practical need and fulfilling a desire to help others. In the following years, TOMS expanded its mission, diversifying its product line and introducing eyewear and coffee. Each product was tied to a different giving initiative—TOMS eyewear helped restore sight to people in developing countries, while the company's coffee sales supported clean water projects. This expansion allowed TOMS to reach new markets while using its platform to support critical global causes. However, TOMS faced criticism over time. Critics argued that simply donating shoes could create dependency and disrupt local economies. In response, TOMS adapted its strategy by focusing on job creation, sustainable practices, and partnerships with local artisans to ensure its positive and long-lasting impact. TOMS Shoes is a powerful example of how a business can thrive while staying true to its purpose. TOMS has shown that companies can play a key role in addressing global challenges by blending profit with social impact. [3+3+3=09] Required:
i. How does TOMS Shoes integrate social responsibility into its business model?
ii. What criticisms did TOMS face in its efforts to make a positive social impact?
iii. How did TOMS respond to criticism about its "One for One" business model?

[4] Display Mermaid diagrams in this vault?Only allow if you trust this vault's contents.Allowflowchart TD subgraph TM ["Traditional Manufacturer (e.g., Hewlett-Packard or IBM)"] direction LR T1[Forecasts demand] --> T2[Makes subcomponents] --> T3[Assembles complete PC] --> T4[Stores PCs in warehouse] --> T5[Ships PCs to retailer] --> T6[PCs sit on retailer's shelf until sold] --> T7[In hands of consumer] endDisplay Mermaid diagrams in this vault?Only allow if you trust this vault's contents.Allowflowchart LR subgraph D ["Dell"] direction LR D1[Customer places order via phone or Internet] --> D2[Contract manufacturers instantly view order information and ship component parts] --> D3[Dell assembles computer from component parts as they arrive and maintains customer relationship] --> D4["Computer is shipped 'direct' to customer via UPS or FedEx"] --> D5[In hands of consumer] end

(a) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: The Ahmed Family Handicraft Business The Ahmed family has been running a traditional handicraft business in Kushtia for over 30 years. Initially started by the father, the business specialized in producing hand-woven nakshi kantha and jute-based products, which became popular among local buyers and tourists. With time, the second generation—two sons and a daughter—joined the venture. However, conflicts have arisen regarding the business's future direction. The father prefers to maintain the traditional model, focusing on loyal local customers. On the other hand, the younger members want to modernize operations—introducing e-commerce, targeting international markets, and adopting professional management practices. Disagreements over succession planning, profit-sharing, and decision-making have created tension. Additionally, the business faces broader challenges common in Bangladesh's entrepreneurial landscape: limited access to financing, bureaucratic barriers in exports, lack of modern infrastructure, and competition from cheap machine-made imports. Despite these hurdles, the Ahmed family recognizes that innovation, professionalization, and a clear strategic plan are vital for long-term survival and growth. [08] Required:
i. What strategic management approaches could help the Ahmed family balance tradition and modernization?
ii. How can succession planning be effectively handled in a Bangladeshi family business context?

(c) Define intellectual property. What are the four key forms of intellectual property? [03]
(d) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Nusrat's Heritage Threads Nusrat, a young entrepreneur from Dhaka, launched an online fashion brand named Heritage Threads, inspired by traditional Jamdani weaving. To stand out, she developed unique fusion designs blending Jamdani patterns with modern cuts. Soon after her business gained popularity, a larger fashion house copied several of her designs and marketed them under a similar brand name, confusing customers. Nusrat was frustrated as she invested heavily in design, brand identity, and online marketing. She realized she had not formally registered her brand name, logo, or applied for design protection. With sales declining due to imitation, Nusrat sought advice on how to protect her creations through intellectual property rights. She wanted to know whether trademarks, copyrights, or design patents would apply in her case and how these protections could help her business survive in a highly competitive Bangladeshi fashion market. [06] Required:
i. What forms of intellectual property protection are most relevant to Nusrat's business?
ii. How can trademark registration help protect Heritage Threads?
iii. What steps should Nusrat take immediately to safeguard her brand and designs?
(a) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Alacritech vs. Microsoft Alacritech, a start-up firm, accused Microsoft of violating two of its patents on technology designed to improve the speed of network-connected computers. Initially, Alacritech shared its technology with Microsoft, hoping the company would license it. However, Microsoft declined and later introduced a similar technology called Chimney. After Alacritech's second attempt to license the technology was rejected, it filed a lawsuit claiming patent infringement. Microsoft argued that its technology was developed independently. The U.S. District Court in San Francisco issued a preliminary injunction preventing Microsoft from selling products with the disputed technology. Eventually, the case was settled out of court, with Microsoft agreeing to license Alacritech's technology. [03+02=05] Required:
i. Define patent. Why is securing and enforcing patents important for start-ups like Alacritech?
ii. Why did Alacritech file a lawsuit against Microsoft?
(b) Define trade secrets with an example. [02]
(c) Define intellectual property. How does it differ from other properties like land, buildings, etc.? [05]
(d) Define copyright. What is protected by copyright? [03]
(a) What are the ethical considerations in entrepreneurship development? [06]
(a) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Dhaka Commercial Evictions The government's drive to force commercial establishments out of residential areas in Dhaka has not only created fears of job loss but also raised questions as to how those establishments operated with government clearance when rules clearly say they cannot. The Rajdhani Unnayan Kartripakkha (Rajuk) has been closing down businesses that have been running in residential areas for years. Dhaka North City Corporation (DNCC) and Dhaka South City Corporation (DSCC) have also warned businesses, which do not operate in Rajuk-approved commercial buildings or in commercial areas, that their trade licences would be cancelled. The DSCC is giving businesses a seven-day deadline to move out. A staggering 18,000 businesses in the capital, 13,500 of them under the DNCC, could lose their trade licences, according to data from the two city corporations. The High Court declared all commercial operations in Dhanmondi Residential Area illegal, with the exception of authorised commercial establishments on Mirpur Road, Satmasjid Road, Dhanmondi Road-2 and Dhanmondi Road-27. It directed the authorities to remove those establishments. The Appellate Division upheld the HC verdict. Utility service providers, like Dhaka Electric Supply Company (Desco), have started issuing notices on commercial establishments in residential areas seeking their occupancy certificates. Most of these businesses -- restaurants, hotels, guesthouses and various retailers -- are in Dhanmondi, Gulshan, Banani and Uttara. The number of guesthouses and hotels would be about 500, according to an estimate of a hotel and restaurant owners' association. They all face closure unless they relocate to commercial areas. However, businesses asked why government agencies, such as the city corporations, utility service providers and VAT offices, issued them trade licences, supplied electricity and provided other services at commercial rates when they were not allowed to do business in residential areas in the first place. Some questioned Rajuk's silence when the business establishments started running in its residential neighbourhoods. The businesspeople think that, "It was the duty of the government agencies to stop the opening of any commercial entities at the very beginning. People may have a tendency to violate rules but there are authorities to enforce the law." Required:
i. Which side do you agree with in this case - Government or businesspeople? Explain your answer. [03]
ii. If you started a business, how would you go about determining the proper licenses and permits to obtain, and whether there are additional government regulations that affect the product or service you plan to offer? Relate your answer to the above case. [04]
(b) Discuss the actions founders can take to establish a strong ethical culture in their entrepreneurial ventures.
(c) Discuss the steps entrepreneurs can take to avoid legal disputes and complications.
(a) Suppose you, as an owner, are struggling to tackle the legal complexities of your start-up business. What are some of the more important criteria you will consider when selecting a consultant lawyer for your new firm? [5]
(a) What do you mean by a founder's agreement? [3]
(b) Describe how to create a strong ethical culture in an entrepreneurial venture. [5]
(c) Discuss the four major forms of intellectual property. [7]
(d) Define liability of newness. How can a new venture overcome the liability of newness? [03]
(a) Why do startup firms need capital investments? Will they be able to sustain themselves without capital investment? [03]
(b) What are the sources of personal financing available to entrepreneurs? [03]
(b) Imagine you want to start a business. As an entrepreneur, explain the sources from where you can arrange funds to start or grow your business. [07]
(c) State the elements of a new venture team. [03]
(a) Describe a new-venture team and discuss the primary elements that form such a team.
(b) What are the common mistakes made in putting together a new-venture team?
(c) What problems do small firms face in financing? Explain briefly. [5]
(a) Why do most new ventures need financing or funding? [3]
(b) Discuss the primary elements of a new venture team. [5]
(a) Some entrepreneurs do not like to seek new venture financing because they feel that venture capitalists are greedy. In your opinion, is this true? Do these capitalists want too much? [7]
(b) In a new-venture evaluation, what are the four stages through which a proposal typically goes? Describe each in detail. [8]
(b) What is debt finance? Discuss the merits and demerits of debt financing for BMRE of an industry. [8]
(c) Explain the internal and external growth strategy for entrepreneurial firms. [05]
(c) Is it possible for a firm to grow too fast? What are the warning signs that a business is growing too fast?
(d) Discuss the six most common reasons firms pursue growth.
(b) Briefly discuss the stages in the organizational life cycle. [5]
(c) What are the steps involved in setting up a franchise system? Differentiate between a product and trademark franchise and a business format franchise with appropriate examples. [5]
(a) Based on the article given below, explain the reasons for business failure. Cite specific examples.
(b) Is it possible for a firm to grow too fast? If so, what are the potential downsides? Did you find any such case in the story below? Explain the case.
(c) Is it possible for something to be an enticing business idea but a poor business? Explain your answer with an appropriate example from the article below. [15] [!info] Article Text Reference: Failures in the Bangladeshi Market & Global Context In the age of mass digitalization, BTCL launched a locally assembled laptop branded as Doel. It was assumed that Doel would capture the entire market of Bangladesh. But Bangladeshi locally assembled laptop Doel failed in marketing competition with HP, Asus and other globally recognized brands. The consumers of Bangladesh are habituated to buy at lower prices, but when it comes to the question of electric equipment, they like to purchase the one of higher quality in spite of premium pricing. This is cent percent true for products like laptops. If you offer someone a laptop of low configuration, he will rather buy a mobile of better configuration with the same price. If you think consumers compromise with brand quality in all cases, you are wrong. 'One size fits all' is a mass marketing concept which has become backdated recently. Walton offered mobile phones and laptops, but because of poor branding, both mobile and laptop lines of Walton did not survive the market competition. Sometimes market leaders also fail for lack of strong succession. If a father cannot leave behind him a strong successor, all fall like a game of cards. The best example is Otobi. Inspired by global brand IKEA, Hatil, Otobi, and many entrepreneurs came to the market of Bangladesh. But failure to retain business by the son of Nitun Kundu, owner of Otobi, caused it to become a bankrupt organization at the day end. Instead of emphasizing company strength, owners of Otobi emphasized business diversification and through fund diversion they tried to revolutionize the power sector. Consequently, both the power sector and home furnishing businesses failed together and now Otobi is in an existential crisis. It would have been better for Otobi to invest more on its house furnishing business instead of the power sector with its retained earnings and bank loans. It is not possible for a global brand to gain popularity in all countries of the world in the same ratio. The common case study is of Starbucks' failure in Australia. In spite of becoming the market leader in the USA and many European countries, Starbucks was below the benchmark compared to coffee shops like Gloria Jean's. Because Starbucks expanded so fast in Australia from the beginning of the year 2000, it did not even get sufficient time to understand Australian customers' appetite. The coffee culture is historical in Australia, but it was a different type of coffee than the one Starbucks offered, since Starbucks failed to understand consumer behavior in Australia. When you fail to understand consumer behavior of some place, the business is bound to meet with failure. When Cell Bazar, an online shopping and delivery service, went into rebranding as Ekhanei.com, it started to lose its market share. Consumers in Bangladesh, especially in Dhaka, were so much acquainted with the name Cell Bazar that the new name just confused them. Again, the way Ekhanei.com tried to rebrand itself was a blunder. Instead of understanding the existing customer base, they tried to bring unnecessary change, mistakenly considering it innovation. Online marketing companies like Bikroy.com, which emerged as a startup and competitor of Cell Bazar, occupied their market share gradually and later became the market leader. At one point of time, the online sale shop Ekhanei.com was shut down with sudden notice. From this marketing failure, the learning is that it is not always the first mover who retains the major market share for long. The world of marketing is not for the first mover, but for the fast mover. Now come to the telecom sector of Bangladesh. Why did all other telecom operators crush before Grameen Phone one by one? Instead of focusing on the reason for Grameen Phone's success story, let us make an autopsy on the failures of its competitors. In spite of becoming the first telecom operator in Bangladesh, City Cell failed to get customers' trust and brand loyalty due to shortsightedness. The case study of CCD, the famous Indian coffee brand, teaches us that if you divert your funds elsewhere from the core business (here coffee sales) while you run it with a bank loan, a day may come when you will be debt-ridden with huge bank loans and the diverted fund will be of no use to save you. This Indian local Coffee brand CCD case study is also applicable to City Cell mobile, which diverted all their earnings elsewhere while they took huge bank loans to run the telecom company, ultimately resulting in huge bankruptcy. Even their internet-based data business under the banner of Zoom failed to recover the company ultimately. On the other hand, Warid Telecom Bangladesh, a subsidiary of Warid Telecom Pakistan, tried to play the best by strong investment in marketing and branding, but Warid Telecom's sudden acquisition by Indian Airtel demanded rebranding and repositioning with huge and fresh investment. Rebranding is also time-consuming after a new entry. Starting afresh, Airtel invested no less than Grameen Phone for branding through newspapers and television advertisements. But Airtel failed to ensure similar network strength and service quality like Grameen Phone. Neither Airtel nor Robi were in a position to invest equally on tower building for network expansion like Grameen Phone. Besides, while Airtel was being defeated in every step by Ambani Group's Telecom called Jio in India, Grameen Phone's parent company Telenor led the global telecom market with desperate success. Grameen Phone inherited and exploited the success of Telenor as a brand image while Airtel failed to fight back with Jio in India. Robi also had the option to revolutionize with 3G and 4G technology, where they also left no significant footprint. Do you know why many globally reputed foreign banks are losing market share in Bangladesh? They failed to explore financial inclusion and financial deepening, which many local banks have been doing successfully by branding credit cards, home loans, auto loans, and app-based service offers etc. The paradigm shift from corporate to retail and SMS banking is something which foreign banks did not address positively. Lastly, international coffee chains like Barista, Gloria Jean's, and the oldest Nescafe's failure before tea companies like Lipton or Ispahani is due to inadequate addressing of Bangladeshi consumers' taste level through branding. Equal branding, marketing, and Public Relations (PR) of coffee by concerned investors like tea investors might have shifted many tea lovers into coffee lovers, just like the paradigm shift from landline phones into mobile phones which took place in the 1990s and onward in Bangladesh. These coffee investors mainly overlooked the growing purchasing capacity of the people of Bangladesh who are already ready for a taste shift. Therefore, changing the signboard, logo, and theme color of an organization is not enough for branding or rebranding unless market penetration and expansion are prudent and judicious. If branding or rebranding gives the wrong message or insufficient message to consumers, the result becomes a disaster rather than a blessing.
(c) Describe the internal and external strategies for firms' growth. [7]
(b) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Shahnaz & Women Empowerment in Rangpur In recent years, Bangladesh has witnessed a remarkable rise in women entrepreneurs, contributing significantly to the economy and social development. One inspiring example is Shahnaz, who started a small handicraft business in Rangpur with just a few thousand taka. Initially, she faced challenges such as limited access to finance, lack of family support, and difficulty in reaching larger markets. However, through perseverance and training from a local NGO, she expanded her business, now employing 25 women from her community. Her enterprise produces eco-friendly products such as jute bags, handmade home décor, and traditional crafts, which are sold both locally and internationally. Shahnaz has become a role model, empowering women by providing employment opportunities and encouraging others to pursue entrepreneurship. Despite her success, challenges remain: accessing larger capital, competing with machine-made cheap imports, and navigating bureaucratic barriers. Yet, stories like hers highlight the resilience of women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh who not only uplift their families but also strengthen the nation's socio-economic fabric. [07] Required:
i. What challenges do women entrepreneurs like Shahnaz commonly face in Bangladesh?
ii. How did training and NGO support contribute to Shahnaz's success?
iii. In what ways can women-led enterprises impact communities and the broader economy?
iv. What policy measures could further encourage women entrepreneurship in Bangladesh?
(a) Would you prefer to be a social entrepreneur, a commercial entrepreneur with social values, or a sustainable entrepreneur? Explain. [04]
(c) State the problems and constraints faced by the entrepreneurs of Bangladesh. [04]
(b) Case Analysis: [!example] Case Study: Anika Rahman & "Crafted by Her" Anika Rahman, a young entrepreneur from Dhaka, Bangladesh, grew up in a family where education and independence were highly valued. She noticed a gap in the local market for affordable, high-quality handmade accessories, particularly those crafted by women in rural Bangladesh. Many of these artisans struggled to access wider markets and often depended on middlemen who took a large portion of their earnings. Determined to make a difference, Anika launched "Crafted by Her," an e-commerce platform connecting skilled women artisans from rural Bangladesh with urban consumers. Anika's vision was to create a sustainable business that not only provided unique, handmade accessories but also empowered women by giving them a direct avenue to sell their products at fair prices. The platform allowed customers to purchase handmade jewelry, bags, and home décor items while the artisans were paid fair wages for their work. Anika faced numerous challenges in starting her business. As a woman in a male-dominated business environment, she struggled to secure initial funding from investors. Building trust with rural artisans, many unfamiliar with e-commerce, also required significant effort. Anika overcame these challenges by partnering with local women's groups, organizing workshops to educate artisans about online selling, and investing her savings into the initial stages of the business. Over time, "Crafted by Her" gained popularity for its unique products and social mission. The platform expanded to include artisans from different regions of Bangladesh, helping to support hundreds of women financially. Anika's business provided women with a source of income and helped them gain recognition for their craftsmanship, boosting their confidence and social standing within their communities. Anika Rahman's story is a prime example of how women entrepreneurs in Bangladesh can use innovation to create businesses that succeed financially and have a lasting social impact. [03+03=06] Required:
i. What challenges did Anika face while building her business, and how did she overcome them?
ii. How does Anika's business contribute to Bangladesh's economic and social development?
(a) "Digital social media explore opportunities for women entrepreneurship in Bangladesh". Explain from a critical perspective. [4]
(c) Identify and explain the technical aspects that stimulate entrepreneurship development. [4]
(b) What are the government and non-government supporting institutions for entrepreneurship development in Bangladesh? Elaborate on the function of the SME Foundation and BSCIC regarding entrepreneurship development. [5]
(a) What are the problems affecting entrepreneurial development in Bangladesh? What roles can trade associations play in solving these problems? [6]
(b) Why is training and development needed for entrepreneurial success? What types of training do the entrepreneurs of Bangladesh receive regularly? [5]
(c) Identify the role and scope of social media for small entrepreneurial development. [4]
(c) Discuss the importance of entrepreneurship development in Bangladesh. [5]
(d) State the individual problems of entrepreneurship development. [3]
(b) Discuss the goals and objectives of the Bangladesh Small and Cottage Industries Corporation (BSCIC). [4]

item.title: ED LO Notes
item.description: Definition of Entrepreneurship: Entrepreneurship is the process by which individuals pursue opportunities without regard to resources they currently control. It involves the identification, evaluation, and exploitation of opportunities to create future goods and services. Corporate Entrepreneurship: This is entrepreneurship practice within established firms. Firms that possess an entrepreneurial intensity highly value risk-taking, innovation, and proactive behaviour, whereas conservative firms take a "wait-and-see" approach and are less innovative. The Importance of Entrepreneurship: Economic Impact: Entrepreneurial firms drive macroeconomic growth by introducing innovations that create entirely new industries and supply chains. Creative Destruction: Originally conceptualised by Joseph Schumpeter, entrepreneurs spark economic evolution by replacing outdated technologies, products, or business models with superior, more efficient options. Historically, research shows that individuals are driven by three major motivations to start their own ventures, ranked in order of frequency: To Be Their Own Boss: Many entrepreneurs have a long-standing desire to break away from traditional corporate hierarchies. They prefer autonomy, self-determination, and frustration with working within traditional corporate structures where their freedom may be restricted. To Pursue Their Own Ideas: Corporate environments often reject or slow down radical innovations. Individuals with a strong desire to see their unique ideas or passion projects come to fruition will establish a new firm to realize that vision. To Pursue Financial Rewards: While financial gain is a motivator, it is typically secondary to autonomy and innovation. Many entrepreneurs find that the financial upside of equity ownership in a successful start-up outweighs the fixed salary upside of corporate employment. While there is no single psychological profile for an entrepreneur, successful founders consistently share four definitive traits: Passion for the Business: This is the number one characteristic. Passion stems from the belief that the business can positively impact customers' lives. It sustains the founder through the inevitable long hours, financial strain, and initial rejections. Product/Customer Focus: Successful entrepreneurs are not just infatuated with the concept of business management; they are obsessed with the product and the customer. They focus on understanding customer pain points and ensuring the product or service solves those problems effectively. Tenacity Despite Failure: The path to launching a venture is filled with setbacks, regulatory hurdles, and market rejections. A successful entrepreneur possesses resilience and treats failures as experimental data rather than definitive endpoints. Execution Intelligence: Ideas are valuable, but execution is everything. Execution intelligence is the ability to fashion a solid business idea into a viable operational entity by assembling a team, creating a business model, securing partnerships, and managing daily operations. To accurately evaluate entrepreneurial behavior, it is vital to debunk five widespread misconceptions: Myth 1: Entrepreneurs Are Born, Not Made: Reality: Entrepreneurship is a fluid discipline composed of skills, processes, and structured mental models that can be studied, practiced, and mastered over time. Myth 2: Entrepreneurs Are Gamblers: Reality: Most entrepreneurs are calculated risk-takers. They do not seek random, high-risk environments; instead, they take deliberate actions to mitigate risks through market research, prototyping, and strategic partnerships. Myth 3: Entrepreneurs Are Motivated Primarily by Money: Reality: As highlighted in the motivations, money is rarely the primary driver. Passion for a product and the desire for autonomy generally trump pure financial gain, which is seen as a byproduct of success. Myth 4: Entrepreneurs Should Be Young and Energetic: Reality: While energy is crucial, data shows that entrepreneurial success is well distributed across age groups. Older entrepreneurs bring deep industry experience, strong professional networks, and access to capital that younger founders often lack. Myth 5: Entrepreneurs Love the Spotlight: Reality: While some high-profile tech founders are famous public figures, the vast majority of entrepreneurs operate quietly, focusing on value creation, customer satisfaction, and private enterprise growth without seeking media attention. Start-up companies differ based on their growth trajectories, capital requirements, and ultimate strategic goals: Salary-Substitute Firms: These are small businesses that yield a level of income for the owner that is similar to what they would earn working at a conventional job. Examples include dry cleaners, convenience stores, and local accounting practices. Lifestyle Firms: These firms allow owners to pursue a particular lifestyle or hobby while earning a living. They are built around the founder's personal passions rather than rapid scalability. Examples include surf shops, ski instructors, and boutique tour guides. Entrepreneurial Firms: These firms bring new products and services to the market by creating and seizing opportunities regardless of their current resource constraints. They focus on growth, innovation, and scaling rapidly into regional, national, or global markets. The modern entrepreneurial landscape is diversifying rapidly away from historical norms. Key expanding demographic segments include: Women Entrepreneurs: Women-owned businesses are growing at a faster rate than the national average, driven by increasing educational attainment, corporate glass ceilings, and dedicated venture ecosystems. Minority Entrepreneurs: There is a significant upward trend in businesses launched by Hispanic, African American, and Asian American founders, changing the corporate landscape and injecting new market innovations. Senior Entrepreneurs: The percentage of individuals aged 55 to 64 starting companies has increased significantly. This trend is driven by longer life expectancies, corporate downsizing, and the desire to leverage a lifetime of industry expertise. Millennial and Gen Z Entrepreneurs: Driven by early exposure to technology and a desire for social impact, younger generations are increasingly looking at entrepreneurship as a primary career path right out of college, rather than a mid-career alternative. Economic Effects: Innovation: Entrepreneurial firms are disproportionately responsible for breakthrough innovations compared to large, stagnant corporations. They introduce pioneering processes, software efficiencies, and new supply chains. Job Creation: Small, young entrepreneurial firms generate the vast majority of net new jobs in global economies, counterbalancing corporate downsizing trends. Societal Effects: Enhanced Productivity: Entrepreneurial innovations make lives easier, safer, and more productive (e.g., smartphones, remote medical platforms, online banking). Social Change: Many ventures target systemic societal challenges—such as renewable energy access or educational tech—transforming how communities interact, learn, and sustain themselves. The entrepreneurial process is a structured, four-step framework that guides a venture from an abstract concept to a fully realised enterprise: Step 1: Deciding to Become an Entrepreneur: Triggered by an event such as corporate frustration, job loss, or a breakthrough discovery, an individual commits to pursuing an independent venture. Step 2: Developing Successful Business Ideas: This phase includes opportunity recognition, conducting initial feasibility analysis, analysing industries and competitors, and constructing a clear, viable business model. Step 3: Moving from an Idea to an Entrepreneurial Firm: The founder begins formalising the venture. This requires preparing a formal business plan, assembling a cohesive founding team, and securing early-stage funding or financing (such as bootstrapping, angel investment, or venture capital). Step 4: Managing and Growing the Entrepreneurial Firm: Once launched, the focus shifts to operations. The entrepreneur manages day-to-day finances, implements marketing strategies, and navigates the challenges of scaling the business over the long term. Opportunity: A favourable set of circumstances that creates a need for a new product, service, or business. To be viable, an opportunity must possess four essential qualities: it must be attractive, durable, timely, and anchored in a product, service, or business that creates or adds value for its buyer or end user. Idea: A thought, an impression, or a notion. An idea may or may not meet the criteria of an opportunity. Many entrepreneurial ventures fail because the underlying idea does not solve a real-world problem or fulfill a genuine market gap. Observing Trends: Analyzing macroenvironmental forces to spot shifts in consumer behavior or market needs. Key forces include: Economic Forces: Changes in disposable income, consumer spending patterns, and economic stability. Social Trends: Shifts in demographics, lifestyle preferences, health awareness, and cultural norms. Technological Advances: Emerging tech innovations that create completely new industries or optimize existing ones. Political Action & Regulatory Changes: New laws, government mandates, or shifting global trade policies. Solving a Problem: Recognizing an everyday challenge, pain point, or inconvenience and engineering a product or service to fix it. These are often discovered via personal experience, consumer complaints, or deliberate industry tracking. Finding Gaps in the Marketplace: Identifying a consumer need that mainstream companies overlook. This frequently occurs when large corporations focus on broad markets, leaving highly specific, local, or specialized niche markets underserved. Prior Experience: Industry-specific experience helps individuals recognize market inefficiencies, understand customer nuances, and establish a network of valuable industry contacts. Cognitive Factors: Entrepreneurial alertness—a heightened awareness that allows certain individuals to notice opportunities without an active, deliberate search. Social Networks: The size and depth of a founder's network directly impacts opportunity exposure. Weak-tie relationships (casual acquaintances) are often more valuable for finding fresh ideas than strong-tie relationships (close friends/family) because weak ties link the entrepreneur to diverse, non-redundant pools of information. Creativity: The cognitive ability to connect seemingly unrelated concepts, resources, or market gaps to form a cohesive, novel solution. Preparation: The foundational phase where an individual gathers background knowledge, education, and industry experience. Incubation: The subconscious phase where the individual mulks over the problem, actively or passively considering various angles without forcing a conclusion. Insight: The "Eureka!" moment where the flash of recognition occurs, and a potential solution or unique opportunity crystalizes in the mind. Evaluation: The analytical stage where the insight is scrutinized for its commercial viability, real-world feasibility, and strategic value. Elaboration: The action-oriented stage where the creative idea is transformed into a tangible entity, such as a prototype, pitch deck, or formal business model. Purpose: Brainstorming is a group dynamic tool designed to generate a high volume of ideas and stimulate creative thinking around a specific problem. Rules of Engagement: To ensure psychological safety and maximum output, brainstorming sessions must strictly adhere to four rules: No criticism or evaluation of ideas is permitted during the generation phase. Freewheeling and wild ideas are actively encouraged. The session prioritizes quantity over quality. Participants are encouraged to build, combine, and iterate on the ideas of others. Focus Groups: A gathering of 5 to 10 consumers who match the profile of the target market. Led by a trained moderator, these groups use open-ended questioning to uncover organic pain points, emotional drivers, and immediate reactions to new concepts. Library and Internet Research: A structured, cost-effective method to validate raw concepts by scanning industry trade journals, market research databases, academic papers, and digital search trends to see if market data aligns with the perceived opportunity. Definition: An idea bank is a centralized, secure digital or physical repository used to log, track, and organize spontaneous insights and potential business concepts. Strategic Value: Promising ideas rarely emerge exactly when a firm has the immediate resources or bandwidth to launch them. An idea bank prevents valuable thoughts from being forgotten, facilitates long-term pattern recognition, and maintains an ongoing pipeline for business pivot options. Because abstract ideas cannot be formally patented or trademarked at the raw conceptual stage, entrepreneurs must practice strict operational security: Documenting the Idea: Maintaining a clear, chronological, and dated log of the idea’s evolution to establish concrete proof of creation. Securing the Assets: Utilizing password-protected files, limited cloud access, and secure storage for all preliminary designs and notes. Non-Disclosure Agreements (NDAs): Requiring prospective partners, contractors, employees, or early investors to sign legally binding agreements pledging not to disclose or misappropriate the proprietary information shared with them. Definition: Feasibility analysis is the process of determining whether a business idea is viable. It serves as a preliminary evaluation of a business concept to decide whether it is worth pursuing. Importance: It introduces objective, systematic, and analytical thinking into the early launch phase, actively stripping away guesswork and emotion. It protects entrepreneurs from wasting significant time, capital, and emotional energy on fundamentally flawed ideas. Timing: The proper time to conduct a feasibility analysis is early in the venture creation cycle, specifically after opportunity recognition but before writing a formal business plan or spending extensive capital. Research Types: Primary Research: Original data collected directly by the entrepreneur (e.g., face-to-face consumer interviews, surveys, focus groups). Secondary Research: Evaluation of pre-existing data gathered by others (e.g., industry analyst forecasts, census bureau summaries, trade journal databases). Purpose: To evaluate the overarching appeal of the proposed product or service before rushing it into mass production or formal development. Issue 1: Product/Service Desirability: Confirming that the concept makes fundamental sense, solves a genuine problem, and is something target consumers will get excited about. Entrepreneurs validate this via: Concept Statement: A clear, one-page summary description of the venture distributed to industry experts and potential buyers to harvest direct, structural feedback. Issue 2: Product/Service Demand: Determining whether there is a true buying intention in the broader market. Common evaluation tactics include: Buying Intentions Surveys: Administering structured questions to target users to measure their explicit willingness to purchase the solution at specific price points. Gumshoe Research: Actively investigating via deep observation—scrounging around for clues, tracking consumer behavior in real-world settings, or interviewing front-line workers. Purpose: To assess the structural strength, maturity, and commercial appeal of the macro industry and the specific micro-market segment the business plan intends to target. Issue 1: Industry Attractiveness: Analyzing the broad landscape of similar companies. From an entry perspective, the most attractive industries are structurally young rather than mature, early in their life cycle, growing rather than stagnant, fragmented rather than dominated by two or three massive monopolies, and characterized by healthy operating margins. Issue 2: Target Market Attractiveness: Evaluating the highly localized pocket of consumers the startup intends to capture first. An optimal target market is large enough to allow the startup to scale profitably, yet small and specialized enough to be overlooked or ignored by established corporate incumbents. Purpose: To gauge whether a proposed startup possesses sufficient internal human talent, professional expertise, and non-financial assets to successfully navigate the launch phase. Issue 1: Management Prowess: Reviewing the ability, passion, and industry network of the core founding team. Founders measure their execution potential based on relevant domain knowledge, social capital (networks), and how effectively their collective skills complement one another. Issue 2: Resource Sufficiency: Determining if the venture can easily secure the critical, non-monetary assets needed to execute day-to-day operations. This includes physical proximity to strategic suppliers, control of necessary intellectual property, access to specialized equipment, and availability of qualified labor pools. Importance: A quick, initial financial assessment is necessary to confirm that the business can realistically generate enough early traction and revenue to stay solvent without requiring continuous, unbacked injections of capital. Issue 1: Total Start-Up Cash Needed: Tabulating every single capital requirement incurred before the business can formalize its operations (e.g., real estate leasing, equipment purchasing, legal filings, raw inventory acquisition, and working capital reserves). Issue 2: Financial Performance of Similar Businesses: Benchmarking the new business against existing operational peers. This relies on collecting data via financial databases, annual corporate filings, or industry association reports to establish standard cost structures. Issue 3: Overall Financial Attractiveness of the Proposed Venture: Forecasting baseline financial returns by estimating steady-state profit margins, early break-even timelines, asset velocity, and the long-term capital efficiency of the business model. Definition: A feasibility analysis template (often referred to as a "First Screen" matrix) is a highly structured, multi-page grading system that lists the vital criteria across all four forms of feasibility analysis. Strategic Importance: It acts as an objective filter that prevents entrepreneurs from falling victim to dangerous wishful thinking or confirmational bias. By standardizing the scoring of product, industry, organizational, and financial viability, it helps founders quickly classify ideas into "go," "no-go," or "rethink" decisions before authoring a complete business plan. Definition: A business model is a firm's plan or recipe for how it creates, delivers, and captures value for its stakeholders. Importance: It serves as a structural extension of a successful feasibility analysis. It provides a holistic framework showing how all the operational, strategic, and financial elements of a business fit together. Strategic Value: An effective business model prevents fatal flaws by forcing entrepreneurs to map out their exact value creation process, helps the core team communicate the company’s vision, and acts as a baseline blueprint before authoring a complete business plan. Standard Business Models: These depict existing, verified plans or recipes that firms use to determine how they will compete and capture value within an established market. Examples include: Advertising: Generating revenue by selling promotional space (e.g., Google, Facebook). Bricks and Clicks: Integrating both physical storefronts and digital e-commerce channels (e.g., Apple). Freemium: Providing a basic service for free while charging a premium for advanced features (e.g., Dropbox, Spotify). Subscription: Charging a recurring fee at regular intervals for continuous access to a product or service (e.g., Netflix). Disruptive Business Models: These are rare, highly impactful models that do not fit the profile of a standard business model. They change or completely reinvent how business is conducted within an industry or specialized niche. Examples include: Direct-to-Consumer: Cutting out traditional retail wholesale intermediaries to sell directly to end-users (e.g., Dell, Warby Parker). Market Creators: Utilizing technology to build an entirely new platform connecting fragmented buyers and suppliers (e.g., Uber, Airbnb). Core Strategy: This describes how a newly formed venture intends to compete relative to its established industry competitors. Business Mission: A clear statement describing why the company exists and what its business model is designed to accomplish. It functions as the firm's financial and moral compass. Basis of Differentiation: The core points that cause a consumer to pick a startup’s products or services over an alternative. This should focus explicitly on consumer benefits rather than technical features. Target Market: A narrow group of customers with highly similar interests, buying patterns, and pain points within a broader macro-market segment. Product/Market Scope: A defined boundary outlining which specific products and geographic markets the firm will concentrate on initially, along with a 3-to-5-year expansion horizon. Resources: The vital tactical inputs an entrepreneur utilizes to produce, sell, distribute, and service an offering. These assets must be difficult to imitate and hard to substitute to build a sustainable advantage. Core Competencies: A specific technical capability, internal process, or specialized expertise that sets a firm apart from its rivals. Startups typically focus on mastering 2 to 3 core competencies. Key Assets: The specific strategic assets a company must own or control to allow its business model to function properly. These are broken into four classes: Physical Assets: Physical space, equipment, corporate vehicles, and distribution infrastructure. Intellectual Assets: Patents, trademarks, copyrights, trade secrets, and institutional brand reputation. Financial Assets: Cash reserves, operational lines of credit, and formal investment commitments. Human Assets: Founders, specialized technicians, key managers, and core strategic advisors. Financials: This section explicitly defines how a company intends to generate revenue and maintain long-term corporate solvency. Revenue Streams: The specific pathways and mechanisms through which the business model captures capital from customers (e.g., one-time transaction fees, licensing, recurring service charges). Cost Structure: Outlines the most significant operational expenses incurred to run the business model. This identifies whether a firm is cost-driven (minimizing costs) or value-driven (maximizing premium value offerings) and documents fixed vs. variable costs. Financing/Funding: A realistic forecast of the total cash needed to fund initial launch operations before the firm reaches a steady state of organic profitability. Operations: This component documents the day-to-day execution framework of the company, bridging internal strategies with external execution networks. Product (or Service) Production: A breakdown of how the firm's core products or services are manufactured, developed, or executed (e.g., in-house production, relying on contract manufacturers, or leveraging automated software delivery). Channels: The direct or indirect distribution touchpoints a company relies on to deliver its value proposition to the end consumer (e.g., direct-to-consumer online platforms, wholesale networks, or physical retail partnerships). Key Partners: The network of strategic alliances, joint ventures, or reliable suppliers necessary to reduce operational risk, optimize performance, and leverage outside capabilities. Definition: A business plan is a written narrative, typically 25 to 35 pages long, that describes what a new business intends to accomplish and how it plans to achieve those goals. Dual-Purpose Document: For most new ventures, a business plan serves two essential functions—one internal and one external: Internal Purpose: It provides the company with a structured "road map" to follow. This helps employees operate in sync, maintain operational alignment, and move forward in a consistent and purposeful manner. External Purpose: It introduces the venture to potential investors and external stakeholders, making a clear, data-driven case that the business concept is viable and has a high probability of success. There are two primary audiences for a firm's business plan, and each reads the document with distinct objectives in mind: A Firm’s Employees: They look for a clear statement of the company's core logic, operational strategies, and strategic goals. The plan acts as a unifying document that helps clarify management expectations and defines how individual roles contribute to the firm's broader objectives. Investors and Other External Stakeholders: Venture capitalists, angel investors, and lenders use the plan to determine if the business concept is financially sound, scalable, and low risk. They look for evidence of a highly capable management team, realistic financial projections, and a compelling market opportunity that guarantees a strong return on investment. To capture an investor's interest and establish corporate credibility, entrepreneurs must adhere to several strict writing and structural parameters: Conventional Structure: The plan must follow a standard, predictable outline. Departing from standard business plan frameworks to showcase "creativity" is generally a mistake; busy investors prefer a familiar format so they can locate key operational metrics quickly. Length and Polish: The document should remain concise, typically staying within a 25-to-35-page window. It must look professional, feature consistent typography, and be entirely free of spelling or grammatical errors. Tone of Content: The narrative needs to strike an equal balance between hard facts and forward-looking excitement. It must project an authentic sense of anticipation about the market opportunity without relying on unbacked hyperbole or overly optimistic financial assumptions. Recognizing Evolving Elements: Entrepreneurs must realize that a business plan is a fluid document. Immersing oneself in the details of the plan and receiving early external feedback will invariably expose new insights, requiring the core team to update and adjust their operational hypotheses. A complete and thorough business plan systematically covers all core elements of the proposed enterprise: Executive Summary: A short, highly impactful 1-to-2-page synopsis of the entire business plan. Because it is the first section read, it is considered the most crucial element; if it fails to captivate the reader, the rest of the document will go unexamined. Industry Analysis: Examines the macro environment in which the startup will operate, evaluating industry size, growth trajectory, structural trends, key success factors, and long-term economic prospects. Company Description: Offers a comprehensive look at the firm, documenting its history, formal mission statement, corporate ownership structure, current developmental milestones, and major strategic partnerships. Market Analysis: Segments the broader industry to isolate the specific target market the startup will capture. It maps out consumer buying behavior, customer acquisition dynamics, and directly charts the strengths and weaknesses of key competitors. The Economics of the Business: Explains the foundational logic of how the venture generates profits. This includes identifying revenue drivers, gross profit margins, fixed versus variable cost breakdowns, operating leverage, and exact break-even calculations. Marketing Plan: Breaks down the firm’s customer acquisition framework, detailing its strategy across the traditional marketing mix (Product, Price, Promotion, and Place/Distribution) and defining the practical workflow of the sales cycle. Design and Development Plan: If introducing a brand-new offering, this outlines the path from initial prototype to commercial production. It outlines development costs, execution milestones, and tracks critical proprietary assets like patents, trademarks, or copyrights. Operations Plan: Outlines how the day-to-day logistics of the business will be executed. It differentiates workflows into "back stage" processes (unseen operational mechanics) and "front stage" processes (the visible interactions experienced by the customer). Management Team and Company Structure: Highlights the background, skills, and professional track records of the founders and early executives. This section is highly scrutinized by investors to ensure the team possesses the execution intelligence to run the business successfully. Financial Projections: Features pro forma (forecasted) financial statements—including income statements, balance sheets, and cash flow statements—typically mapping out a realistic 3-to-5-year financial window. The Presentation Deck: When invited to present to investors, entrepreneurs should bring a highly streamlined slide presentation, typically limited to 10 to 12 polished slides. The presentation must cleanly outline the core problem, the proposed solution, market size, the business model, competitive advantages, and financial milestones. Managing the Q&A Session: The presentation is followed by a rigorous question-and-answer block from investors. To build trust, presenters must avoid becoming defensive when challenged. They should demonstrate absolute domain expertise, maintain intellectual honesty if a specific data point is missing, and show a thorough, deep command of their underlying financial assumptions. Lead by Example: The most important action an entrepreneurial team can take. When founders behave ethically, communicate openly about values, and prioritize integrity over short-term financial gains, they set a cultural benchmark that employees naturally mirror. Establish a Code of Conduct: A formal, written document that explicitly states a firm's values, ethical expectations, and social responsibilities regarding internal and external business relationships. It acts as a clear reference point for appropriate organizational behavior. Implement an Ethics Training Program: Structured internal programs that teach employees how to identify, analyze, and successfully navigate complex ethical dilemmas. These programs clarify corporate policies and guide personnel to make choices aligned with company values. Organizational Benefits: Cultivating an ethical environment creates substantial operational payoffs. These include enhanced brand reputation, higher employee alignment and retention, increased customer loyalty, and reduced legal and regulatory exposure. Choosing an Attorney Early: Founders should select legal counsel as early as possible. The chosen attorney should specialize in early-stage startups, possess deep experience in the company's specific industry, understand venture financing, and be willing to offer flexible or deferred payment structures. Ethically Departing a Former Employer: To avoid intellectual property and contractual disputes, departing employees must behave professionally. They must provide adequate notice, perform all assigned duties until departure, and leave behind all data, proprietary files, and trade secrets belonging to the former employer.
