Conclusion: The proximate cause of death is the accidental scratch on the leg (an accident). The septic pneumonia was not an independent disease but rather a terminal symptom and direct consequence of the physical injury. The insurance claim is fully payable to the family, and they should challenge any initial denial based on the following justifications: In insurance law, if an accidental event directly causes a sickness or disease that ultimately results in death, the entire loss is contractually attributed to the accident. Because the proximate cause of the loss was an accident, and the policy explicitly covers death by accident, the policy exclusion for death by disease does not apply to consequential illnesses arising directly from an accidental injury. The insurer is legally bound to fulfill the policy obligations and pay out the death benefits.

item.title: IRM 2021 Exam Q6
item.description: Marine insurance provides financial protection against losses resulting from maritime perils that occur during a marine adventure. The subject matter of a marine insurance contract can be broadly categorized into four primary components: Hull Insurance (Ship or Vessel): This refers to the insurance of the physical structure of the vessel, including its machinery, hull, tackle, apparel, fittings, and onboard equipment. It protects the shipowner or ship operator against physical damage or total loss of the ship caused by marine hazards like collisions, stranding, sinking, storms, or fire while navigating at sea or resting in port. Cargo Insurance: This covers the goods, merchandise, commodities, and property being transported by the vessel from the point of origin to the final destination. It protects the cargo owners (exporters, importers, or merchants) against physical loss, damage, or theft of the cargo during transit via ocean routes, including associated inland transit legs. Freight Insurance: Freight is the financial consideration or payment received by the shipowner for the safe carriage and delivery of goods. Under maritime law, if the cargo is lost and cannot be safely delivered to its destination, the shipowner loses the right to collect the freight charges. Freight insurance protects the shipowner or operator against this specific loss of revenue resulting from a covered marine peril. Liability Insurance (Protection and Indemnity - P&I): This covers the legal liabilities incurred by shipowners or operators to third parties due to maritime operations. This includes liability for injuries or loss of life of crew members and passengers, damage to other ships during collisions, damage to harbors, wharves, or piers, and environmental liabilities such as oil spills and ocean pollution. The fundamental principles of insurance apply to marine contracts with distinct, tailored legal nuances reflecting the unique nature of international maritime trade.The insured must have a legally recognized financial relationship with the subject matter of insurance, meaning they benefit from its safety and suffer a financial loss from its damage or destruction. Application in Marine Insurance: Unlike life or fire insurance, where insurable interest must exist at the inception of the policy, in marine insurance, the insurable interest must exist at the time of the loss. This exception accommodates international trade, where goods frequently change ownership while in transit. For instance, an importer buying cargo under an F.O.B. (Free on Board) contract acquires an insurable interest once the goods cross the ship's rail, even if the policy was arranged prior to shipment. A contract of marine insurance is based on mutual trust. Both parties—the insured and the insurer—are legally obligated to act with complete honesty and disclose all material facts transparently. Application in Marine Insurance: The proposer must volunteer information about every material circumstance that would influence a prudent underwriter in determining the premium rate or deciding whether to accept the risk. This includes detailing the vessel's true age, condition, exact nature of cargo, and the specified route. Because the insurer cannot physically inspect a ship at sea or cargo packed in container yards, any non-disclosure, concealment, or misrepresentation gives the insurer the statutory right to declare the policy void ab initio (from the beginning). The principle of indemnity ensures that the insured is restored to the same financial position following a loss as they occupied immediately prior to it, without the possibility of making a profit. Application in Marine Insurance: While marine insurance is fundamentally a contract of indemnity, it operates as a modified indemnity. Marine policies are almost exclusively Valued Policies, where an agreed value is determined between the insurer and insured at policy inception. This value typically encompasses the cost of goods, freight charges, insurance premiums, plus a standard 10% markup to represent anticipated profit. In the event of a total loss, the insurer pays this fixed agreed sum, regardless of whether the actual market value of the cargo fluctuated during the voyage. This prevents complex valuation disputes mid-transit. Standardized clauses are embedded within marine policies—predominantly governed by the Institute Cargo Clauses (ICC) developed by the London market—to precisely delineate coverage boundaries, perils, and liabilities. Transit Clause (Warehouse-to-Warehouse Clause): This clause defines the exact duration and spatial scope of the coverage. It states that insurance attaches from the moment the goods leave the shipper's warehouse or place of storage named in the policy, continues throughout the ordinary course of transit, and terminates either upon safe delivery to the consignee's final warehouse or upon the expiry of 60 days after completion of discharge overside from the overseas vessel at the final port, whichever occurs first. Perils of the Sea Clause: This defines the traditional maritime hazards covered by the policy. It encompasses extraordinary natural actions of the elements such as heavy weather, stranding, sinking, capsizing, shipwreck, and collisions, as well as man-made perils like fire, jettison (throwing cargo overboard to lighten the vessel in an emergency), piracy, and barratry (fraudulent or wrongful actions committed by the ship's master or crew against the owner's interest). Institute Cargo Clauses - Core Categories: Modern cargo insurance is standardized into three distinct sets of clauses reflecting varied coverage depths: Institute Cargo Clauses (A): Offers the widest coverage under an "All-Risks" framework. It covers all accidental physical losses or damages except for specifically excluded perils (such as willful misconduct, ordinary leakage, wear and tear, or improper packing). Institute Cargo Clauses (B): A more restrictive, named-perils policy. It covers major casualties like burning, stranding, sinking, plus risks like earthquake, volcanic eruption, lightning, water entry into the hold, and total loss of any package dropped during loading or unloading. Institute Cargo Clauses (C): Provides the bare minimum, lower-premium coverage. It covers only major catastrophic accidents such as fire, explosion, stranding, sinking, overturning of land conveyance, collision, and voluntary jettison. Sue and Labour Clause: This clause places a legal and operational duty on the insured (and their agents) to take all necessary, reasonable measures to mitigate or prevent further loss to the insured property when an accident occurs. Crucially, the clause guarantees that the insurer will reimburse any reasonable expenses ("sue and labour charges") incurred by the insured while attempting to salvage or protect the property, in addition to paying any claim for damage. Waiver Clause: As a protective supplement to the Sue and Labour clause, this guarantees that any action taken by either the insurer or the insured to recover, save, or preserve the endangered property will not be interpreted as a waiver of their respective rights, nor will it be construed as an implicit acceptance or refusal of an abandonment notice. Change of Voyage and Deviation Clause: Under maritime conditions, a ship must follow the customary, designated geographical route for its voyage. If a vessel deviates from this route or changes its final destination without a legally justifiable reason (such as saving human lives or seeking safety from severe storms), the insurer's liability ceases immediately from the point of deviation. The deviation clause outlines the specific conditions under which coverage may be extended or reinstated upon the payment of an additional premium. War, Strikes, Riots, and Civil Commotions (SRCC) Exclusion Clause: Standard marine policies exclude losses resulting directly from war, hostilities, civil wars, strikes, lockouts, labor disturbances, or acts of terrorism. To secure coverage against these risks, an insured must specifically pay an extra premium to append specialized War and Strikes Clauses to the core marine policy.

item.title: IRM 2022_4th Exam Q3
item.description: The legal framework of insurance contracts relies on several core principles that establish trust, equity, and functionality between the insurer and the insured. Principle of Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei): This principle dictates that both parties to an insurance contract must display absolute honesty and disclose all material facts accurately. A material fact is any information that would influence the decision of a prudent insurer to accept the risk or determine the premium level. Non-disclosure or misrepresentation of these facts makes the contract voidable at the option of the aggrieved party. Real-World Example: If an individual applies for life insurance and deliberately conceals a pre-existing chronic heart condition, they have violated the principle of utmost good faith. If the individual passes away due to heart complications, the insurance company has the legal right to deny the claim and void the policy. Principle of Insurable Interest: The insured must have a legal and financial relationship with the subject matter of insurance, meaning they stand to benefit from its safety or continuous existence and suffer a direct financial loss from its damage, destruction, or loss. Insurable interest must exist at the inception of a life insurance policy, but it must exist at the time of loss for property and liability insurance. Real-World Example: A homeowner possesses an insurable interest in their own residential property because its destruction by fire results in a direct financial loss to them. Conversely, an individual cannot legally purchase a fire insurance policy on their neighbor's house because they lack an insurable interest in it and cannot profit from its destruction. Principle of Indemnity: This principle states that an insurance contract is designed to compensate the insured for the actual financial loss sustained, restoring them to approximately the same financial position they occupied prior to the loss. The insured is prohibited from collecting an amount greater than the actual loss, thereby preventing them from profiting from an insured event. (Note: This principle does not apply strictly to life insurance and personal accident policies, which are valued contracts). Real-World Example: If a commercial warehouse worth Tk. 50,00,000 is partially damaged by fire, causing actual physical damage calculated at Tk. 12,00,000, the insurance company will pay a maximum indemnity of Tk. 12,00,000. Paying the full face value of Tk. 50,00,000 would violate the principle of indemnity by allowing the owner to profit. Principle of Subrogation: Subrogation places the insurer in the legal position of the insured after a loss has been fully indemnified. It permits the insurance company to pursue legal action against any third party responsible for causing the loss to recover the claim amount paid out to the insured. This prevents the insured from collecting twice for the same loss (once from the insurer and once from the negligent party). Real-World Example: If a negligent driver crashes into an insured motorist’s parked vehicle, causing Tk. 2,00,000 in damages, the insured's own automobile insurer pays for the repairs. Under the principle of subrogation, the insurer then acquires the legal right to sue the negligent driver (or their liability insurer) to recover the Tk. 2,00,000. Principle of Contribution: Contribution applies when an insured holds multiple indemnity policies with different insurance companies covering the exact same risk and interest. In the event of a loss, the insured cannot claim full compensation from every insurer. Instead, the total loss is distributed proportionally among the respective insurance companies based on the ratio of coverage each company provides relative to the total sum insured. Real-World Example: A business owner insures a commercial building against fire with Company A for Tk. 10,00,000 and with Company B for Tk. 20,00,000 (Total coverage = Tk. 30,00,000). If a fire causes a loss of Tk. 3,00,000, the insurers contribute proportionally: Company A pays: Company B pays: An insurance policy is highly structured and organized into distinct sections that define the boundaries of coverage, operational requirements, and the financial obligations of both parties.The global insurance landscape is experiencing structural changes driven by technological disruptions, climate volatility, and shifting macroeconomic factors. Insurance companies are adapting through strategic shifts in underwriting, distribution, and product design. Integration of Insurtech and Artificial Intelligence (AI): Insurers are modernizing legacy operations by integrating advanced AI and automation algorithms. Machine learning frameworks are applied to streamline underwriting processes, execute automated risk assessments, and speed up claims processing through image recognition (e.g., assessing vehicle damage via smartphone photos). This minimizes administrative expenses and elevates consumer satisfaction. Big Data and Telematics-Driven Pricing: Instead of relying strictly on historical pool-averages, insurance companies leverage real-time data streaming from Internet of Things (IoT) devices. In auto insurance, telematics tracking infrastructure ("Pay-How-You-Drive" models) assesses real-time velocity, braking intensity, and route selections to price premiums dynamically based on individual behavior. Similarly, smart home sensors and wearable health tech are shifting the insurance paradigm from passive indemnification to proactive loss prevention. Climate Change and Predictive Environmental Modeling: The increasing frequency and severity of catastrophic weather anomalies (such as severe flooding and cyclones in Bangladesh) have challenged traditional historical actuarial models. Insurers are adopting sophisticated geospatial modeling and predictive analytics to price catastrophe risks more accurately. Furthermore, the industry is scaling up Parametric Insurance schemes, which disburse automated, immediate payouts whenever an objectively verified weather threshold (e.g., wind speed or rainfall levels) is breached, omitting the prolonged traditional loss-adjustment cycle. Addressing New Cyber-Risk Paradigms: The widespread shift toward digital infrastructure has accelerated the exposure of corporations to ransomware, systemic network downtime, and massive data breaches. Insurance entities are rapidly developing standalone cyber liability insurance frameworks, coupling these policies with real-time cybersecurity monitoring and risk consulting services to mitigate losses before they manifest.

item.title: IRM 2019 Exam Q4
item.description: Private insurance companies play a transformative role in driving the economic development of Bangladesh by acting as financial stabilizers, mobilizers of domestic savings, and catalysts for capital formation. Their contributions can be analyzed through the following core economic dimensions: Mobilization of Savings and Capital Formation: Private life insurance companies collect micro-premiums from thousands of individual policyholders spread across both urban and rural areas. By pooling these scattered items of small savings, they create substantial investable funds. These long-term capital resources are subsequently channeled into government securities, infrastructure bonds, and capital markets, bridging the national investment gap. Risk Mitigation and Business Continuity: Industries, manufacturing plants, and service sectors are perpetually exposed to uncertainties such as fire, machinery breakdown, and operational liabilities. Private non-life insurance companies underwrite these commercial risks. By promising financial compensation in the event of a disaster, they provide entrepreneurs with the confidence to undertake high-risk, high-return industrial projects, safeguarding business continuity and employment. Facilitating International and Domestic Trade: International trade is a primary driver of the Bangladeshi economy, especially through the Ready-Made Garments (RMG) sector. Private insurance providers issue essential marine hull, cargo, and aviation policies. Without these risk-transfer mechanisms, commercial banks would not open Letters of Credit (LCs), effectively halting import-export transactions. Employment Generation: The private insurance sector is a major source of employment in Bangladesh. It provides direct professional opportunities for thousands of executives, underwriters, actuaries, and loss assessors, alongside generating extensive indirect employment for a vast network of insurance agents operating nationwide. Reduction of Burden on Government Finances: By offering health, accident, and life insurance products, private insurers reduce the socio-economic burden on the state. In the event of industrial mishaps or personal tragedies, private insurance claims absorb the financial shock, minimizing the need for direct government relief and rehabilitation spending. Sadharan Bima Corporation (SBC) is the sole state-owned non-life insurance and reinsurance corporation operating in Bangladesh. Established under the Insurance Corporations Act of 1973, it holds a unique, dual-functional status within the country's financial architecture, serving both as a direct insurer and the national reinsurer.Display Mermaid diagrams in this vault?Only allow if you trust this vault's contents.Allowgraph TD SBC[Sadharan Bima Corporation] --> Underwriting[Direct Underwriting Functions] SBC --> Reinsurance[National Reinsurance Functions] SBC --> Regulatory[Market Stabilization & State Support] Underwriting --> PubAsset[Insuring Public Sector & Government Properties] Underwriting --> Specialized[Specialized Schemes: Crop & Export Credit] Reinsurance --> CompCession[Managing Mandatory 50% Reinsurance Cessions] Reinsurance --> ForeignRet[Minimizing Capital Flight / Retaining Forex] Regulatory --> PriceStability[Setting Benchmark Rates] Regulatory --> DevSupport[Supporting IDRA Initiatives]The principal functions of Sadharan Bima Corporation are detailed below: Underwriting Public Sector Risks: By statutory mandate, SBC is responsible for underwriting 100% of all non-life insurance policies related to public sector properties, government departments, statutory bodies, and state-owned enterprises. It also retains 50% of this public sector business and distributes the remaining 50% equally among private non-life insurance companies. Acting as the National Reinsurer: SBC serves as the central clearinghouse for reinsurance within Bangladesh. By law, all private non-life insurance firms operating in the country must cede a mandatory percentage (currently 50%) of their total reinsurable risks to SBC. SBC handles the management, evaluation, and settlement of these domestic reinsurance pools. Conservation of Foreign Exchange: Prior to the establishment of SBC, domestic risks had to be heavily reinsured with foreign corporations, resulting in a continuous outflow of hard currency. SBC retains a substantial portion of national risk within domestic borders, preventing capital flight and conserving the foreign exchange reserves of Bangladesh. Implementation of Socio-Economic Insurance Schemes: SBC designs and manages specialized, non-commercial insurance products aimed at vulnerable segments of the population. These include the Crop Insurance Scheme to safeguard farmers against natural calamities, and the Export Credit Guarantee Scheme (ECGS), which protects local exporters from default risks associated with foreign buyers. Market Stabilization and Technical Leadership: SBC plays a vital role in stabilizing premium rates and maintaining market discipline. It frequently provides technical expertise, historical loss data, and risk-assessment frameworks to the Insurance Development and Regulatory Authority (IDRA) and private insurers to foster structural stability across the industry. The insurance sector in Bangladesh faces a notable paradox: despite the country's rapid GDP growth, national insurance penetration remains among the lowest in South Asia. Resolving this requires understanding both the deep-seated challenges and the emerging drivers within the industry.Emerging Growth Drivers The structural transformation of the economy of Bangladesh offers several key growth vectors for forward-looking insurers: The Demographic Dividend and Middle-Class Expansion: The continuous expansion of a consumerist middle-class population with growing disposable income represents a massive untapped market for individual life, health, and pension insurance products. Mega Infrastructure Developments: Massive state-backed infrastructure undertakings—including deep-sea ports, economic zones, metro rail networks, and nuclear power plants—generate substantial demand for high-value engineering and non-life insurance policies. Takaful (Islamic Insurance) Expansion: Given the demographic profile of Bangladesh, Shariah-compliant insurance structures (Takaful) possess immense growth potential. Standardizing and expanding these operations can successfully draw millions of faith-conscious citizens into the formal financial fold. Insurtech and Digital Intermediation: The proliferation of mobile financial services (MFS) like bKash and Nagad enables the distribution of micro-insurance products directly to remote rural populations, bypassing costly traditional agent networks and lowering administrative expenses. Climate Risk Management: As a nation highly vulnerable to climate change, the demand for structured crop insurance, flood protection covers, and catastrophe bonds is set to grow exponentially, backed by international development initiatives.

item.title: IRM 2019 Exam Q6
item.description: Premature death can be defined as the death of a family head with unfulfilled financial obligations. This occurs when an individual dies before reaching full retirement age or normal life expectancy, leaving behind dependents who rely on their income, outstanding financial liabilities (such as mortgages, loans, or credit card debts), and future financial goals (such as funding children's higher education) that remain uncompleted. The financial cost of premature death is substantial because the human life value of the deceased is lost forever. In addition to the loss of future earnings, the family incurs immediate expenses such as funeral costs, medical bills, and probate or estate settlement expenses.The financial consequences of premature death vary considerably depending on the structure and socio-economic context of the family. In Bangladesh, these impacts are heavily influenced by cultural norms, the lack of robust state social safety nets, and the prevalence of joint family systems. Single People: General Impact: For single individuals without dependents, the financial impact of premature death is relatively low, primarily involving funeral costs and the settlement of personal debts or credit lines. Bangladeshi Context: In Bangladesh, many single working adults act as secondary or primary financial support providers for aging parents, younger siblings, or extended family members. Therefore, their premature death can still significantly disrupt the financial stability of their parental household. Traditional Families: General Impact: A traditional family typically consists of a single breadwinner (usually the husband) and a non-working spouse who takes care of the home and children. Bangladeshi Context: The premature death of the sole breadwinner in a traditional Bangladeshi family is financially devastating. It causes an immediate cessation of the family income stream, often forcing the surviving spouse into low-paying labor or complete dependency on relatives. The family faces an immediate degradation of their standard of living, inability to pay rent or utilities, and a high risk of pulling children out of school due to a lack of tuition fees. Sandwiched Families: General Impact: A sandwiched family is one in which a working adult supports both dependent children and aging parents. Bangladeshi Context: This is a very common family structure in Bangladesh due to traditional filial obligations. The premature death of the primary earner delivers a severe dual blow: it leaves young children without care and future security, and leaves elderly parents without critical medical care, food, and housing support. The financial distress is compounded by rapidly rising medical healthcare costs for seniors. Single-Parent Families: General Impact: This structure consists of one parent living with dependent children due to divorce, desertion, or the previous death of a spouse. Bangladeshi Context: The financial impact here is catastrophic. The single parent is both the sole economic engine and the primary caregiver. Upon premature death, the children lose all immediate financial support. If substantial life insurance or liquid assets are not available, the children face severe institutional risk, poverty, or complete reliance on the charity of relatives. Two-Income Earners with Children: General Impact: In these families, both parents work outside the home and contribute to the household income. Bangladeshi Context: While the survival of one working parent provides a partial safety net that prevents absolute destitution, the premature death of one earner significantly lowers the family's overall standard of living. Dual incomes are typically required to afford urban housing (such as apartments in Dhaka or Chattogram), private schooling, and car loans. The loss of one income makes meeting these combined obligations exceptionally difficult, requiring rapid lifestyle downscaling or asset liquidation. To determine the amount of additional life insurance Shelly needs to purchase, the Total Financial Needs must be calculated and then offset by her Total Existing Financial Assets. Immediate Cash / Clean-up Fund: Funeral costs and uninsured medical bills: Income Support for Son: (Note: Since the rate of return on policy proceeds is assumed to equal the inflation rate, the real interest rate is , meaning no discounting is required.) Debt Clearance: Pay off mortgage on home: Pay off car loan and credit card debts: Special Future Goals: College education fund for son: Checking account: Individual Retirement Account (IRA): 401(k) plan: Individual life insurance: Group life insurance: Conclusion Based on the needs approach, Shelly should purchase an additional TK. 583,000 of life insurance coverage to fully ensure her financial goals and her son's future needs are met.

item.title: IRM 2020 Exam Q1
item.description: Risk is traditionally defined as the uncertainty concerning the occurrence of a loss. In a broader business context, risk is dual-natured: it encompasses both negative deviations (threats or pure risks) and positive deviations (opportunities or speculative risks). The relationship between risk and uncertainty is that uncertainty is the subjective or objective state of mind characterized by a lack of knowledge or doubt about the future outcome, whereas risk is the actual quantifiable or identifiable exposure to those varying outcomes.Pharmaceutical R&D Venture A pharmaceutical firm invests BDT 500 million into researching a new oncology drug. The Threat: The clinical trials could fail, or regulatory approval could be denied, resulting in a complete write-off of the invested capital with zero financial return. The Opportunity: If successful, the drug cures a major illness, obtains exclusive global patent rights, and captures massive market share—generating billions in revenue and maximizing shareholder wealth. In risk management, it is crucial to clearly separate the cause of a loss from the underlying factors that exacerbate it. Fire: A fire breaks out inside a commercial warehouse, physically consuming the structural building and inventory. Earthquake: A high-magnitude seismic event occurs, directly causing the structural collapse of a factory facility. Physical Hazard (Defective Wiring): An industrial facility operates with frayed, outdated electrical wiring. This physical condition significantly increases the frequency and severity of the peril of fire. Morale/Attitudinal Hazard (Carelessness): An employee leaves a secure bank vault open or leaves security keys unattended on a desk due to a careless attitude, which directly increases the likelihood of the peril of theft. A manager can utilize several fundamental risk-control and risk-financing techniques to spread and diversify corporate loss exposures: Product and Market Diversification: Spreading risk across multiple distinct product lines, service categories, or geographic regions. If one market faces a downturn or localized disaster, profits from other regions stabilize the firm. Subcontracting and Outsourcing (Non-Insurance Transfer): Transferring risky operational steps—such as product distribution, specialized manufacturing, or IT hosting—to third-party specialists through contractual agreements. Financial Hedging: Utilizing derivative contracts (such as forward contracts, futures, or options) to spread and offset macroeconomic price fluctuations in raw materials, foreign exchange rates, or interest rates. Contractual Liability Distribution: Incorporating protective clauses, such as hold-harmless agreements and indemnity provisions, into vendor contracts to legally shift the financial burden of operational liabilities to external parties. Insurance Risk Pooling: Combining uncorrelated risk exposures with commercial insurance underwriters, effectively transferring volatile financial exposures into a stable, predictable premium expense. An explosion that produces major structural and operational damage to a manufacturing facility generates distinct tiers of financial consequence: Direct Losses: The immediate physical destruction of the plant's brick-and-mortar buildings and infrastructure. The total loss of specialized factory machinery, heavy manufacturing equipment, and automated assembly lines. The physical ruin of stored raw materials, work-in-progress components, and completed finished goods inventory. Indirect Losses: Business Interruption Loss: The complete halt of production operations, resulting in a severe loss of sales revenue while the plant is physically rebuilt. Continuing Fixed Expenses: The mandatory obligation to pay ongoing fixed overhead costs despite zero manufacturing output (e.g., executive salaries, debt interest installments, property taxes, and security costs). Extra Expense: Emergency funds spent to lease temporary production facilities, outsource manufacturing to competitors to satisfy existing client orders, or pay expedited shipping fees for replacement equipment. Loss of Market Share: Long-term customers switching to competing manufacturers due to extended delivery delays, causing permanent competitive damage. A toxic chemical leak that damages local ecosystems and prompts extensive legal action exposes a business to severe liability-driven losses: Direct Losses: The out-of-pocket costs required to settle civil lawsuits filed by affected communities, landowners, or agricultural entities. Substantial legal defense fees, including retaining specialized attorneys, environmental scientists, court costs, and expert witness fees. Statutory fines, economic penalties, and mandatory remediation expenses levied by environmental protection authorities to clean up contaminated soil and waterways. Indirect Losses: Reputational Damage: Severe degradation of the company's brand image and public goodwill, leading to consumer boycotts and plummeting sales. Capital Market Contraction: A sharp collapse in the company's publicly traded stock price, along with reduced access to credit as banks refuse to finance an environmentally compromised business. Human Capital Flight: Difficulty in recruiting and retaining top-tier talent or professional managers due to the firm's toxic public image. Surging Risk-Financing Costs: Extreme hikes in future commercial liability insurance premiums, or the total denial of environmental impairment liability coverage by primary insurers.

item.title: IRM 2020 Exam Q2
item.description: The distinction between maximum possible loss and maximum probable loss is critical for risk managers when determining appropriate risk-retention levels and insurance limits: Maximum Possible Loss (MPL): This is the worst-case scenario that could happen to an organization's exposure during its lifetime. It represents the maximum financial damage that could occur if everything goes wrong, all protective barriers and loss-control measures fail simultaneously, and the absolute worst event takes place. Maximum Probable Loss: This is the worst-case scenario that is likely or reasonable to happen. Unlike the maximum possible loss, it factors in the operational reality that some loss-control systems (such as automated fire sprinklers or fire walls) will function as intended, meaning a total, absolute destruction of all assets simultaneously is highly improbable. Avoidance is a proactive risk-control technique that involves eliminating any possibility of a loss. This means a firm or individual either decides never to acquire or accept a particular loss exposure in the first place, or chooses to completely abandon an existing exposure. Characteristics: While avoidance reduces the probability of a specific loss to zero, it has two major drawbacks: it may not be practical or possible for all risks, and avoiding a risk means the entity also forfeits any potential profits or strategic benefits associated with that activity. Loss prevention focuses on reducing the frequency or probability of a particular loss occurring. It involves taking specific measures before an event happens to stop the peril from manifesting. Characteristics: This technique directly targets the hazards that cause losses. Examples include conducting regular safety training for machine operators to prevent workplace injuries, installing security cameras to prevent theft, and performing routine vehicle maintenance to prevent road accidents. Loss reduction focuses on minimizing the severity or financial impact of a loss after it has already occurred. It accepts that a peril may manifest but aims to contain the resulting damage. Characteristics: Measures can be implemented both before a loss (pre-loss reduction measures like installing fire sprinkler systems or smoke detectors that activate during an event) and after a loss (post-loss reduction measures like executing disaster recovery plans, salvaging damaged goods, or establishing first-aid stations). Ignoring the time value of money (TVM) when making risk management decisions can lead to flawed economic evaluations and severe financial misallocations due to the following effects: Inaccurate Cost-Benefit Analysis: Risk control investments (such as buying high-end safety equipment or paying insurance premiums) require certain cash outflows today. Conversely, the financial benefits (avoided losses or insurance payouts) occur in the future. Ignoring TVM treats a dollar spent today the same as a dollar saved five years from now, leading firms to overvalue or undervalue long-term risk mitigation programs. Suboptimal Selection of Techniques: When comparing risk retention (paying for losses as they occur over time) versus risk transfer (paying an upfront premium to an insurer), failing to discount future loss payments will make retention look artificially more expensive than it actually is. Mispriced Risks and Reserves: For long-tail risks where claims take years to settle (e.g., liability lawsuits), ignoring the interest that could be earned on reserved funds over time will result in over-funding reserves and dragging down corporate profitability. The goals of a risk management program are divided based on whether a loss event has occurred: Pre-Loss Objectives: Economy: Preparing for potential losses in the most cost-effective manner. This involves analyzing the costs of safety programs, insurance premiums, and retention methods to find the optimal mix. Reduction of Anxiety: Minimizing the fear, stress, and uncertainty associated with potential catastrophic risks for executive management, shareholders, and employees. Meeting Legal Obligations: Ensuring strict compliance with statutory mandates, such as installing required environmental safety controls, purchasing workers' compensation insurance, or adhering to building accessibility codes. Post-Loss Objectives: Survival of the Firm: Ensuring that after a severe, catastrophic loss occurs, the company does not go completely bankrupt and can resume its existence in some form. Continuity of Operations: Maintaining the ability to supply products or services without vital interruptions. This is crucial for competitive industries where a temporary shutdown means permanently losing customers to rivals. Stability of Earnings: Shielding net income and earnings per share from volatile drops, thereby maintaining investor confidence and stock value. Continued Growth: Ensuring that a major loss does not permanently derail the long-term strategic expansion plans of the enterprise. Social Responsibility: Minimizing the adverse impact that a corporate disaster can have on external stakeholders, such as avoiding mass employee layoffs, preventing community environmental contamination, and keeping critical supplier chains intact.

item.title: IRM 2020 Exam Q3
item.description: Understanding the frequency (how often a loss occurs) and severity (the financial size or magnitude of the loss) of a potential loss is the foundation of the risk management process. By quantifying these two variables, a risk manager can systematically evaluate a risk exposure and select the most efficient and cost-effective risk management technique. This relationship is typically structured using a Risk Management Matrix, which classifies exposures into four distinct quadrants, each requiring a different operational strategy:By evaluating these dimensions, organizations can prevent over-insuring minor risks (which wastes premium capital) or under-insuring catastrophic risks (which could lead to insolvency).From a purely economic perspective, the financial needs arising from a total and permanent disability are substantially greater than those caused by premature death. This phenomenon is often described as the "living death" due to its compounding financial impact: The Double Financial Blow: In the event of premature death, the individual's future income stream is permanently lost, but their personal living expenses (food, clothing, personal care, transit) cease. In the event of a total disability, the income stream is also completely wiped out, but the individual remains alive. Consequently, their normal, day-to-day living expenses continue to accrue. Incurrence of New Medical Costs: A disabled individual often requires continuous medical treatment, long-term care, prescription medication, physical therapy, and specialized medical equipment. Home and Vehicle Modifications: Severe disabilities may necessitate expensive structural alterations to the individual's home (such as installing wheelchair ramps or stairlifts) and vehicles to make them accessible. Depletion of Family Care Resources: Family members may have to reduce their own working hours or quit their jobs to act as full-time caregivers, leading to a secondary drop in household income. An individual who experiences a temporary or permanent disability can look to several primary resources to mitigate the loss of income and handle rising medical costs: Social Insurance and Government Welfare: Workers' Compensation: Provides medical benefits and wage replacement if the disability occurred as a direct result of employment. State/National Welfare Programs: Government-sponsored safety nets or grants intended for citizens with severe physical or mental impairments. Employer-Sponsored Benefits: Group Disability Insurance: Many employers offer short-term disability (STD) and long-term disability (LTD) plans that replace a set percentage (e.g., 50% to 70%) of the worker's gross salary. Paid Sick Leave: Provides short-term continuation of regular salary during the initial days of illnesses or injuries. Provident Funds/Gratuity: Partial or early withdrawal allowances from employment retirement accounts on medical grounds. Individual Private Insurance Policies: Individual Disability Income Policy: Privately purchased coverage that guarantees a monthly cash benefit during the period of disability. Life Insurance Riders: Policies featuring a Waiver of Premium Rider (which suspends premium payments while keeping coverage active during total disability) or a Total and Permanent Disability (TPD) Rider (which pays out a lump sum or accelerated death benefit). Personal Savings and Liquidation of Assets: Emergency cash funds, stock portfolios, or fixed deposits can be utilized to cover short-term shortfalls. In severe cases, non-liquid assets (such as real estate or vehicles) may be sold to finance long-term survival. Retirement exposes an individual to a unique matrix of long-term financial and systemic risks that can threaten their economic security during old age: Longevity Risk: The risk that a retiree outlives their accumulated financial assets and savings. As life expectancies rise, individuals run a higher risk of depleting their retirement nest egg while still requiring regular income. Inflation Risk: The gradual loss of purchasing power over time. Because retirees often rely on fixed pension payouts or fixed annuities, steady inflation over a 20-to-30-year retirement window can severely degrade their real standard of living. Health and Medical Expense Risk: The high probability of developing chronic medical conditions during old age. Escalating healthcare costs, nursing home fees, and the cost of specialized geriatric care present an unpredictable and massive drain on retirement funds. Investment and Market Risk (Sequence of Returns Risk): The risk that fluctuations in the financial markets will depress the value of the retiree's investment portfolio. Experiencing a severe stock market downturn in the early years of retirement, combined with ongoing asset withdrawals, can prematurely deplete a retirement fund beyond recovery.

item.title: IRM 2020 Exam Q4
item.description: An insurable risk is a specific type of risk that meets the ideal operational criteria required for an insurance company to efficiently pool, calculate, and cover potential financial losses. In the insurance market, pure risks (situations involving only the chance of loss or no loss) are generally considered insurable, whereas speculative risks (which involve the chance of gain) are not. Large Number of Exposure Units: There must be a massive pool of similar exposure units (e.g., houses, automobiles, lives) to enable the Law of Large Numbers to operate effectively. This allows the insurer to predict aggregate future losses accurately. Accidental and Unintentional Loss: The loss must be fortuitous, unforeseen, and outside the control of the insured. This minimizes moral hazards and preserves the random nature of the risk pool. Determinable and Measurable Loss: The loss must have a distinct time, place, cause, and amount. The insurer must be able to verify whether a loss occurred and quantify its exact financial impact. No Catastrophic Loss: A large proportion of the exposure units must not experience a simultaneous loss. If a single event (like a nuclear war or a widespread regional catastrophe) damages all units at once, the pooling mechanism fails, threatening the insurer with insolvency. Calculable Chance of Loss: The insurer must be able to estimate both the frequency and severity of losses to establish an accurate and equitable premium rate structure. Economically Feasible Premium: The cost of the premium must be substantially lower than the face value of the policy. If the chance of loss is too high, the premium will become too expensive, making it unattractive to potential buyers. Example of an Insurable Risk Standard fire insurance on a residential brick house represents a classic insurable risk. There are millions of similar houses (large exposure units), residential fires are usually accidental and unintentional, the structural damage is easily determinable and measurable by a loss adjuster, a fire in one house rarely spreads to damage the entire national housing stock (non-catastrophic), historical fire data allows accurate premium calculation, and the premium is highly affordable relative to the total value of the house. Insurable interest is a fundamental legal principle in insurance stating that the insured must stand in a legally recognized relationship to the subject matter of insurance, whereby they benefit from its safety or well-being and suffer a direct financial loss or face legal liability upon its damage, destruction, or loss.An insurer must rigorously verify and determine the presence of an insurable interest for three primary reasons: To Prevent Gambling and Wagering: If insurable interest were not required, individuals could buy insurance policies on completely unrelated properties or lives (e.g., buying a policy on a stranger's house or life) simply to speculate on a loss event. This would turn insurance into a socially destructive gambling mechanism. To Reduce Moral Hazard: If an individual has no financial stake or emotional bond with the insured item, they have no incentive to protect it. In fact, they might be highly motivated to intentionally cause the loss (e.g., committing arson or murder) to collect the policy proceeds. Requiring an insurable interest ensures the policyholder only seeks protection against genuine financial hardship. To Measure the True Extent of the Loss: In indemnity insurance (such as property and liability policies), the maximum amount payable by an insurer is strictly limited to the value of the insured’s financial interest at the time of the loss. It prevents the insured from collecting more than what they actually lost. Insurance is broadly classified into distinct categories depending on the subject matter and the specific nature of the exposures handled.

item.title: IRM 2020 Exam Q5
item.description: The Principle of Utmost Good Faith (Uberrimae Fidei) is a fundamental legal doctrine governing insurance contracts. It states that a significantly higher degree of honesty and disclosure is imposed on both parties to an insurance contract than is required in standard commercial contracts. Because the insurer relies heavily on the information provided by the applicant to assess risk and determine premiums, the applicant is legally obligated to disclose all material facts accurately and completely. This principle is supported and enforced through three primary legal doctrines: Representations: These are statements made by the applicant for insurance during the negotiation process (e.g., statements regarding age, health history, or occupation). An insurer can void the contract if a representation is material, false, and relied upon by the insurer. A statement is material if knowledge of the true fact would have caused the insurer to refuse the risk or charge a higher premium. Concealment: This is the intentional failure of the applicant to disclose a known material fact to the insurer. If an applicant purposefully hides information that they know is highly relevant to the risk assessment (such as a pre-existing terminal illness), the insurer has the legal right to void the policy because the contract was not entered into with utmost good faith. Warranties: A warranty is a statement of fact or a promise made by the insured that becomes an explicit part of the insurance contract and must be strictly true. Any breach of a warranty—even on a minor or non-material point—traditionally allows the insurer to deny a claim and cancel the policy. The financial needs created by a total and permanent disability are generally considered greater than those resulting from premature death due to a phenomenon known as "economic death." Disability inflicts a severe dual financial blow on an individual and their family: Loss of Earning Capacity: Similar to premature death, a severe disability completely cuts off or severely limits the individual’s ability to work and generate an active income stream for the household. Incurrence of Additional Expenses: Unlike premature death, the disabled individual remains alive, meaning their personal consumption costs continue. Furthermore, disability introduces massive new financial obligations, including continuous medical treatments, specialized rehabilitation, structural home modifications, and potentially long-term assistive care. Cost Summary In premature death, the income terminates, but the deceased individual's personal living expenses also cease. In disability, the income terminates, but personal living expenses persist and are compounded by escalating medical and care costs. The necessity and optimal amount of life insurance vary dramatically depending on an individual’s dependency structure and family obligations: Single Individuals: Generally, single individuals without dependents have a very low or non-existent need for life insurance. They do not have anyone relying on their active income stream. Their primary insurance need is typically restricted to a small policy to cover final expenses, such as funeral costs and outstanding personal debts. Childless Couples: This group faces a moderate need for life insurance. If both partners work and maintain a lifestyle built on a dual-income foundation, the premature death of one partner can significantly degrade the survivor’s standard of living. Insurance is needed to clear joint debts, settle shared mortgages, and provide transitional financial support. Persons with Children: This segment possesses the absolute highest need for substantial life insurance. The premature death of a parent can cause immediate economic devastation. Life insurance is critical to replace the lost income needed to cover the ongoing costs of raising children, funding future higher education, liquidating residential mortgages, and ensuring long-term family stability. The statement "The effect of the income loss due to premature death depends on the circumstances" signifies that the economic severity of death is not uniform across society; instead, it is directly contingent upon the specific financial role the deceased played within their unique family unit. The variation in impact can be observed across different real-world scenarios:Term life and endowment insurance represent completely different approaches to life insurance design, altering how benefits are paid and how equity accumulates.

item.title: Syllabus 4th Semester
item.description: Marks: 100 Credit: 3 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Insurance and Risk Management is a core course of business administration discipline of University of Chittagong. It is designed to provide an introduction to the basic principles of risk and insurance prevalent in financial decision making. To acquaint students with the basic knowledge of the principles of risk and insurance and the methods of risk management found in strategic planning. To provide students with a basic knowledge of general, life and health insurance. To help students develop a sound personal insurance program for meeting the major risks in our society. To give students some basic principles of insurance buying, with an emphasis on how to develop a strong insurance and financial estate planning program. To offer a systematic framework for analysing any insurance contract. To learn about the ethical issues facing business and an appreciation of the framework for making ethical decisions. Introduction to Risk Management: Concept, Types of Risk, Risk Faced by Businesses and Individuals; Risk Management, The Risk Management Process and Methods, and Business Risk Management Organisation, Factors affecting risk. Objective of Risk Management: The Need for a Risk Management Objective, Understanding the Costs of Risk, Firm Value Maximisation and the Cost of Risk, Individual Risk Management and the Cost of Risk, and Risk Management & Societal Welfare. Risk Identification and Measurement: Risk Identification; Basic Concepts from Probability and Statistics; and Evaluating the Frequency & Severity of Losses. Risk Management by Individuals and Corporations: Risk Aversion and Demand for Insurance by Individuals - the Effects of Insurance on Wealth, Risk Aversion, Other Factors Affecting an Individual's Demand for Insurance; and Business Risk Management - Shareholder Diversification - Closely Held Business - Why purchase insurance when shareholders are diversified. Introduction to Insurance: Definition and Basic Characteristics of Insurance, Requirement of an Insurable Risk, Adverse Selection and Insurance, Insurance and Gambling Compared, Insurance and Hedging Compared, Types of Insurance, Benefits and Costs of Insurance to Society. Life Insurance: Life Insurance Product Overview, Traditional Products: Term, Endowment, and Whole Life Insurance, Product Innovation: Universal and Variable Life Insurance, Tax benefits from Life Insurance Policies, Annuity Contracts, Life Insurance Pricing, How much Life Insurance should be covered, and Life Insurance Cost Comparisons. Fire Insurance: Meaning - Principles, Elements of Contract - Classification of Fire Insurance Policies - Policy Conditions - Determination of Premium - Fire Claims. Marine Insurance: Meaning - Subject Matter - Importance - Marine Insurance Contract - Types of Marine Policies - Policy conditions - Marine Losses - Claims and their Settlement. Other Insurance: Health, Automobile, Social Insurance, and other Miscellaneous Insurance Policies. Insurance Practices in Bangladesh: Insurance Acts and Regulations of Bangladesh, Organization and Functions of Jiban Bima Corporation and Sadharan Bima Corporation, Role of Private Insurance Companies, and Problems & Prospects of Insurance Business in Bangladesh. Harrington Niehaus – Risk Management & Insurance (2nd Edition) George E. Rejda – Principles of Risk Management and Insurance (10th Edition) M. N. Mishra – Insurance Principles and Practices (22nd Edition) Azizul Huq Chaudhuri – Risk and Insurance (2nd Edition) Shahiduddin Ahmed – Insurance Business in Bangladesh: A Study of the Pattern, Problems & Prospects Publications of Insurance Development and Regulatory Authority (IDRA) Publications of Government of Bangladesh regarding laws relevant to insurance, rules & regulations issued from time to time. Publications of Jiban Bima Corporation & Sadharan Bima Corporation. Marks: 100 Credit: 3 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)The course aims at understanding business ethics, its application, and management. To achieve the objectives, the course will highlight the theories of business ethics. The course will also elaborately explain the roles and responsibilities as well as rights and privileges of different stakeholders in the context of business ethics. Introduction to Business Ethics: Definition, Importance, Globalization – a key context of business ethics? Sustainability – a key goal for business ethics? Theories of Business Ethics: Normative ethical theories – Individual vs. Institutional morality, Questioning vs. accepting capitalism, Justifying vs. applying moral norms, Traditional ethical theories – Consequentialist Theories: Egoism, Utilitarianism, Non-consequentialist Theories: Ethics of duties, Ethics of rights and justice, Limits of Traditional Theories, Contemporary ethical theories – Virtue ethics, Feminist ethics, Discourse ethics, Postmodern ethics. Making Decisions in Business Ethics: Ethical decision, Models of ethical decision-making, Individual influence on ethical decision-making, Situational influence on decision-making. Managing Business Ethics: Business ethics management, Setting standards of ethical behavior: designing and implementing codes of ethics, Managing stakeholder relations, Assessing ethical performance, Organizing for business ethics management. Shareholders and Business Ethics: Introduction: reassessing the importance of shareholders as stakeholders, Shareholders as stakeholders: understanding corporate governance, Ethical issues in corporate governance: Executive accountability and control, Executive remuneration, Ethical aspects of mergers and acquisitions, The role of financial markets and insider trading, The role of accountants, Reforming governance. Employees and Business Ethics: Employees as stakeholders, Ethical issues in the firm-employee relation, Employing people worldwide: the ethical challenges of globalization. Consumers and Business Ethics: Consumers as stakeholders, Ethical issues, marketing, and the consumer, Globalization and consumers: the ethical challenges of the global marketplace, Consumers and corporate citizenship: consumer sovereignty and the politics of purchasing, Consumer sovereignty, Ethical consumption. Suppliers, Competitors and Business Ethics: Suppliers and competitors as stakeholders, Ethical Issues and suppliers, Ethical issues and competitors, Globalization, suppliers, and competitors: the ethical challenges of global business networks, The corporate citizen in the business community: ethical sourcing and fair trade. Civil Society and Business Ethics: Introduction: what is civil society? Civil society organizations as stakeholders, Ethical issues and CSOs, Globalization and civil society organizations, Corporate citizenship and civil society: charity, collaboration, or regulation? Civil society, business, and sustainability. Government, Regulations and Business Ethics: Government as a stakeholder, Ethical issues in the relation between business and government, Globalization and business-government relations, Corporate citizenship and regulation: business as a key player in the regulatory game. Marks: 100 Credit: 3 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)Entrepreneurship skills accelerate economic growth by transforming a population burden into a demographic dividend. The main motto of offering this course is to inspire students to explore their potential to become entrepreneurs and to equip them with guiding principles to become effective entrepreneurs. In order to attain learning outcomes, the course has been designed considering the basic principles of entrepreneurship, the state of global environmental forces, and the dynamics of the Bangladeshi entrepreneurial environment. It covers knowledge and skills about identifying new business ideas, assessing the feasibility of those ideas, preparing a business plan, starting new ventures, conducting managerial operations, maintaining growth, and facing emerging business challenges effectively and efficiently. Introduction to Entrepreneurship: What is entrepreneurship? Why become an entrepreneur? Characteristics of successful entrepreneurs; Importance of entrepreneurship; The entrepreneurial process; Approaches to entrepreneurship development; What is corporate entrepreneurship? The nature of corporate entrepreneurship; The need for corporate entrepreneuring; Corporate venturing obstacles; Conceptualizing corporate entrepreneurship strategy. (Case Study: 1.1 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer, 4th Edition) Recognizing Opportunities and Generating Ideas: Identifying and recognizing opportunities; Finding gaps in the marketplace; Techniques for generating ideas; Encouraging and protecting new ideas. (Case Study: 2.2 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Feasibility Analysis: Product/service feasibility analysis; Industry/target market feasibility analysis; Organizational feasibility analysis; Financial feasibility analysis. (Case Study: 3.2 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Writing a Business Plan: Reasons for writing a business plan; Who reads the business plan? Guidelines for writing a business plan; Outline of the business plan; Presenting the business plan to investors. (Case Study: 4.1 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Developing an Effective Business Model: The importance and diversity of business models; How business models emerge; Potential fatal flaws of business models; Components of an effective business model. (Case Study: 5.1 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Entrepreneurship Development through Small Business: Modern small business enterprises; Setting up a small business enterprise; Strategic management in small business; Family business. (Case Study: 6.1 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Ethical, Legal and Financing Issues: Initial ethical and legal issues facing a new firm; Obtaining business licenses and permits; The importance of intellectual property; Patents; Trademarks; Copyrights; Trade secrets; Financial objectives of a firm; The process of financial management. (Case Study: 7.2 & 12.2 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Building a New Venture Team and Getting Funding: Creating a new venture team; The role of professional advisers; The importance of getting funding for a new venture; Sources of funding. (Case Study: 9.1 & 10.1 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Managing and Growing an Entrepreneurial Firm: Preparing for growth; Reasons for growth; Managing growth; Challenges of growth; Internal growth strategies; External growth strategies. (Case Study: 14.1 - Basic Text: Bruce R. Barringer) Contemporary Issues in Entrepreneurship: Women entrepreneurship; Social entrepreneurship; Challenges of entrepreneurship development in Bangladesh; Role of government and non-government institutions in entrepreneurship development in Bangladesh; Role of Information and Communication Technology (ICT) in entrepreneurship development. Assignments: Two (on any of the contents) Bruce R. Barringer and R. Duane Ireland – Entrepreneurship: Successfully Launching New Ventures (4th Edition) Donald F. Kuratko – Introduction to Entrepreneurship (8th Edition) Poornima M. Charantimath – Entrepreneurship Development and Small Business Enterprises (1st Edition) Tahlil Azim – Entrepreneurship Development Marks: 100 Credit: 3 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)This course focuses on the foundation of individual and group behavior at work. Special emphasis is given on the psychological roots, causes, and consequences of human behavior in organizations. Major topics include dynamics of individual and group behavior, motivation, leadership, power and politics, conflict management, and organizational change and stress management.Upon successful completion of the course, students will be able to: Apply organizational behavior concepts to individual work experiences. Recognize how different personalities and other issues with different experiences may perceive and react to situations in different ways. Examine own behavior and beliefs about managerial behavior and to contrast and integrate these ideas with the theories and observations of others. Work more effectively in a group and team environment. Learn how organizational power and politics have been exercised. Understand how organizational conflicts and negotiation have to be managed. Learn how organizational change and stress have to be managed. Introduction: Meaning and Concepts of Organizational Behavior (OB); Contemporary Issues in OB; Disciplines that Contribute to the OB Field; Challenges and Opportunities for OB; OB Model; Global Implications. Diversity in Organizations: Diversity; Discrimination; Biographical Characteristics; Ability; Implementing Diversity Management Strategies; Global Implications. Attitudes and Job Satisfaction: Attitudes; Main components of Attitudes; Major Job Attitudes; Job Satisfaction; Measuring Job Satisfaction; Global Implications. Emotions and Moods: What are Emotions and Moods; Emotional Labor; Affective Events Theory; Emotional Intelligence; OB Applications of Emotions and Moods; Global Implications. Personality and Values: What is Personality; The Myers-Briggs Type Indicator; The Big Five Personality Model; Values; The Importance of Values; Linking an Individual's Personality and Values to the workplace; Global implications. Perception and Individual Decision Making: What is Perception? Person Perception: Making Judgments About Others; The link Between Perception and Individual Decision Making; Decision Making in Organizations; Influences on Decision Making: Individual Differences and Organizational Constraints; Global Implications. Motivation: From Concepts to Application: Motivating by Job Design; Employee Involvement; Other Concurrent Methods to Motivate Employees. Foundations of Group Behavior and Understanding Work Teams: Defining and Classifying Groups, Stages of Group Development, Group Properties, Group Decision Making; Differences Between Groups and Teams; Types of Teams; Creating Effective Teams; Turning Individuals into Team Players, Global implications; Relevant Case Analysis. Leadership: Why Leadership; Charismatic Leadership and Transformational Leadership; Authentic Leadership; Mentoring; Challenges to the Leadership Construct; Creating Effective Leaders; Relevant Case Analysis. Power and Politics: Definition of Power; Contrasting Leadership and Power; Bases of Power; Dependency the key to Power; Power Tactics; Politics, Causes and Consequences of Political Behavior; Global Implications; Relevant Case Analysis. Conflict and Negotiations: Definition of Conflict; Transitions in Conflict Thought; Conflict Process; Negotiation; Negotiation Process; Global Implications; Relevant Case Analysis. Organizational Change and Stress Management: Change; Resistance to Change; Approaches to Managing Organizational Change; Creating a Culture for Change; What is Stress; Source of Stress; Consequences of Stress; Managing Stress; Relevant Case Analysis. S.P. Robbins & Others – Organizational Behavior (Latest Indian Edition) Keith Davis and John Newstrom – Human Behavior at Work: Organizational Behavior Fred Luthans – Organizational Behavior J.M. Ivancevich, R. Konopaske, and M.T. Matteson – Organizational Behavior and Management (McGraw Hill, Current Edition) A.A. Arif and M.A. Taher – Organizational Behavior Joseph Reitz – Behavior in Organizations Marks: 100 Credit: 3 hours (Written: 75, Internal Evaluation: 20, Viva: 05)The general objective of this course is to understand and evaluate Bangladesh as an emerging country along with its economic growth and development. There are a number of specific objectives of starting this course in the BBA program, such as: To have a clear idea about the history of Bangladesh as an emerging country. To investigate the diverse constituents of the business environment of Bangladesh. To critically evaluate fundamental economic development theories and models. To understand the development strategies and policies for enhancing economic progress. History of Bangladesh: People of Bangladesh, origin and Anthropological identity; Territories of Bangladesh in Ancient Time; Muslim Rule and British Colonial Rule in Indian Sub-Continent; The Pakistan Movement and the Birth of Pakistan; Language Movement, 1948-52; Juktafront Elections, 1954 and Six Point Program, 1966; Mass Upsurge of 1969 and Elections, 1970; and Birth of Bangladesh. Physical and Natural Resources of Bangladesh: Physical Features of Bangladesh: Location, Climate and major Physiographic Units; Surface Water Inflow and River Systems of Bangladesh; Pattern of Agriculture and types of Forest in Bangladesh; Mineral Resources, Energy, Transportation and Communication, Industrial Setup in Bangladesh; Distribution of Population in Bangladesh. Political, Administrative and Legal Structure of Bangladesh: Forms of Government and State Mechanism (Executive, Legislatures, Judiciary) of Bangladesh; Constitutions of Bangladesh and its Amendments; Administrative Structure of Bangladesh; Political Parties of Bangladesh; Different Political Regimes of Bangladesh. Socio-culture of Bangladesh: Social Structure and Social Stratification in Bangladesh; Population Migration from Rural to Urban areas in Bangladesh; Ethnic Minorities in Bangladesh; Social and Cultural Problems of Bangladesh. Concepts and Approaches of Economics of Development: Meaning of Economic Development; Economic Development vs Economic Growth; Measurement of Economic Development; Alternative Measures of Economic Development, PQLI and HDI; Determinants of Development; Challenges to economic Development; Factors of Economic Growth. Development Theories and Growth Models: An overview of the General Theories of Development; Theories of Economic Development: the Classical Theory, the Schumpeterian Theory, Rostow's Stages of Economic Growth, the Marxian Theory, Big-push theory, Lewis' Theory; Growth Models: The Solow Model, The Harrod-Domar Model, The golden rule of accumulation. Fundamental Issues and Strategies of Economic Development of Bangladesh: Fundamental Issues: Poverty, Balance of Payment, NGO Activities, Micro Credit Programs, Income Inequality, Unemployment, Inflation, Blue economy, Financial Administration; Strategies: Five year plans, SDG, Technology Transfer, and Women Empowerment. Local and International Measures for Economic Development: Local Measures: Capital formation, Role of agriculture and industry, Fiscal policy and monetary policy, Deficit financing as an investment, population growth, Entrepreneurship Development; International Measures: Role of foreign trade, Debt problem of LDCs, NIEO, Foreign capital and aid, Foreign Direct Investment (FDI), Role of MNCs. Comparative Analysis of Developed countries and Lessons for Bangladesh: Comparative analysis of USA, CANADA, UK, GERMANY, JAPAN, FRANCE and CHINA; lessons for the developing and less developing countries and Bangladesh. Prof. Sirajul Islam (Ed.) – Banglapedia: National Encyclopedia of Bangladesh (Latest Edition, 2006) Sirajul Islam – History of Bangladesh: Social and Cultural History, Political History, Economical History A.F. Salauddin Ahmed (Ed.) – Bangladesh National Cultural and Heritage: An Introductory Reader M. L. Jhingan – The Economics of Development and Planning (Revised edition) Debraj Ray – Development Economics (Princeton University Press, 1998) Michael P. Todaro – Economic Development in the Third World (7th Edition, Longman) G.M. Meier – Leading Issues in Economic Development (7th Edition) M. Gillis et al. – Economics of Development (2nd Edition, W.W. Norton, 1985) S. Ghatak – An Introduction to Development Economics (2nd Edition, Allen and Unwin, 1986) R. L. Meier – Development Planning (McGraw Hill, 1995) M. P. Todaro – Development planning: Models and Methods (Oxford University Press, 1971) Akhtar Hossain – The Economics of Development and Planning (30th Edition, Konark, New Delhi) CPD (Centre for Policy Dialogue) – Various Publications
